News.title: Early release scheme prisoner jailed days after leaving
News.content:
A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme.

Michael Bogle, 38, was released from HMP Wandsworth on 1 October as part of the first wave of prisoners to be let out under the plan.

Speaking to reporters outside the prison following his release, Bogle said the conditions inside were "awful" and said "people like me" should not be in prison "for a long time".

In the four days after his release, Bogle stole more than Â£100 worth of detergent from supermarkets in north London.

He was arrested on Tuesday and admitted the offences in court on Wednesday, resulting in an eight-month sentence.

The previous 32-week sentence he was released from early had been suspended but he was jailed for breaching its terms. He served 78 days.

Asked if he had a message for Prime Minister Andy Burnham after his early release, Bogle said: "Keep the early release going. It's good."

The scheme was brought in to relieve pressure on prisons across England and Wales which were dangerously close to reaching full capacity.

It is understood the force's highest ranking commander in north-west London referred to his case in a letter raising concerns about the early releases.

Det Ch Supt Luke Williams outlined the details of the "astonishing" case in correspondence to local politicians, which was later shared by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp.

Without naming Bogle, the letter, sent on Wednesday, said he had been identified as a high-risk offender by the probation service but was released on 1 October.

"Just one day after his release" he was recorded on CCTV stealing, Williams said.

News.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
News.content:
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.

But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime â attacking civilian infrastructure â allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".

Both he and his country have denied any involvement.

Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

News.title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fourth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.

While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.

Friday's episode saw the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.

And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).

When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.

"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."

Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."

Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."

On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.

"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.

"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.

"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."

I guess now we'll never know.

News.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
News.content:
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.

"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.

"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.

Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.

"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

News.title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
News.content:
When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.

But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history.

"Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."

The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.

Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.

She says the whole process took its toll.

"I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.

News.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago, why are they resuming now?
News.content:
They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.

By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.

That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.

The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.

That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

News.title: Ashe was too scared to cancel her wedding - the story became a hit song
News.content:
No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

Its name? Stop the Wedding.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before â but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

News.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
News.content:
Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

News.title: NI secretary intervenes to ban Drumcree parade
News.content:
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has banned the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.

The dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.

Sir Chris said the PSNI chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".

His decision has been welcomed by Sinn FÃ©in and the SDLP, but the DUP leader said he now needs to "explain what his government intends to do to restore confidence in the rule of law".

The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

The Portadown District Lodge has submitted a notification to complete the full march for the past 28 years, with exceptions such as during the Covid pandemic - but every year has been denied permission by the Parades Commission.

For decades, the situation at Drumcree has settled into a relatively minor stand-off that no longer made headlines, however that changed when the Parades Commission ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place.

That parade did not happen and, after a series of talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state has banned the procession.

Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following input from the police.

Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn FÃ©in and the SDLP to stop the parade.

Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.

On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect.

"Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably.

"As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined."

Boutcher said his "current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted".

"Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention.

"Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long-term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process."

In a statement, the Parades Commission said it "recognises the importance of resolving the issues arising from this dispute and hopes that a way forward can be found through constructive engagement between those concerned".

News.title: Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
News.content:
Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.

The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.

Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.

Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and he "of course" had not questioned that.

The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.

Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali - who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.

Following the by-election, Lichtenstein was asked whether it would be right for Polanski to continue as leader of the party. She told Times Radio: "No, I think he should resign."

Earlier in the week, Lichtenstein, who has been a member of the Green Party for nearly three decades, told Radio 4's Today programme it was "quite possible" she would leave the party after the Zionism row.

Speaking to the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire on Friday, she said she would not resign immediately because she is having conversations about how to "detoxify" the party.

When asked if she had confidence in Polanski's leadership, Lichtenstein said: "At the moment, no I don't." She added that she was "very disappointed" in him.

Calling on Polanski to apologise, she said: "I don't think that any Jew in the party is going to be in any danger...

"There just might be some unpleasant people who will direct some unpleasant comments, and some of us are going to have to deal with them robustly."

Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.

The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski on Friday, and said he was now working to reverse the motion.

"A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he told the BBC's Politics East, when asked if Polanski should still lead the party.

"[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for."

News.title: Four murder arrests after teenagers attacked
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died and another suffered life-threatening injuries in Stoke-on-Trent.

A cordon remains in place on Brookhouse Road, in Meir, after police were called to reports of violence at 23:45 BST on Friday.

A man in his late teens was confirmed dead at the scene, Staffordshire Police said, and another man, also in his late teens, was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical but stable condition.

Two 18-year-old men, a 20-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, all from Stoke-on-Trent, were arrested on suspicion of murder, while the boy was also arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. All remain in police custody.

"This is a devastating time for all those affected by what has happened overnight," said Det Insp Katie Gregory.

She added: "I'd like to reassure the community that there is no wider risk to them, and we are doing all we can to understand the circumstances that led to this tragic incident."

The force has urged anyone with information about the attack to contact police.

News.title: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow
News.content:
Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s.

"As teenagers you read a lot of romances. It was the moment of Lady Chatterley, under our pillows, reading that by torchlight. You know the minute something is forbidden, you want to get hold of it," she said about the novel that had been at the centre of an obscenity trial.

The Queen spoke about memorable moments in her own reading for BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, and about the life-changing power of literacy and books.

She gave a glimpse of how regular reading is part of her royal marriage: "It's like the best tonic in the world. My husband and I actually read before dinner, just sitting quietly and reading.

"He loves biographies, and PG Wodehouse. I occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something," said the Queen about the King's affection for the author of the Jeeves and Wooster comic novels.

"It's very off-putting, I can't get back into my book, or I'll suddenly start weeping. But it's a lovely, quiet time. I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever," she said.

The Queen also revealed more of her own youthful reading, saying she was "mesmerised" by Charles Dickens's Tale of Two Cities and its depiction of those watching the guillotine during the French Revolution.

"Those ghastly women sitting there knitting while everybody had their heads chopped off," she said.

The Queen, who is 79 years old, said she was part of a generation of women who missed out on higher education, which made reading and books even more important.

"I left school quite young. In my day, women didn't go to university, so I think reading has been most of my education," she said.

News.title: 'Thuggish' behaviour could see balaclava ban in more cities
News.content:
Matthew Evans, one of two Newport councillors who proposed the ban, said people were wearing "intimidating" face coverings to "rob, burgle and deal drugs in our city centre" and "avoid detection".

He proposed "exemptions for religious reasons" and said this was not an "attack on the human rights of young people".

This follows a recent joint police and council crackdown, Operation Krypton, external, which led to hundreds of arrests.

Supt Esyr Jones from Gwent Police said 321 arrests had been made since July to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour across Newport.

Newport council said the current Public Spaces Protection Order (PSPO) was due for review, "and any potential amendments can be considered as part of that process".

It said the PSPO could potentially include face coverings, "and this too is being explored in relation to its practical implication and legalities".

But added there would be "exemptions for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, medical, occupational, weather or personal safety reasons".

In Nottingham, a senior police officer said offenders who wore them to hide their identity caused "substantial" problems.

Now, police there are allowed to ask people to remove their face covering if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or antisocial behaviour.

Anyone who refuses could face a Â£70 fixed penalty notice or a maximum fine of Â£1,000.

Marcellus Baz, who helps run a youth project called Switch Up in Nottingham, said young people were being influenced by social media and the drill music scene to wear balaclavas, which had increased with the rise in use of masks since the pandemic.

He said the use of balaclavas had also coincided with a rise in antisocial behaviour and knife crime so enforcing the removal of such masks was the "right step moving forward".

However, he was concerned mask-wearing could be displaced to other areas without a consistent and nationwide strategy which, he said, needed to be implemented "correctly so we don't have more distance between young people and institutions".

Baz said with cuts to things like youth services in the past, it "feels like the chickens are coming home to roost now".

"We've got to be proactive as a society and look at the root causes rather than just putting a plaster on this."

News.title: Weekend showers and sunshine for UK ahead of warmer air next week
News.content:
It will be a weekend of two halves weather-wise for most people with many seeing a cool start on Saturday.

A strengthening north-westerly wind will carry showers across the UK. But Sunday looks calmer with sunshine in the north and east and rain creeping into the south and west.

Looking further ahead, next week will see a return to above average temperatures.

Tuesday looks set to be the warmest day of the period and could reach 21C for some. However a deep area of low pressure is likely to bring some stormy weather across the north.

News.title: Leah Croucher: 'Not knowing was torture, knowing is as bad'
News.content:
When Leah Croucher's body was found three years after she went missing her family thought their torture would end. Instead it continued with conspiracy theories, fear and heartbreak haunting their lives.

The 19-year-old was walking to work on 15 February 2019 when she disappeared. Her parents say they went through more than three years of "absolute torture" before her dismembered body was discovered in a house in Milton Keynes, less than half a mile (0.8km) from her home in 2022.

She had been killed by a repeat sex offender Neil Maxwell, a man who her parents have branded "an animal". He was on the run from police at the time.

Despite overwhelming evidence of Maxwell's guilt, her parents Claire and John say they have been subjected to "devastating" speculation online, with some pointing the finger at her brother.

Leah's parents are now calling for 'Leah's Law', a mandatory minimum sentence for anyone convicted of a third sexual offence.

Haydon Croucher took his own life nine months after his sister went missing. Leah's parents say he struggled to cope with not knowing what had happened to her.

The Crouchers believe Leah's Law would have saved Leah and by extension Haydon.

News.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
News.content:
"My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything."

From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two.

Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort.

But research into the life story of Venke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers.

About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945.

After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow.

The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile.

News.title: ‘Much-loved mum’ whose body was found in burning van was pregnant, say police
News.content:

A “much-loved” mum whose body was found in a burning van in North Wales was pregnant, police have said.

Samantha Natalie Phythian’s body was found after emergency services were called to reports of a van on fire on Gas Works Lane in Prestatyn at around 11:30pm on Sunday 4 October. Thomas Bell, 38, appeared at Mold Crown Court on Wednesday charged with her murder, and has been remanded into custody.

A postmortem examination has now revealed the 35-year-old was pregnant at the time of her death, North Wales police said in a statement.

open image in gallery Police released a picture of Samantha Natalie Phythian ( North Wales Police )

“We can confirm that the person who sadly died in a van fire on Gas Works Lane, Prestatyn on the evening of Sunday 4th October was 35 year old Samantha Natalie Phythian from Rhyl, known as Sammi by her family,” the force said. “A postmortem examination has revealed that Sammi was pregnant at the time of her death.”

Police released a picture of Ms Phythian alongside a moving tribute from her family, who described her as a “much-loved mum, daughter, sister, auntie and friend” who will be “deeply missed”.

“Samantha, who everyone knows as Sammi, will be remembered for the special place she held in the hearts of everyone who knew and loved her,” they said.

“Her tragic and untimely death has left her family and friends devastated, struggling to come to terms with the loss of someone who meant so much to so many. No family should ever have to endure the pain of losing a loved one in such circumstances.

“While her life has been cruelly cut short, the memories she created, the love she gave and the lives she touched will never be forgotten. She will forever be cherished by those who loved her, and she will be deeply missed.”

They also urged people not to speculate on the circumstances surrounding her death, asking people to be “mindful and respectful of rumours circulating over social media platforms”.

North Wales Police said Ms Phythian’s family are being supported by specialist officers, and echoed the family’s call for people to avoid speculation.

Senior Investigating Officer, Detective Chief Inspector Zoie Dunkerley said: “My thoughts are with Sammi’s family and friends. I would also urge the community to be careful of commenting anything which would add to the family’s distress or interfere with the ongoing active legal proceedings.”

News.title: New Zealand v Australia LIVE: Result and reaction after All Blacks surge away from Wallabies to retain Bledisloe Cup
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

( Getty )

New Zealand produced a show of force at Eden Park as they surged away from Australia to retain the Bledisloe Cup.

The All Blacks extended their unbeaten streak at their Auckland fortress to 54 matches with a dominant performance in the second half particularly, with the Barrett brothers among their best in an all-round strong showing. With Damian McKenzie illustrating from fly half, the hosts blended collision dominance with backline creativity to turn a three-point half-time lead into a 31-point winning margin, controlling proceedings almost totally after the interval.

For the Wallabies, this was a first defeat under Les Kiss and a bit of a reality check after beating South Africa a fortnight ago. Having begun brightly, they could not consistently get their game on the park, and will have to improve greatly if they are to hit back when the two sides meet again in Sydney next week.

Follow all of the latest from Eden Park with our live blog below:

News.title: All Blacks produce show of force to extend Eden Park and Bledisloe Cup streaks against Australia
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park.

The Wallabies were in touch at 17-14 down at half time but the All Blacks scored five tries after the break to ensure they will retain the ⁠symbol of trans-Tasman supremacy for a 24th straight year ahead of next week's second Test in Sydney.

Tries from Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, skipper Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan combined with 15 points from the boot of fly half Damian McKenzie got the All Blacks back to winning ways after three straight losses to South Africa.

Australia, who came into the ​game ⁠unbeaten in six matches and looking for a first win at Eden Park since 1986, scored first-half tries through fullback Tom Wright and captain Harry Wilson and earned a ⁠late consolation score from hooker Josh Nasser.

open image in gallery The All Blacks retain the Bledisloe Cup for another year ( Getty )

The Wallabies, buoyed by a win over world champions South Africa last month, dominated the opening exchanges and got their reward in the eighth minute when full-back Wright cleverly straightened up an attacking move to score the opening try. The aerial battle was always going to be a key factor and ‌New Zealand were enjoying the better of it with Jordie Barrett ‌winning one duel and feeding McKenzie, who scythed through the defence before feeding flanker Lakai to level up the scores.

The All Blacks were also getting a width in the attack that was causing Australia problems and the home side cashed in to take a 14-7 lead in the 16th minute, when Vaa'i barrelled low and hard through the defence at the end of a multi-phase attack. Ryan Lonergan missed a kickable penalty for Australia in the 24th minute, but McKenzie made no mistake from closer range nine minutes later to extend the lead to 10 points.

open image in gallery New Zealand were dominant in the second half in Auckland ( AP )

The five minutes before halftime is traditionally a fruitful stage of the game for New Zealand, but it was Australia who scored three minutes before the break, with Ben Donaldson scooting through a gap in the defence and finding Wilson in support. Australia again came firing ​out of the blocks in the second half but New Zealand earned the first ‌points after 50 minutes when scrum half Roigard darted ⁠over the line off the back of a rolling maul to extend their lead ⁠to 24-14.

The All Blacks were now relentless in attack and hooker Taylor, captaining the side for the second time, scored their fourth try five minutes later. News.title: India locks down capital city as protests against election chief intensify
News.content:
Central Delhi was put under a police lockdown as the youth-led “cockroach” movement sought to organise protests in the India capital on 10 October, intensifying a nationwide campaign against a contentious revision of voter lists and fuelling anger against Narendra Modi’s government and the country’s election authorities.

Thousands of protesters were expected at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the city, to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief, prompting authorities to impose sweeping restrictions, including suspension of mobile internet.

The site was cordoned off with metal barricades and thousands of police personnel were deployed in and around the area.

Police said on Friday they had denied permission for the protests because the request was submitted late.

Restrictions on train and metro rail services disrupted travel in and around the capital and made it harder for protesters to reach the venue.

News.title: 2 Inflation reports, retail sales and big bank profits all arrive in the coming week
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The upcoming week promises to deliver notable updates on inflation, a topic sure to dominate the U.S. midterm elections now less than a month away. A separate report will show how retailers are faring in an inflationary environment, while the nation's biggest banks roll out financials details from the most recent quarter.

The price of oil will be front and center as the U.S. war with Iran drags into its eighth month. Renewed violence has sent oil prices back above $100 per barrel and average gasoline prices remain well above $4 per gallon, while diesel remains just below the record high prices reached in September. That has all fueled inflation, putting more pressure on household budgets and businesses.

Here's a look at some of the events that will be front and center in the week ahead.

Good news for the US housing sector may be that things have not gotten worse

No news is good news lately in the U.S. housing market. On Tuesday, the National Association of Realtors reports existing home sales for September, and economists believe sales held steady from August. But August was awful, with sales declining to their slowest annual pace in more than a year. Prospective home buyers are being thwarted by rising mortgage rates which, as Freddie Mac reported Thursday, marched higher for the seventh consecutive week. The average long-term U.S. home loan rate is now higher than it's been in nearly three years. The housing sector has been in a slump since 2022 and sales of previously occupied homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low.

Inflation does not appear to be going away soon

The U.S. reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East. More of the same is expected for September with all sides in the Iranian conflict unwilling to concede ground. The Labor Department is expected to report Wednesday that its consumer price index rose by two-tenths of a percent month over month and rose 3.6% compared with a year ago at this time. A day later, the department will release its producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. Same story there. Economists expect an increase from the 5.4% registered in August, which was up from 4.8% in July. Last week, PepsiCo said it was raising prices on Doritos and other favorites, citing rising costs for fuel, aluminum and commodities.

Shopping is still hot for US consumers, but economists expect less of it

Economists believe that Americans pulled back on shopping in September with the holiday shopping season just around the corner. Most expect a 0.65% bump. That said, consumers surprised just about everyone in August. As they griped about higher prices at the pump and at the grocery store, Americans spent heartily, expanding retail sales by 1.2%, nearly twice what forecasters had expected. Also next week, the National Retail Federation releases its forecast for the holidays.

Banks expected to report more profit gains amid volatile stock market and consumer spending

Banks have notched record profits this year as their trading desks benefit from a volatile stock market while the U.S. war with Iran drags on. Big swings in markets tend to increase activity on trading desks, leading to higher commissions and fee revenue for the banks. Meanwhile, consumers keep spending despite pressure from high prices, and that helps boost fee and lending revenue.

Wall Street expects more of the same from the third-quarter updates. Analysts expect JPMorgan Chase to report a 47% boost in profits and Citigroup to report a 61% profit jump when both release earnings Tuesday. Bank of America is expected to tally a profit gain of 36% when it announces results Wednesday. Several other banks and financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley, will also report results during the week.

Households and businesses are also facing high interest rates that allow banks to charge more for loans and that won't likely change anytime soon. The Federal Reserve recently raised its benchmark interest rate in an effort to cool inflation and is leaning toward another rate hike by the end of the year.

News.title: Black British Business Awards 2026 winners revealed
News.content:
The chief executive of Dr. Martens has been named the Black British Business Person of the Year at the 2026 Black British Business Awards (BBBAwards).

Ije Nwokorie, who became chief of Dr. Martens in January last year and is the only black chief executive in the FTSE 250, was awarded in recognition of his role shaping Dr. Martens’ growth strategy.

He is recognised inside Dr. Martens for his strong communication with staff, according to the judges.

Before joining Dr. Martens, Mr Nwokorie spent more than 11 years at Wolff Olins, the marketing giant, before working as a senior director at Apple.

Born in the US but brought up from age six against the backdrop of post-civil-war Nigeria, Mr Nwokorie has described how he and his family went from the lifestyle trappings of 1960s America to a small Nigerian village and a home with no running water.

On winning the award, Mr Nwokorie said: “This recognition means a lot to me. While this award bears my name, it reflects the talent, dedication and generosity of the incredible teammates, mentors and leaders who have shaped me as a person and a professional.

“It is a powerful reminder that there is nothing more important in our leadership journeys than the time we invest to help others thrive.”

Alongside his executive career, he has served as a trustee at Charity: water for nearly a decade and held board roles at cultural and humanitarian organisations including the Institute of International Visual Arts and Malaria No More UK.

He also served as chairman of trustees for the Chineke! Orchestra, a British orchestra championing change and the first in Europe to feature a majority of black and ethnically diverse musicians.

The Black British Business Awards started in 2014 to celebrate the achievements of black people in British business. The Telegraph is the national media partner for the awards.

Mr Nwokorie was presented with the award at an exclusive ceremony sponsored by JPMorgan Chase at London’s Hilton Park Lane hotel.

Speaking at the ceremony, Sophie Chandauka, the executive founder of the awards, said: “You lend the BBBAwards credibility not simply to celebrate excellence, but to ensure the best and brightest from all communities get a fair shot. That commitment has made the BBBAwards the UK’s premium awards programme for black business achievement.”

A spokesman for JPMorgan Chase said: “We couldn’t be prouder to support and celebrate such an outstanding breadth of black British talent.

“Their accomplishments continue to inspire future generations and demonstrate the exceptional value they bring to businesses, communities and the wider UK economy.”

This year’s winners are as follows:

Black British Business Person of the Year: Ije Nwokorie, chief executive of Dr Martens

News.title: Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it
News.content:
England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

News.title: What is the XFG Covid strain? Symptoms and what to know as the variant hits the UK
News.content:
Cases of Covid-19 have risen sharply across the UK this month, driven largely by a variant of the virus known as ‘XFG’.

Sometimes referred to as ‘Stratus’ and the ‘American strain’, owing to the fact that it is now the most common strain in North America, it was first identified in January 2025 and has since spread worldwide.

Between August and September, Covid cases in Britain jumped 230 per cent, from 1,374 to 4,589 new infections, half of which were caused by the XFG strain.

Hospitalisation rates have also increased by 15 per cent in the same period, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The true number of cases is likely to be much higher, as most people who contract Covid-19 experience a milder illness and will not visit hospital or receive an official diagnosis via their GP.

What are the symptoms, and how is it different from other variants?

Symptoms of XFG are similar to other variants of Covid-19 like Delta and Omicron, and typically begin with a sore throat, before developing into a cough and fever.

However, experts have noted that patients diagnosed with XFG tend to present with a characteristic hoarse, croaky voice, which is distinctive from older strains.

More than 30 other symptoms have been known to be associated with XFG and other Covid strains, including diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of taste and smell, shortness of breath, headache, and muscle aches.

Why are cases rising?

Current data does not suggest that XFG leads to more severe illness than any other variant in circulation, according to the UKHSA.

As the UK moves into winter, colder and wetter weather naturally influences the rise in respiratory illnesses like Covid-19 and the flu, given people spend more time indoors and in closer proximity to each other, where viruses can more easily transmit between them.

It has also been roughly a year since the last significant wave of Covid-19 cases, meaning that the population-wide immunity has somewhat waned, making people more susceptible to the disease, the UKHSA said.

Can you be vaccinated against XFG?

The current Covid-19 vaccine is designed to protect against XFG and related strains specifically, after modelling suggested it would become the dominant variant this season.

Those eligible for a Covid-19 autumn booster include adults over the age of 75, residents in care homes, and anyone over six months old with a weakened immune system, due to a health condition or treatment.

Covid vaccines are also available to buy privately for those who are not eligible for a free jab, and typically cost around £98 per dose.

What should you do if you suspect you have XFG?

The NHS no longer advises that people with symptoms of Covid-19 take a test, unless they want to do so.

If you feel unwell or have a high temperature, health authorities advise you to try and stay home and avoid contact with people until you feel better.

They also recommend avoiding contact with vulnerable people, like those undergoing chemotherapy or the elderly, for at least 10 days.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Harry’s Invictus Games challenge in Kenya is helping veterans battle physical and mental scars
News.content:
Wounded veterans from 10 countries have gathered in Kenya’s Great Rift Valley for a week of endurance challenges, organised by the charity behind Prince Harry’s Invictus Games.

Twenty-five serving and former personnel, among them a Ukrainian who survived a direct bomb hit in Donetsk and a Danish combat engineer who cleared roadside bombs in Afghanistan, will run, hike or cycle up to 120km across the area on Saturday October 10, World Mental Health Day.

The Invictus Games Foundation, the charity the Duke of Sussex founded in 2014 for wounded, injured and sick service personnel, has organised the event.

For Vasyl, a Ukrainian soldier, it will be his first time in Africa and his first long-distance challenge.

After three weeks of military training in the UK, the 34-year-old joined a brigade in Donetsk as a reconnaissance squad commander, spending more than 19 months on the front line. He was wounded when a drone dropped a grenade three metres from him, and the shrapnel still causes frequent pain in his leg which can sometimes make walking difficult.

But he said the physical injury was easier to bear than the loss of the friends he made in the trenches.

“There is a level of kindness between comrades in a trench that you will never find in civilian life,” he said. “If someone made a mistake or said something wrong, we immediately forgave them and thought nothing more of it.

“For me, the pain of loss is the hardest thing the war has left behind.”

News.title: From Yale to the Congo: The mathematician who became one of Africa’s most intrepid reporters
News.content:
Sundaram has a lot of experience with the Rwandan methods of control. After spending 17 months in DRC, he moved to Kigali and he is eloquent about the convoluted effects of dictatorship. “Living in Rwanda taught me so much about how dictatorships function internally and how counter-intuitive they can be. A friend of mine who was working in public health told me ‘When we ask people in India to wash their hands we get a 30 per cent success rate from a campaign, but when we need people in Rwanda to wash their hands, we just need to slip a line in one of Kagame’s speeches and we get a 90 per cent success rate. That’s fantastic isn’t it?’

“And I said, ‘well is it? It’s great for short term health outcomes but what does that say about society? Isn’t democracy about people choosing freely? What if the government tells them to do something bad – like what happened in the genocide when people were told to kill all the Tutsis?’

“Kagame and his army stopped the genocide, and he has restored peace, but he governs using the same system that was used to perpetrate the genocide.”

In Bad News: Last Journalists in a Dictatorship, the book Sundaram went on to write about his time in Rwanda teaching journalists, he describes a more extreme version of this phenomenon, recalling how Kagame once commented that thatched roofs on huts were primitive. “And the local authorities took that as a sign that he didn’t like thatched roofs, and that they should get rid of them. And without replacements being built, people climbed up and dismantled their own thatched roofs. And I saw these villages with houses which just had mud walls without roofs, and the families were sitting outside with their children and their goats, the thatch strewn on the ground. In the rain, quite often. The children would get sick, and it was like a war zone.

“At the end of my time in Congo, I was at a UN base and they were digging latrines, when they found some human bones. They stopped digging and alerted the press, and I happened to be in Goma nearby.” He subsequently found out that it was one of a series of mass graves containing the bodies of Congolese killed by forces controlled by Kagame. “And so when I arrived I had a sense of what Rwanda had done in Congo, but I didn’t fully appreciate the extent to which it was totalitarian. I’d heard that the country was a shining example of progress – aid programs were successful, and poverty reduction programs. The streets were clean, public services functioned. I was living in a nice house with a big garden provided by the journalism programme I was working in.”

Many European governments, including Britain, are enamoured with Rwanda, because, says Sundaram, “dictatorships can be very efficient”. But it is a “mirage of a country”, he says.

The teaching programme he was running was briefed not to challenge the government on any level, and an embassy official told him that if any of the journalists mentioned repression they would be expelled.

“Layer by layer, as I began to talk to the journalists I was training, the true story unravelled. The first instance was when one of them left the programme, and I heard him on the radio one day praising the president, but with a degree of flattery that was completely exaggerated, and I didn’t understand why. The rest of the class were reluctant to talk about it but eventually I learned that another student had been beaten to a coma on the day he criticised the president.

“I started to realise that my class contained some of the most courageous journalists in the country.” As a foreigner, if he transgressed, Sundaram could have his visa cancelled or get kicked out, or even locked up for a couple of days, but for the Rwandan journalists, everything was at stake. They could be killed or their families threatened.

“But still they persisted, and they took me around the country and showed me all the things the government didn’t want anyone to see – things they couldn’t report on because it was too dangerous, so they wanted to show me because they wanted somebody to speak up. It’s really a book about them – they’ve been my greatest teachers in journalism.”

News.title: I tried Amazon’s new iPad rival – and there’s one standout feature
News.content:
Amazon says that this tablet has three times the computing power and nine times the graphics power of any previous Amazon tablet, so this is a significant boost in performance to previous models.

That will make light tasks, such as crunching through emails, browser-based activity like online shopping and document work. With a keyboard factored in, it could work as a laptop alternative for some. The same could be said of the iPad Air, although with recent price increases from Apple and the matte screen, for my money, this is a better proposition.

The premium makeover that comes with the Alexa Tablet Pro includes a slim aluminium design, with flattened edges, so it looks like an iPad or Samsung tablet, only 6.5mm thick. The Pro version only comes in the Graphite colour seen here. All models in the new line-up feel more grown-up and less like kid’s tablets than the Fire range. Plus the switch to proper Android over Fire OS is welcome and will result in better app compatibility (although I noticed that these tablets were running Android 16, which is now an old version).

It has a battery that’s good for 16 hours of video playback and supports 27W charging. There are cameras front and rear although like any tablet, these won’t be as good as your phone, while there’s support for Dolby Atmos from the speakers, so your movies will sound decent.

The AI capabilities are a step up

As the name suggests, Amazon is keen to promote the AI element here. It has customised the interface slightly with access to Alexa+ meaning you can utilise Amazon’s AI at any time to ask about what’s on the screen, to control smart home devices or search for content. If you are a keen Alexa user, then that will be a plus, but for me it’s not the headline news.

Sports.title: Unassuming London park is piece of English football history after being made from rubble of iconic 82,000-seat stadium
Sports.content:
Next

WHEN Wembley was renovated and reopened in 2007, not many of us were thinking: What are they going to do with all that rubble?

You might be surprised to learn that they did indeed use said rubble and laid the foundations for a new park in London.



Wembley used to be defined by the ‘twin towers’ at the front of the ground, but in 2003 those iconic pillars were stripped away as part of the rebuild.

They stood together for 80 years, but now Wembley’s arch, which is sometimes even lit up in the country’s colours, parades the London skyline.



But the ruins of old Wembley did indeed find a new home.

Next to the A40 in west London sits Northala Fields, which opened one year after the new Wembley did.



It has four distinct, climbable hills, all of which were made out of the ruins of old Wembley.

As well as the man-made hills, the park has several fishing lakes, a large field area, a children’s play area and adjacent cafe.

The name Northala supposedly comes from how the old manor of Northall (Northolt) was recorded in Domesday Book in 1086.

Wembley Stadium was originally built all the way back in 1923.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

It was the site where England won their one and only World Cup, but by the turn of the Millennium, it was outdated and no longer safe.

Now, the home of English football remains the biggest stadium in the country with 90,000 seats.

It held 96,000 people for Anthony Joshua‘s fight with Daniel Dubois while 98,000 packed in to see an Adele concert.

In 2028, it will also host the finals of the Euros, just like it did in 2021.

Sports.title: Awkward moment Mark Goldbridge squirms as Jamie Carragher calls him ‘the biggest fraud’ on launch of new podcast
Sports.content:
Next

JAMIE CARRAGHER took the first chance he got to have a go at YouTube star Mark Goldbridge when the pair sat together alongside Gary Neville on a new episode of Overlap Daily.

Neville’s The Overlap empire paid a seven-figure sum earlier this year for Goldbridge’s The United Stand and That’s Football YouTube channels, which have a combined subscriber count of around four million.



The move has seen The United Stand become ‘Stick to United’ as part of The Overlap’s lucrative deal with Disney and Goldbridge is hosting alongside Man United legend Wayne Rooney.

That’s Football was also rebranded to Overlap Daily as part of the deal, with the YouTuber continuing to broadcast his watchalongs on the channel.



He will host the Friday edition of that show with Carragher, Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel set to be regular co-hosts.

And Liverpool legend Carragher made sure he got off to a flying start with the often viral presenter.



In the opening salvo from the show, Carragher highlighted Goldbridge’s real name – Brent Cleminson – while claiming the YouTube star is really a Nottingham Forest supporter, not a Man United fan.

That could be viewed as the worst kept secret in the YouTube football space, but Carragher put it on him anyway.

He said: “Are you going to be yourself on the show? I keep reading that you’re not going to be yourself, you’ve sold out,” Carragher quipped, much to Neville’s laughter.

Goldbridge responded: “I was actually thinking on the way up, you know, your punditry career is a bit like your playing career, isn’t it?”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Carragher eagerly replied: “Go on, have you got your lines ready and all that? I’ve got my lines ready for you.”

“Used to be a policeman, didn’t you?”

Once Goldbridge responded ‘yeah,’ Carragher took the chance to call him a fraud again.

Trying to play it nicer, Goldbridge tried to joke: “This is why I’m here, for the Man City stuff,” referencing the recent independent commission decision to find City guilty of over 100 financial rule breaches, which the club has appealed.

But Carragher went back at him leaving Goldbridge squirming awkwardly in his chair.



“Yeah, but you are the biggest fraud though, aren’t you, when you think about it?” Carragher continued, with Goldbridge responding “Why’s this?”

“Your name’s Mark, but it’s really Brent, and you say you’re a Man United fan, but you’re really a Nottingham Forest fan,” Carragher said.

“You know what I mean, you want to start with that?”



Goldbridge’s attempt at a comeback referenced Carragher wearing an Everton kit, having supported the club as a youngster, before ultimately becoming a club legend at their arch rivals Liverpool.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Some might view this as banter, others might suggest Carragher has very little, if any respect for Goldbridge and saw a good chance for a joke.

Either way, Goldbridge will have to work on his material because he’ll no doubt be working with Carragher again as the season continues.

Sports.title: Masked Man and Wellington Arch tackle Chepstow's Silver Trophy
Sports.content:
We have a busy day's racing on Saturday with action from Chepstow, Hexham and Southwell, live on Sky Sports Racing...

4.02 Chepstow - Wellington Arch and Masked Man spearhead classy field

The feature Wasdell Group Silver Trophy Handicap Hurdle at Chepstow looks a belter with Masked Man and Wellington Arch among a host of contenders.

Masked Man has been at the head of the market all week and this lightly raced five-year-old must be feared on handicap debut. He scored on two of his four hurdles starts last season while running with credit in Graded company and ought to be involved.

Wellington Arch has a very different profile having landed a pair of handicaps on his last two outings. Ultra-impressive when landing a strong Aintree contest, he will need more again to defy a further seven-pound rise.

Melon claimed an Aintree handicap on his last hurdling run and arrives fit from a spin on the Flat.

Glynn Brae and The Mighty Celt are others will obvious each-way chances as well as last year's victor Rambo T.

3.45 Hexham - Prolific Passing Diamond faces Tiddesley Wood

Prolific Passing Diamond takes on three rivals in a trappy Cast Novices' Limited Handicap Chase at Hexham.

The Ben Haslam-trained six-year-old has relished the switch to fencing winning both starts at Cartmel and deserves a crack at this better race. A natural jumper, he ought to take some catching.

Tiddesley Wood is the chief danger as he makes his debut for trainer Adrian Keatley. He doubled his tally over hurdles when landing a Kempton novice on his final start for Fergal O'Brien and remains of interest over fences.

Ballykinlar and Passengerontheship complete the quartet.

7.30 Southwell - Recent scorer Tanjen contests strong heat

Recent winner Tanjen features among a field of nine for the competitive Pilsner To The Post Handicap at Southwell.

Tim Easterby's four-year-old has won over this course and distance and arrives on the back of a comfortable success at Hamilton. Up seven pounds, he switches back to the all-weather and will be fancied to follow up.

Star Noir bounced back to life with an eight-and-a-half length victory at Catterick and reverts to handicaps with strong claims.

David O'Meara's top-weight Goyard was only just denied over this course and distance last month and a similar effort would put him in the frame despite a one-pound rise.

Sports.title: 'You will see me back' - Smith vows 2027 return after Swiss Darts Trophy win
Sports.content:
Former world champion Michael Smith says he plans on "playing 100 per cent of the tournaments" in 2027 after an opening win at the Swiss Darts Trophy.

'Bully Boy' Smith fought back from 3-1 down to beat Rob Owen, hitting 50 per cent of his doubles in just his fourth European Tour event of the season.

"I've missed this. I want to apologise and also make a promise in 2027 I will be playing 100 per cent of the tournaments. You will see me back," said the 2023 world champion.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Smith revealed he has been playing in discomfort after being diagnosed with arthritis in his wrists in 2025, but despite this setback he believes he can get back to his best and challenge for titles again

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch how Michael Smith overcame several setbacks to become a world darts champion in 2023

Smith is chasing down the final spots in the European Championship race and the St Helens thrower beat Owen 6-4 to set up a meeting with Jermaine Wattimena for a place in Sunday's action.

Rob Cross was Friday's standout performer for the second event in a row, averaging 105.95 in his 6-3 success against Mario Vandenbogaerde and will take on Luke Woodhouse on the back of his brilliant opening round performance at the World Grand Prix.

Bradley Brooks also produced an excellent display of darting brilliance in his opening round contest against Niels Zonneveld, as the former World Youth Champion averaged over a ton in a 6-4 victory over the World Grand Prix quarter-finalist, in a game that saw both players average over a ton and hit 13 maximums between them.

Brooks has now won four out of a possible four round-one games in European Tour events this year, and will take on Chris Dobey for a place in the final day of action at St Jakobshalle.

Karel Sedlacek's hopes of sealing a spot at the European Championship continue into Saturday's action as he swept aside Sebastian Bialecki to stay alive in the race for place in Dortmund later this month.

The Czech star averaged upwards of a ton and came back from 4-3 down to defeat the Pole 6-4, which included a brilliant 86 checkout on the bull to break the throw for the first time in the contest.

Image: Stefan Bellmont defeated Andrew Gilding to send the Swiss crowd wild in Basel

Stefan Bellmont produced a brilliant display on home soil in Basel as he created history by becoming the third Swiss player to win a match at the tournament, as he beat Andrew Gilding 6-3.

The 37-year-old, who featured in his tenth European Tour event in his career, pinned five legs on the spin to defeat the former UK Open champion, and has his eyes set on a place in Saturday's action.

"Playing in front of your home crowd is very special and I wanted to win so much." Bellmont reflected, who managed to win only his third match on the European Tour and will face Krzysztof Ratajski in round two.

"There were quite a few nerves in the early stages of the match, but thankfully I was able to raise my game.

"I know I will have to play better tomorrow but for now I just want to enjoy this amazing moment."

Maik Kuivenhoven ended a losing streak of almost five years in Basel, as the Dutchman beat compatriot Raymond van Barneveld 6-3 to deny van Barneveld his first European Tour victory of the year.

Dave Chisnall and Tom Bissell both secured last-leg victories in their opening round contests against Alan Soutar and Joe Cullen respectively.

Cristo Reyes' first win on the European Tour since May came in style, as the Spaniard beat Scotsman Cameron Menzies with an average of 98 and will face Ryan Searle next.

The Swiss Darts Trophy continues with a bumper double session on Saturday, as the 16 seeded representatives enter the fray on Day Two in Basel.

Sports.title: Opetaia could fight Wilder on Fury-AJ undercard: 'He’s ready to go!'
Sports.content:
Deontay Wilder could fight Jai Opetaia on the undercard of the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua blockbuster clash on December 11.

Fury and Joshua meet in a long-awaited, much-anticipated all-British heavyweight fight at the Principality Stadium.

Wilder, the hard-punching former world heavyweight champion, is eyeing a place on the bill against elite cruiserweight Jai Opetaia.

Dana White, who promotes Opetaia, told Sky Sports: "Jai Opetaia is more than likely going to be on the undercard. [Wilder] is one that we've been talking about and working on."

It would be a first high-level heavyweight fight for Opetaia, the unbeaten Australian who has been a force at cruiserweight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jai Opetaia landed a powerful flurry of shots in the ninth round to force a stoppage victory over Noel Mikaelian and accepted the challenge of David Benavidez. Fight footage courtesy of DAZN

Wilder is now 40 years old but the former WBC titlist is still known for his fearsome punch-power.

"The guy's willing to fight anybody," White said of Opetaia. "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.

"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."

Opetaia would likely return to cruiserweight afterwards. He and David Benavidez are considered the two best fighters in the 200lb weight class and Benavidez remains Opetaia's ultimate target.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jai Opetaia showed off his spiteful combinations as he punished Jack Massey and forced the stoppage in round six

"That's the fight he really wants. He wants that fight so we've got to figure that one out," White said, adding: "He wants to stay active, he wants to fight and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever, he's ready to go."

Wilder had an epic trilogy with Tyson Fury and came close to setting a fight with Anthony Joshua, only to lose to Joseph Parker.

In his last fight Wilder battled to a points win over British contender Derek Chisora at The O2 in London in April.

Sports.title: Arteta says conscience clear over time at Man City
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has said he has a clear conscience over his former club Manchester City's serious breaches of financial rules.

An independent commission found that between 2009/10 and 2017/18, City artificially inflated their revenue by £830m. The club have lodged an appeal and deny all wrongdoing.

The investigation covered two years in which Arteta was working as assistant to manager Pep Guardiola but, in an otherwise guarded press conference, the Arsenal boss answered "yes" when asked if he had a clear conscience.

Arteta, who this week signed a new four-year contract as Arsenal manager, faced a string of questions over the City verdict by journalists but repeatedly insisted he would not comment further until the outcome of City's appeal is known.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How Arteta and other managers reacted to questions about the Man City case

"The thing is that this has been going for various years," he said.

"The process is still not finished, so it's very difficult to express how I feel because it's not resolved. When it's resolved, I can talk with clarity and tell you exactly how I feel.

"I think that process has to be resolved in a way. And we need to trust that the people who are in charge doing that will do it in the timeframe that they believe is best for everybody."

Arteta spent three-and-a-half seasons working with Guardiola, including the 2016/17 and 2017/18 campaigns, when City won back-to-back Premier League titles, an FA Cup and two League Cups, before leaving the club to take charge of Arsenal in 2019.

Image: Arteta worked with Pep Guardiola at Man City

According to the independent commission, City artificially inflated their sponsorship income by £264.3m across the 2016/17 and 2017/18 seasons, a period during which their signings included John Stones, Aymeric Laporte, Bernardo Silva, Ederson and Kyle Walker.

Arteta refused to comment when asked if his memories of working at City had been tainted.

When asked whether he was pleased to have won the Premier League title for Arsenal before the verdict, he said: "I feel proud and very emotional when I think about how we won it, the moments that we had together. It's a unique and genuine feeling that I have."

Arteta: Premier League still best in the world

Arteta insisted the Premier League will "100 per cent" continue to be the best league in the world despite questions of integrity being thrown up by the City verdict.

"It's the best league in the world for many reasons," he added.

"I've been here for over 20 years and it will continue to be the best league in the world. I feel privileged to be where I am.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Premier League managers including Frank Lampard, Marco Rose and Daniel Farke have their say

"And there are a few clubs who have been extremely good and managed resources in an intelligent way. And we suffered from that a few weeks ago [with their defeat to Brighton]."

However, following comments by Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner, who said the Premier League has been "damaged" by City being found guilty, Arteta admitted he was unsure about the impact on the competition's reputation globally.

"I want to think that it doesn't [damage the Premier League] but I don't know," he said. "And certainly it's not in our control.

"In our control is to bring everything we can individually to the club, to maintain the position we have to be the best league in the world."

Sports.title: Wainwright opens Leicester account with Gloucester win in front of Prince Harry
Sports.content:
Wales back-rower Aaron Wainwright scored his first try for Leicester Tigers as they defeated Gloucester 38-31 in a forward-dominated contest in the Gallagher Prem watched by The Duke of Sussex, Prince Harry.

The hosts found themselves 14-0 down after just 10 minutes at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, but a sustained period of dominance led to them scoring 31 unanswered points that put them well on the way to their second straight win.

For the Cherry and Whites, this was a first league loss of the season as they fell short in a match that saw eight of the nine tries scored by forwards.

Image: Prince Harry (centre) was spotted in the stands

Prince Harry, who had a beer in his hand, is a keen rugby fan and was in attendance with Andrea Pinchen, the Tigers chief executive.

Harry returned to the UK with Meghan and their children in August after six years away in the US.

It was Leicester who quickly found themselves under pressure when they had fly-half Billy Searle sin-binned just three minutes in for deliberately knocking Ben Loader's pass forward inside his own 22.

The Cherry and Whites quickly made the most of their one-man advantage when Wales flanker Jac Morgan squeezed his way through after a succession of pick-and-goes from his fellow forwards.

Try number two for the visitors soon followed when a driving maul powered its way over, with loosehead Dian Bleuler grounding the ball. Caolan Englefield converted both early scores stylishly from out wide.

Shortly after Searle returned to the field, Leicester were on the board when Finn Carnduff managed to force himself over the whitewash from close quarters.

The Tigers began to dominate territorially and found themselves level after half an hour when England tighthead Joe Heyes blasted through from a couple of metres and Searle added the extras.

The turnaround was then completed in the 36th minute when Jamie Blamire scored off the back of a driving maul to give Leicester a 21-14 half-time lead.

To make matters worse for Gloucester, they had Thomas sin-binned immediately after the try had been awarded as their evening threatened to unravel.

They had a lifeline after an hour when a superb carry from Morgan took them close to the line before Englefield's pass allowed Will Trenholm to power in down the left.

But their hopes of a comeback were ended with 10 minutes remaining when Ollie Hassell-Collins became the first back from either team to score when Adam Radwan's pass sent him scurrying in at the corner.

There was still time, though, for the visitors to claim two bonus points late on as Jack Innard scored their fourth try before George Barton knocked over a penalty with the final kick.
