World.title: SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 under REVIEW
World.content:
SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 are still under review for the coming month. Unbelievably, after not affecting any October 2026 top-ups, the agency cannot confirm next month’s payment arrangements either, due to local government elections (this is the case at the time of publishing) …

As you can imagine, this isn’t good optics for new department head Dina Pule, who is the first minister to date to have such a clash. SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 were originally scheduled for Tuesday 3 November 2026 – a 32-day gap between disbursements.

SASSA OLDER PERSON GRANTS IN NOVEMBER 2026

However, in exceedingly tough economic times, the country’s four-million elderly could do without such indecision. And to await pronouncements on a reviewed payment date for SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 is only adding insult to injury. The only small sliver of hope is that Finance Minister Godongwana’s Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS) – scheduled for Wednesday 21 October 2026 – may bring some late-onset good news.



The South African Social Security Agency only increased Older Person Grants by R80 back in April 2026. And there has been no confirmation of further increases since:

SASSA Old-Age Grants 60 to 74 years old – R2 400 (up from R2 320)

(up from R2 320) SASSA Old-Age Grants 75 years and older – R2 420 (up from R2 340)

WHY ARE SASSA OLDER PERSON GRANTS IN NOVEMBER 2026 UNDER REVIEW?

We can only assume that new SASSA minister Dina Pule doesn’t hold much sway with the National Treasury to bring in any significant grant increases. Image: File

Civil society groups say they’re not entirely sure why SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 are even under review. The perceived clash with local government elections only impacts SASSA Disability – on Wednesday 4 November 2026. So, why Older Person and Childcare should be changed isn’t abundantly clear to anyone, besides clashing with a public holiday.

Nevertheless, while the agency continues to employ strict review and eLife certification policies, the Auditor-General just revealed something more worrying in Parliament. According to latest reports, more than R260 million in SASSA grants is drawn annually by government employees. This is completely and utterly illegal. And every million stolen could feed more than 100 households on SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026.



BENEFICIARY REVIEWS FOR SASSA OLDER PERSON GRANTS IN NOVEMBER 2026

A reminder that SASSA cross-references all personal data with other government departments and banks. Therefore, anyone claiming a government grant that shouldn’t be could be in trouble. For those who are reviewed by SASSA and clear their names, they receive a deferred payment on a fourth payment date. It was schedule for Friday 6 November 2026 but is also under review next month. And don’t forget agency’s income (means) and asset eligibility limits for SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026:

Your income must be less than R9 350 (single) or R18 700 (married) per month.

(single) or (married) per month. This adds up to R112 200 (single) or R224 400 (married) per year.

(single) or (married) per year. Total assets (property) in your name cannot be worth more than R1 584 000 (single) or R3 168 000 (married).

WHAT TO BRING TO YOUR SASS APPLICATION APPOINTMENT

Official RSA identity document (ID) preferably a Smart ID Card with digital ID photo and biometrics.

Valid three months’ statement certified by your bank, plus copies.

All documents proving your marital status, plus death certificates, if necessary.

Proof of residence (a utility bill with your name on it, not older than three months).

Documents proving your income and/or financial dividends (very important).

Comprehensive information regarding assets/valuation of any property you own.

Full declaration of any and all private pension in your name.

Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) membership book, or discharge certificate from your previous job.

A copy of your will, first and final liquidation and distribution accounts if your spouse has passed away in the last five years.

HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE TO BE APPROVED?

Make sure all your personal and banking details are up to date with the agency before SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 roll off to avoid delays. Image: File

SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 typically take around three months to be processed. So, if you apply today, you will receive your first payment in the New Year. However, the good news is you will be back paid to the date of your first application, a first tranche of three months in one go. But that’s assuming you have all your above documents correct at the first time of asking.

It is now possible to complete eLife certification and biometric verification online to save time and beat the queues. You can do so HERE on the SASSA Service Portal. However, it has been offline often recently. Plus, if you’re too old, sick or live in a remote rural area you can get a loved one to help with your SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 application. All you need is a letter from your doctor. And all of the above documentation copied and certified by a commissioner of oaths. If you are denied the grant you do have three months to appeal the decision with the agency.



You can try to contact SASSA directly here:

SASSA toll-free line: 0800 601 011

Head Office of SASSA: 012 400 2322

Email SASSA: grantsenquiries@sassa.gov.za

But what do you think? Would you like to see SASSA Older Person Grants in November 2026 go ahead on the stipulated date? Do you have any insights in the agency’s service of late? Be sure to share your ideas in the comments section below …

World.title: SASSA grant reviews: What beneficiaries need to know
World.content:
The South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) has clarified its intensified social grant reviews and verification measures. Image: Facebook @SASSANewsZA

The South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) has clarified its intensified social grant reviews and verification measures, saying these are necessary to protect the integrity of the social assistance system and prevent fraudulent payments.

The agency issued the statement on Friday following media reports about money paid to beneficiaries who were allegedly not eligible to receive social grants during the 2025/26 financial year.

SASSA also acknowledged issues raised before the Portfolio Committee on Social Development on Wednesday, 7 October, and welcomed continued scrutiny of the administration of public funds.



The agency said social assistance is a constitutional obligation and a critical safety net for millions of vulnerable South Africans but stressed that the system needs to be protected against fraud, abuse, errors, misrepresentation and payments to people who no longer qualified for assistance.

“The integrity of the social grants system cannot be protected by avoiding reviews simply because reviews may be uncomfortable or inconvenient,” SASSA said.

REMEMBER | Win R2 000 every month in The South African’s SASSA survey

Criticism

SASSA said the reviews and eLife certification measures had attracted criticism from some sections of society and interest groups, amid concerns that the interventions were intended to exclude legitimate beneficiaries.

The agency rejected these concerns, saying the processes were designed to establish whether beneficiaries continued to meet the prescribed eligibility requirements.

“A social grant is not an unconditional entitlement that continues irrespective of changes in a beneficiary’s circumstances. Beneficiaries have a responsibility to inform SASSA when circumstances that may affect their eligibility change,” the agency said.



These changes include income, employment, marital status, banking details, residential circumstances and other material personal circumstances.

SASSA said reviews were an important administrative and control mechanism to verify whether beneficiaries remained eligible for the grants they received.

The agency added that beneficiaries who legitimately qualified for social assistance should not fear processes intended to verify their continued eligibility.

eLife certification and biometric enrolment

SASSA said it had also intensified eLife certification to establish whether beneficiaries were still alive and were the legitimate recipients of social assistance.

The process seeks to prevent public funds from being paid where a beneficiary has died, where there is uncertainty about their continued existence, or where another person may be unlawfully accessing the grant.

“Social grants reviews and eLife certification are therefore not designed to arbitrarily terminate grants. They are a control mechanism intended to confirm the continued existence and eligibility of beneficiaries and to prevent fraudulent payments,” SASSA said.

Another intervention is Beneficiary Biometric Enrolment, which the agency said would strengthen identity verification and improve the security of social grant transactions.

The process forms part of broader efforts to reduce opportunities for impersonation and fraudulent transactions, while ensuring that grants reach their rightful recipients.

SASSA said the measures were particularly important given the substantial public resources managed by the social assistance system and the millions of beneficiaries it serves.

The agency maintained that it could not rely indefinitely on historical information, as systems, identities, personal circumstances and payment arrangements changed over time.

“Controls must therefore evolve accordingly,” SASSA said.

World.title: First time travelling abroad? The checklist nobody gives you, until now
World.content:
Travelling abroad for the first time is exciting, but there's plenty to sort out before you fly. Image: Pexels.

First time travelling abroad? It’s exciting. It’s also a little overwhelming.

There’s the passport, the visa, the money, the insurance and a dozen small things nobody tells you about.

Most first-time travellers only find out what they’ve forgotten at the airport.



This checklist will help you avoid that.

From paperwork to phone bills, here’s what every South African should know before their first trip overseas.

1. CHECK YOUR PASSPORT CAREFULLY

Having a valid passport isn’t always enough.

Many countries require your passport to be valid for six months from the day you arrive.

Thailand, Indonesia, China, India and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are among them.

The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) also advises that your passport should have at least two blank pages.



2. FIND OUT IF YOU NEED A VISA

South Africans can visit many countries visa-free. But popular destinations like the UK, the US and most of Europe require a visa.

Apply early.

A Schengen visa for Europe can take up to 45 days in busy periods, and a UK visa can take four to six weeks from start to finish.

Don’t book non-refundable flights or accommodation until your visa is approved.

3. CHECK YOUR TRANSIT RULES TOO

A layover can need paperwork as well.

South Africans usually need a transit visa to change planes in the UK, even without leaving the airport.

In Dubai, you don’t need a visa if you stay in the transit area. But you will if you need to collect your luggage and check in again.

4. GET TRAVEL INSURANCE BEFORE TRAVELLING ABROAD FOR THE FIRST TIME

Medical treatment abroad can be extremely expensive, and your medical aid may not cover you overseas.

Travel insurance can cover medical emergencies, cancelled flights and lost luggage.

Some bank cards include basic travel insurance if you pay for your flights with them.

Check exactly what your card covers, since it may not be enough for a long trip.

5. CHECK WHICH VACCINATIONS YOU NEED

Some countries require proof of certain vaccinations.

The most important one for South Africans is yellow fever.

According to the government, South Africa requires a valid yellow fever certificate from anyone over one year old who travels from a yellow fever risk country, including South African citizens.

The vaccine must be given at least 10 days before you travel. A travel clinic can tell you what you need for your destination.

6. SORT OUT YOUR MONEY FOR YOUR FIRST TIME TRAVELLING ABROAD

Let your bank know you’re travelling, so it doesn’t block your card for unusual activity.

Carry more than one way to pay, such as a bank card, a travel card and a little cash in the local currency.

South Africans can take money out of the country under the single discretionary allowance (SDA).

In 2026, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) increased the allowance to R2 million per adult per calendar year.

It covers travel, gifts and other transfers.

7. REGISTER YOUR TRIP WITH DIRCO

This is the step most first-time travellers skip.

DIRCO offers a free, voluntary registration service for South Africans abroad.

It helps the department reach you, or your family, in an emergency such as a natural disaster or civil unrest.

You can register through the DIRCO Travel Smart App, by emailing rosahelp@dirco.gov.za, or at the nearest South African embassy.

8. MAKE COPIES OF YOUR DOCUMENTS

Take photos of your passport, visa, insurance policy and bookings.

Save them somewhere you can access without your phone, such as your email, and leave copies with someone at home.

If your passport is lost or stolen, contact the nearest South African embassy or consulate.

9. WATCH OUT FOR ROAMING CHARGES

Using your South African SIM card overseas can get expensive very quickly.

Before you leave, check your network’s roaming rates, or consider a local SIM card or an eSIM at your destination.

10. KNOW THE AIRPORT RULES BEFORE TRAVELLING ABROAD FOR THE FIRST TIME

If you’re a dual citizen, South African law requires you to use your South African passport to enter and leave South Africa.

Check your airline’s baggage rules before you pack, since extra or overweight bags can cost you.

And give yourself plenty of time at the airport. International check-in usually closes earlier than domestic.

I’ll be honest. My first trip abroad came with a few lessons I wish I’d learnt sooner.

The good news? Most travel stress comes from things you can sort out at home.

My advice? If it’s your first time travelling abroad, work through this list a few weeks before you fly.

Then all you have to worry about is enjoying the trip.

World.title: ANC to appeal court ruling in Andile Lungisa candidate list dispute
World.content:
ANC NEC member Andile Lungisa (In white T-shirt) during a door-to-door campaign in the Eastern Cape. Image: X/@mrlungisa

The African National Congress (ANC) says it will appeal the Johannesburg High Court ruling in favour of Andile Lungisa over his removal from the party’s proportional representation (PR) candidate list for the Nelson Mandela Bay Municipality.

Lungisa reportedly appeared on the ANC’s initial candidate list but was removed from the final list submitted to the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) for the 4 November local government elections.

After being urged to use the party’s internal structures to resolve the dispute, Lungisa approached the court, arguing that his removal was unlawful. The Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg subsequently ruled in his favour.



COURT RULES IN FAVOUR OF ANDILE LUNGISA

In a ruling delivered on Friday, 9 October, Judge Nelisa Mali directed the ANC to restore Andile Lungisa’s name to its internal proportional representation candidate list. The party was also ordered to submit his name to the IEC, provided it is legally permitted to amend its list.

Lungisa had alleged that ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula removed his name after the candidate-selection process had reached its final stages. However, the court did not hold Mbalula personally liable, the Daily Maverick reported.

[BREAKING] The High Court in Johannesburg invalidates Andile Lungisa’s removal from the ANC’s candidates list. Mbalula, the ANC & the NEC have been ordered to take immediate steps to ensure that Lungisa’s name is reinstated to the party’s internal list.@Newzroom405 pic.twitter.com/jjxstevfq7 — Zoleka Qodashe (@ZOLEKV_Q) October 9, 2026

ANC TO APPEAL COURT JUDGEMENT

The former ruling party said it respected the independence of the judiciary and the constitutional authority of the courts but had resolved to appeal the judgment.

The party said the ruling “raises fundamental questions concerning the organisational autonomy of political parties and their authority to regulate internal democratic processes”.

Andile Lungisa with ANC members during a door-to-door campaign in ward 55. Image: X/@mrlungisa

The ANC maintained that selecting candidates for public office was an organisational responsibility governed by its constitution, established guidelines and collective decision-making structures.



“The ANC believes that the judgement raises important legal questions regarding the interpretation and application of these internal rules, particularly the authority to enforce candidate eligibility requirements and uphold organisational discipline.

“These matters warrant further judicial consideration to ensure clarity on the constitutional relationship between political parties, their internal democratic processes and the courts,” ANC spokesperson Mahlengi Bhengu said.

World.title: Anglo-Boer War ammunition found in the Northern Cape
World.content:
DE AAR - Approximately 15 000 rounds of historic ammunition, with an estimated value of R7 million, has been found in De Aar.

The discovery was made by municipal workers who alerted authorities.

In a statement, the police said the ammunition was identified as .303 rounds, believed to date back to the Anglo-Boer War.

“A multi-disciplinary team comprising members of the Local Criminal Record Centre (LCRC), Explosives Unit, K9 Unit and Sunrise detectives was deployed to the scene.

“An enquiry was subsequently registered to facilitate further investigation into the discovery,” the statement read in part.

The surrounding area has since been declared safe, and investigations into the circumstances surrounding the discovery are ongoing.

“The public is reminded not to handle or tamper with any suspected ammunition or explosive materials, but to immediately report such discoveries to the police.”

World.content:
The three suspects were certified dead at the scene, while two AK-47 rifles, multiple rounds of ammunition and magazines were found inside their vehicle.

“The injured victims were transported to hospital for medical attention,” she said.

According to Nevhuhulwi, the shootout followed a crime intelligence operation in which law enforcement officers received information about a group using two vehicles allegedly planning to commit a robbery in Roodepoort.

READ | Alleged CIT robbers killed in shootout with KZN police

She said the white vehicle involved in a high-speed chase with police was spotted on Kliprivier Road.
