World.title: South Africa: Zuma Remains in Hospital as Conflicting Reports Emerge Over His Health
World.content:
Former South African president Jacob Zuma has remained at a private hospital in Pietermaritzburg. However, there have been conflicting accounts about his health following his admission.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party said Zuma had attended a routine medical check-up, a procedure he undergoes twice a year, and reassured supporters that he was "healthy and in good spirits".

According to News24, his brother Khanya said that Zuma was unwell and remained in hospital. He said the situation was concerning and that the family was praying for Zuma's recovery.

The 84-year-old former president is set to testify before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) cases inquiry in two weeks.

Zuma was president from 2009 to 2018.

He now leads the uMkhonto weSizwe Party. His hospitalisation comes as his party continues its campaign activities for the local government elections on 4 November.

World.title: Nigeria: American Lobbying Firms Disagree Over $57m U.S. Lawsuit Against Tinubu
World.content:
DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.

American lobbying firm DCI Group has rejected allegations made by Washington-based lobbyist Karl Von Batten in a $57 million lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, former aviation minister Femi Fani-Kayode and the firm.

DCI has been hired by the Nigerian government for lobbying activities in the United States, while Mr Von Batten is doing the same work for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office also told PREMIUM TIMES that he had not been formally served with the court papers and maintained his earlier denial of the allegations.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The case, filed at the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on 28 September, concerns allegations of defamation and a conspiracy to kidnap and physically harm Mr Von Batten. The claims are disputed and have not been established by a court.

DCI, Fani-Kayode respond

In an email to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Craig Stevens of DCI Group dismissed the allegations.

"Mr. Von Batten's allegations are so far past unfounded that they reach the point of the absurd," Mr Stevens said.

He said DCI's work for the Nigerian government focused on strengthening relations between Nigeria and US policymakers and referred the newspaper to the firm's disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr Stevens did not address the specific allegations individually.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office, responding separately, answered "No" when asked whether the former minister had been formally served. It also confirmed that he stood by his earlier denial of the allegations.

Mr Fani-Kayode had previously indicated that he would pursue a $100 million counterclaim against Mr Von Batten.

Asked whether the counterclaim had been filed or lawyers instructed to commence proceedings, his office replied: "All in good time."

The response did not confirm any filing.

What the lawsuit alleges

The US federal court docket identifies the case as Von Batten v. Tinubu et al., No. 1:26-cv-03374, before Judge Randolph D. Moss.

The defendants include President Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, Mr Fani-Kayode, DCI Group AZ, LLC, and 10 unidentified persons.

In a public announcement, Von Batten-Montague-York said it was seeking $36 million jointly from President Tinubu and the Nigerian government, $3 million from Mr Fani-Kayode and $18 million from DCI.

The firm alleged that the defendants were involved in efforts to defame, kidnap or physically harm Mr Von Batten over his advocacy concerning US government records relating to President Tinubu.

Close 

The publicly accessible docket records the filing and issuance of summonses, although this does not establish that the defendants have been formally served.

PREMIUM TIMES has requested the complete file-stamped complaint and exhibits to examine the allegations and the damages sought.

Presidency, others yet to respond

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Presidency through Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, seeking its response to the allegations, confirmation of any formal service and its position on the court's jurisdiction.

The enquiries were sent by email and WhatsApp, followed by telephone contact and reminders.

The newspaper also contacted Mr Atiku's ADC campaign to establish whether the former vice president or his representatives knew about the lawsuit before it was filed and whether they endorsed its allegations.

The campaign was further asked about the status of Mr Atiku's $1.2 million lobbying agreement with Mr Von Batten's firm, payments made and their source.

Mr Von Batten was separately contacted for the full complaint, supporting documents and his response to the denials by DCI and Mr Fani-Kayode. PREMIUM TIMES also sought clarification on the alleged threats, the damages claimed and whether the incidents had been reported to US law-enforcement authorities.

During a telephone call to his firm's office on Thursday, an answering-service representative took the reporter's contact details and said the enquiry would be forwarded.

By the time this report was filed, the Presidency, the ADC campaign and Mr Von Batten had not provided substantive responses.

World.title: Kenya: U.S. Report Flags Kenya's Failure to Act On Officials Linked to Human Trafficking
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report said Kenyan authorities investigated three Ministry of Labour officials suspected of accepting bribes to facilitate potential trafficking involving migrant workers travelling to the Middle East, but highlighted broader concerns over alleged collusion between public officials and recruitment networks.

The report also found that the government had not reported action against recruitment agencies allegedly owned by government employees and suspected of facilitating trafficking, with authorities frequently pursuing lesser offences such as failure to register recruitment companies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action during the year," the report stated.

The findings raise questions about accountability within institutions responsible for regulating overseas recruitment and protecting Kenyans seeking employment abroad.

Media reports cited in the assessment indicated that more than 10 per cent of Kenyan government officials held ownership interests in private employment agencies, including firms recruiting migrant workers for jobs overseas, creating potential conflicts of interest.

Observers also alleged that criminal syndicates colluded with law enforcement and immigration departments at border checkpoints and airports to transport trafficking victims into and within Kenya.

The report further cited allegations that some Kenyan embassy officials in Saudi Arabia demanded sex or cash payments from women seeking government assistance to escape abusive employers and return home.

The allegations come against the backdrop of declining anti-trafficking prosecutions and convictions.

Kenya convicted six traffickers in 2025, down from 21 in 2024, while prosecutions fell from 44 cases to 14.

The government investigated 43 trafficking cases during the year, compared with 42 in 2024.

The report also detailed allegations involving the fraudulent recruitment of more than 1,000 Kenyan men to fight for the Russian military in the war against Ukraine, with officials reporting that Kenyan and Russian officials had colluded with illicit recruiters to facilitate the recruitment.

Despite the concerns, Kenya remained on Tier 2 in the US assessment, which recognises significant efforts to combat trafficking while finding that the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating the crime.

Close 

The report credited Kenya with identifying more victims, repatriating citizens exploited in overseas online scam operations, and securing its first civil judgment against a fraudulent recruiter.

However, it said persistent concerns over official complicity continued to hamper law enforcement and victim identification, while protection services for adult survivors remained limited.

World.title: South Africa: Navi Pillay's Nobel Win Draws Attention To Her Work Defending Media Freedom And Beyond
World.content:
Navi Pillay speaking at the South African National EditorsÂ Forum (SANEF) Nat Nakasa Award for Courageous Journalism in 2022.

Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights — including the right to report freely and safely.

Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Friday, 9 October, is drawing attention to her support for media freedom and a career spanning some of the most consequential developments in international human rights law.

The South African jurist has backed initiatives to strengthen legal protections for free expression and promote a free and pluralistic information space.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Pillay is the fifth South African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, following Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk.

Announcing the Nobel, Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes linked Pillay’s early legal work under apartheid to her later role in international justice, from defending Nelson Mandela and others who opposed apartheid to serving as a judge in major international cases.

The committee said she had helped strengthen the international legal order and institutions responsible for holding perpetrators of serious crimes accountable. It also highlighted the uneven application of international law and the ability of powerful states and leaders to evade responsibility.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence," the committee said.

Pillay’s win is particularly being celebrated by the media fraternity in Africa, most of whom are citing her efforts in defending media freedom.

Reacting to the announcement, Moky Makura, executive director of Africa No Filter said Pillay “embodies African agency”.

“For decades, she has worked tirelessly to create the change she wants to see in the world. This Nobel Prize shines a well-deserved spotlight on her extraordinary contribution. It is a reminder that African progress is not always about what is happening, but also about what the world is failing to see,” Makura said.

Churchill Otieno, president of The African Editors Forum (TAEF), also said Pillay’s record held particular significance for journalists because of its emphasis on accountability and the right to report freely.

“From her struggle against apartheid to her work in international human rights and law, she has shown that peace cannot endure without accountability,” Otieno said.

“For us journalists and media workers, her record also speaks directly to the right to report freely and safely. As UN High Commissioner, she called for journalists to be protected from political interference and physical threats. Her recognition affirms that defending human dignity, press freedom and the rule of law takes courage, especially when powerful interests resist scrutiny.”

In February 2025, Pillay delivered the keynote address at the launch of South Africa’s Free Expression Legal Network in Johannesburg. Developed by the South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF), the Press Council, the Campaign for Free Expression and other organisations and legal experts, the network connects journalists and others facing legal threats over their expression with support, including legal representation.

Information and digital rights activist Izak Minnaar notes that Pillay had actively supported the network and advanced media freedom initiatives internationally.

“As the only South African on the global Information and Democracy Commission, she has been spearheading initiatives to support media freedom in South Africa and beyond,” Minnaar explained.

Anton Harber, director of the Henry Nxumalo Foundation, said Pillay had been particularly consistent in defending independent journalism.

“Navi Pillay has stood firm on many human rights issues, but has had particularly clear, strong and consistent views in defence of media freedom and the importance of independent journalism.”

“Whenever called upon to defend the media, she has been quick to stand up and be counted, even when it was not an easy thing to do. Her prize will be celebrated by journalists,” Harber added.

At the network’s launch, Pillay stressed the value of collective action. “If you clap with a single hand, nobody yells for you. But if a lot of people form a network clap, they will be heard,” she said, according to SANEF.

In its statement congratulating her, SANEF recalled Pillay’s call for governments to promote a free press that can “combat disinformation, build public trust and advance the promotion and protection of human rights.”

She also emphasised the need to protect those who help journalists expose wrongdoing. “I would say that such action must also protect media sources and whistle-blowers,” she said, according to SANEF.

Pillay served on the International Commission on Information and Democracy, convened by Reporters Without Borders in 2018. The 25-member commission developed principles for protecting freedom of expression and democratic debate in the global information space. Its declaration described information and communication as a common good and called for freedom, pluralism and reliable information.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award recognised Pillay’s contributions to peace and human dignity in South Africa and internationally.

“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place,” Ramaphosa said.

Mameltwe Sebei, president of the General Industries Workers Union of South Africa (Giwusa) and an attorney at Lawyers for Human Rights, described the Nobel as recognition of Pillay’s legal career serving oppressed and marginalised people.

Her work defending anti-apartheid activists and involvement in international cases concerning atrocities, including the Rwanda genocide and the occupied Palestinian territory, made the award a source of pride for South Africans, he said.

“Most importantly, this should affirm our commitment to the principles of justice that underpin the work of any lawyer who stands on the side of the oppressed,” Sebei said. “She represents that type of jurist, that type of lawyer, and this Nobel Peace Prize is a well-deserved recognition of that.”

South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on International Relations and Cooperation also described the award as a source of national pride, citing Pillay’s contribution to international justice and accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

Na’eem Jeenah, Senior Researcher at Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection (MISTRA) and political analyst said the award carries significance beyond South Africa.

“This then is an honour not only for South Africa but for the whole of Africa, a continent that is battling with its own conflicts and violations of international law,” Jeenah said.

While he believes the Nobel Prize would not change conditions for Palestinians nor stop the violence in Gaza, it “adds to the body of moral and legal evidence against Israel, including several UN reports (including on genocide), and the ICJ genocide case”.

Born on 23 September 1941 in Clairwood, Durban, to a family of Indian Tamil descent, Pillay grew up under apartheid. She graduated from the University of Natal with a bachelor’s degree in 1963 and an LLB in 1965.

In 1967, she became the first Black woman to open her own law practice in Natal, now KwaZulu-Natal. She represented political detainees and exposed abuses including torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she successfully challenged restrictions preventing political prisoners from accessing legal counsel, according to South African History Online.

After earning postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, she became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in Natal in 1995. She also participated in the Women’s National Coalition during the country’s constitutional transition and co-founded Equality Now, an organisation campaigning for the rights of women and girls.

In 1995, Pillay joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. She became its president in 1999, serving until 2003.

A landmark case during her time on the tribunal was the trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former local official convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part.

Pillay later served in the International Criminal Court’s Appeals Division from 2003 to 2008. She became United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, serving until 2014, a period that included the Arab Spring uprisings and the Syrian civil war.

Close 

Her later work included international proceedings and investigations into alleged serious crimes. In December 2019, she was appointed an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over alleged genocide against the Rohingya minority. The court confirmed its jurisdiction and ruled the application admissible.

From 2021 to 2025, Pillay chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.

In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected the conclusion. The finding was made by a UN commission of inquiry, not a final judgment by an international court.

The commission’s work highlighted a central challenge for international law: translating findings of serious violations into consequences for those responsible, particularly when powerful states are involved.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said the award underscored the importance of international law at a time when its institutions face growing pressure.

“Throughout her long career, Navi Pillay has set a high moral example, speaking out and standing up for justice, accountability and the rule of law,” said SIPRI director Karim Haggag.

Haggag said the award also recognised the institutions Pillay had served, warning that powerful states were increasingly resorting to power politics and transactionalism while international law and its institutions faced attack.

South African investigative organisation Open Secrets also welcomed the award, saying it affirmed the importance of international law and its promise of holding human rights abusers to account.

Pillay was a panellist at the first People’s Tribunal on Economic Crime in the arms trade, convened by Open Secrets and civil society partners in 2018. The tribunal sought accountability for arms companies and politicians in the aftermath of apartheid and State Capture.

The announcement also prompted a lighter moment. Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay joked with supporters, “If you clap a little bit louder, I may share this prize with Trump,” according to an amateur social media clip.

World.title: Liberia: 'Stop Following America' - Sirleaf Urges Liberians
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has urged Liberia to reduce its dependence on the United States for policy direction and embrace homegrown solutions that reflect the country's development priorities and national interests.

Sirleaf said Liberia must break away from longstanding patterns of dependency and take greater responsibility for shaping its future through policies, institutions and development strategies suited to its own circumstances.

"We have to stop following the United States of America. Let's join the new era of sovereignty, respectability," the former president declared.



Her remarks signal a call for greater national ownership of Liberia's development agenda, particularly in a changing global environment where countries are increasingly reassessing their political and economic relationships.

Sirleaf made the statement during a brief interview with journalists on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, following her participation in a one-day symposium organized by the Governance Commission on 3rd Street in Monrovia.

The symposium, held as part of activities marking Good Governance Month, was organized under the theme, "Promoting Good Governance Through Accountability and Transparency in Liberia."

The observance was established by presidential proclamation in keeping with the Governance Commission's founding Act of October 9, 2007.

Speaking to journalists, Sirleaf emphasized the need for Liberia to rethink traditional approaches to governance and development, arguing that the country must adapt to changing global realities rather than continue relying on policies and systems developed elsewhere.

Her comments come against the backdrop of Liberia's longstanding diplomatic, historical and development relationship with the United States, a partnership that remained particularly strong during her 12-year presidency.

Sirleaf, who served from January 2006 to January 2018, became Africa's first elected female head of state after defeating George Manneh Weah in Liberia's 2005 presidential runoff election.

Her administration inherited a country devastated by years of civil conflict and prioritized post-war reconstruction, international debt relief, infrastructure development, institutional reforms and the restoration of Liberia's international standing.

During her presidency, the United States remained one of Liberia's major development and diplomatic partners, providing substantial assistance in governance, economic recovery, health, education and security-sector reform.

Sirleaf also maintained close relationships with successive American administrations.

In March 2006, shortly after assuming office, she addressed a joint session of the United States Congress, highlighting Liberia's recovery efforts and appealing for continued international support.

Then-U.S. President George W. Bush visited Liberia in February 2008, while his successor, Barack Obama, hosted Sirleaf at the White House in 2010 and 2015.

The relationship became particularly significant during the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic, when the United States provided major emergency assistance to Liberia, including medical personnel, logistical support and resources to help contain the outbreak.

Her administration also secured substantial international debt relief and development assistance as part of efforts to rebuild Liberia's economy and strengthen public institutions.

Against this historical background, Sirleaf's latest remarks represent a notable emphasis on national self-reliance by a former president whose administration benefited significantly from close American cooperation.

However, her statement did not explicitly call for Liberia to abandon its diplomatic relationship with Washington or reject international partnerships.

Close 

Rather, her comments focused on the need for Liberia to exercise greater independence in determining its national priorities and developing solutions to its governance and economic challenges.

The former president did not outline specific policy changes or identify particular American-supported programs that Liberia should reconsider.

Nevertheless, her remarks raise broader questions about how Liberia can balance its longstanding relationship with the United States against the need to strengthen domestic institutions, promote economic self-reliance and exercise greater control over its development agenda.

For a country whose reconstruction and development efforts have depended heavily on international assistance, Sirleaf's message places renewed attention on the distinction between maintaining strategic partnerships and relying on external powers to shape national policy.

Her central argument is that Liberia must increasingly take ownership of its future while engaging international partners on terms that reflect its own priorities and interests.

World.title: West Africa: Russia-Ukraine Conflict Finds New Battleground in Africa's Sahel
World.content:
Ukraine has vowed to counter Russia wherever it can, even "in the scorching sands" of the Sahelian desert, as evidence mounts that Kyiv is backing Tuareg separatists battling Mali's army and its Russian allies.

Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso -- all led by military juntas that have turned their backs on former colonial ruler France and moved closer to Russia -- have reacted by severing diplomatic relations with Kyiv.

They accuse Ukraine of supplying weapons to the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) -- a predominantly Tuareg armed separatist group loosely allied to Al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"In Africa and the Sahel, (Ukraine) is providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop alleged at the United Nations in September.

Niger's Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine singled out France and Ukraine, alleging they were directing "proxies" along his country's northeastern borders to attack military positions and oil facilities.

Ukraine's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment on the allegations.

The accusations followed posts on X by Kyrylo Budanov -- a former Ukrainian intelligence chief who became President Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff in January -- in which he hinted at the presence of Ukrainian agents in Africa's Sahel region.

"From Russia to Africa... the Main Intelligence Directorate protects Ukrainian interests across the globe by all means... in the scorching sands of deserts and the freezing snows of Antarctica," Budanov wrote on September 7.

The post was accompanied by a photo showing four white men, their faces blurred, alongside armed, turbaned men in pickup trucks in a desert.

Five days later, a CNN report said Ukrainian military intelligence officers had confirmed that drone operators in the Sahel had provided training and support to the FLA.

- Training -

Armed groups are increasingly using low-cost, remotely piloted technologies for reconnaissance and strikes -- tactics possibly inspired by the war in Ukraine.

Details of what the Ukrainians are doing in sub-Saharan Africa are disputed.

A source within the FLA told AFP the Malian separatists "maintain contact with the Ukrainians".

But the source stressed: "All the fighting over the past few months has been carried out by the FLA and JNIM."

He denied Kyiv had provided logistical, material or intelligence support and dismissed Budanov's photos as "just Ukrainian propaganda".

Kyiv had provided some instruction, though, he said.

In 2023, "three or four Ukrainians" travelled to northern Mali to train some FLA fighters and several combatants underwent "an intensive 30-day course in Ukraine on the use of FPV (first-person view) drones", he said.

The training course in northern Mali "took place near the Mauritanian border", a second source within the FLA said, adding the photos posted by Budanov were "either from that time or were taken in Syria".

- Mauritania -

A diplomat based in the region, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the Ukrainians had "a definite presence in northern Mali, where they move about and collaborate with Tuareg rebels".

They said the border with Mauritania was the main crossing point for exchanges between the Ukrainians and the FLA and the drones used by the separatists came from Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that Kyiv opened an embassy in Nouakchott in 2024, given that Mauritania serves as a rear base for FLA leaders," the diplomat said.

Close 

The diplomat said the FLA systematically denied or underplayed reports of Ukrainian assistance to avoid creating problems for Mauritanian authorities.

In November, a study by US think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace indicated that Kyiv had been supplying drones to the separatists since early 2024.

In July of that year, Ukrainian military intelligence official Andriy Yusov hinted that Kyiv had provided information to FLA and JNIM fighters, who carried out an attack in northern Mali which killed dozens of Russian mercenaries and Malian soldiers.

In recent years, Ukraine has opened several embassies across Africa as it seeks to boost its influence in a continent where Russia has a significant presence.

In March Ukraine laid out its first strategy for extending its reach in Africa and in August Zelensky asked his ambassadors to pay close attention to certain African regions, including the Sahel.

World.title: South Africa: South Africa-Born Navanethem "Navi" Pillay Wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
press release

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.

This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.



In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time.

The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the peace prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War.

However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim.

Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world.

At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity.

And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence.

In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice.

History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench.

Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda.

Close 

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form.

Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.

World.title: Liberal hot spot residents can’t agree on what socialism means as far-left movements gains steam
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans can't seem to get on the same page when it comes to what defines socialism even though new polling shows the movement's favorability is at an all-time high.

Whether far-left factions are able to rally around the label could come down to understand its principles.

Fox News Digital took to the streets of a Maryland liberal hotspot, Takoma Park, for its annual street festival to talk with attendees about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals.

"The fact is that there's no…one answer," Nina Gilden Seavey said when asked to define socialism.

"Just the idea of like, you've been paying all these things to set up these programs and then you're actually giving them to the people," Jaw Blake said describing his view of the political movement. "It's not a special group that gets to have them, it's just available."

LIBERAL HAVEN FESTIVAL-GOERS WEIGH GOVERNMENT SEIZURE OF THEIR HOMES: 'I'D BE SO GAME'

Jenny Sniderman had a more direct answer, claiming that "public libraries, the police department, the fire department, all our public services, utilities," are all part of what makes up socialism.

A September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans have a positive image of socialism — the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010.

But the survey asks respondents their image of socialism without providing a definition of the ideology or asking whether they would actually support adopting it in the U.S.

The same festival-goers were pressed on socialism as an economic system, questioning their favorability of collective ownership. They shared some skepticism when Fox News Digital asked whether they would personally surrender their private property to government or collective control.

"Do I want to give up my private property? Of course I don't want to give up my private property," Sniderman said. "Are they going to reimburse me fairly? That would be helpful in making my choice."

"I don't know that I would necessarily love it," Blake said. "But I mean, if it was something that was beneficial, I'd at least consider it."

DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

"Nobody wants what they have to be taken away from them," he continued. "But there is something to be said about…you can set up things so that they're available for everybody."

"I think the government is not the greatest steward…of assets," Seavey said. "It's not to say that capitalism is somehow without flaw, but the fact is that there is an idealism that can come from thinking, 'Oh, if we had some more centrality, if…there was some kind of uber organization in charge of reallocation.'"

Documentary filmmaker and self-described historian Seavey also questioned the idea of government control over private assets, but argued that the growing democratic socialist movement in the U.S. should not be confused with traditional socialism.

"This is not socialism. This is democratic socialism. It's different. There's socialism, there's communism, there are all kinds of 'isms.' Democratic socialism is essentially what we have a growing movement in this country," Seavey said.

"Socialism is where there is a massive redistribution of wealth. We are not having redistribution of wealth in this country."

But the Democratic Socialists of America, the largest socialist organization in the U.S., advocates redistributing wealth from wealthy individuals and corporations to workers and lower-income Americans. The DSA also calls for public stake in major corporations and essential industries rather than private ownership.

THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM

The differing interpretations among festival-goers reflect a broader debate over what socialism means in America — one that has taken on new political significance as socialist candidates gain ground within the Democratic Party heading into midterm elections.

In a 2018 survey asking Americans to define socialism in their own words, just 17% described it in terms of government ownership or control of businesses or the means of production. Another 23% associated it with equality, while 10% pointed to social benefits and services. Nearly a quarter could not provide an answer.

Seavey argued that political labels themselves have distorted the conversation.

"Let's think about it differently and let's take away these ridiculous stigmas that have to do with these crazy labels that we have allowed the right wing to foment onto the rest of America," Seavey said.

But as socialist-aligned candidates compete for office, the growing movement raises a question that favorable polling alone cannot answer: whether voters are embracing its promises on affordability and equality, or also support its broader proposals for economic ownership and control.

President Donald Trump returned to his home state of New York on Friday night, showcasing America's "New Golden Age" and promising to help Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman flip the Empire State red as the GOP makes its final push toward November's midterm elections.

Trump rallied supporters in Syracuse with a sweeping celebration of his administration's economic and immigration agenda, pledging to help New Yorkers secure lower taxes, cheaper energy and safer streets by electing Republicans up and down the ballot.

"We're in the Golden Age of America," Trump told the crowd, urging supporters to deliver the same enthusiasm that powered his presidential campaigns.

TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG

"Please pretend I'm on the freaking ballot," Trump urged. "And in a really, in a certain way, I am on the ballot because they can take away everything that we, that we got."

The president took Blakeman's challenge to Democrat Gov. Kathy Hochul as the centerpiece of the rally, promising direct support from Washington if elected.

"[Blakeman will] save this state. He'll turn the state around and I'll help him from the White House," Trump said. "I'll be helping him for governor."

Trump blasted Hochul over New York's taxes, utility bills and public safety, arguing that Blakeman could unleash the state's economic potential by embracing domestic energy production and cutting costs for families.

DEBRA MESSING SAYS COST OF LIVING, SUBWAY VIOLENCE PUSHED HER TO BACK TRUMP-ENDORSED REPUBLICAN

The president also hailed his administration's economic agenda as proof of what Trump described as a remarkable national turnaround.

He singled out Micron's planned $100 billion semiconductor complex in central New York, a project the company says is expected to generate 50,000 jobs across the state, including 9,000 directly with Micron.

"This will soon be the home to the largest semiconductor manufacturing facility ever built in the Western Hemisphere," Trump said.

Blakeman joined Trump onstage and echoed the president's message of a Republican resurgence, promising to cut taxes and utility bills, focus on public safety and make New York more attractive to both businesses and families.

"We have to create good jobs, good benefits to keep our young people here," Blakeman said. "We gotta look at business not as the enemy, but as a partner."

Trump also threw his support behind Republican congressional candidates Kailee Buller, who is challenging Democrat Rep. John Mannion in New York's 22nd District, and Anthony Constantino, who is running for the state's open 21st District seat, pledging to help Republicans compete for both seats.

The rally also notably featured a brief but memorable on-stage appearance by legendary former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson, whom Trump invited up before the crowd.

"I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump," Tyson said. "And, there's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump. Thank you. Thank you very much."

Trump responded with a laugh, recalling Tyson's notorious reputation.

"I don't want to fight him," Trump joked, before complimenting the former champion. "You look good. Mike. What the h— are you doing?"

"We're going to elect a Republican House and Republican Senate," Trump said.

World.title: Gov Kathy Hochul signs New York onto Trump's school choice program despite teachers union opposition
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Friday signed on to join President Donald Trump’s school choice program despite opposition from teachers unions.

"Every parent wants their child to have a great education and the best possible chance to succeed. That’s what guides my decisions as governor," Hochul announced Friday.

"New York’s public schools are the backbone of communities across this state," she added. "That’s why I’ve made historic investments in public education, increasing school funding by more than $10 billion and fully funding Foundation Aid for the first time."

GOV HOCHUL'S PLAN TO OPT NEW YORK INTO FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DRAWS UNION OPPOSITION

Despite Hochul's stated intention to participate, major labor groups and teachers unions remain staunchly opposed. A coalition of teachers unions and other public school advocates launched a petition demanding that Hochul reject the program.

"Gov. Hochul plans to opt New York in starting in 2027. But most New Yorkers haven’t even heard of this program or know how it will affect New York," the petition states. "Tax dollars would help pay private tuition for families who never used public schools."

Sydney Altfield, Scholarships for All founder and Teach Coalition CEO, told Fox News Digital, "This is a tremendous day for New Yorkers. Millions of children across our state will now have access to scholarships that can help pay for tutoring, after-school programs and other educational needs.

"Gov. Hochul has kept her promise to New York families, helping put money back into the pockets of hardworking parents while expanding educational opportunities for children across the state."

PRO-TRUMP GROUP LEADS NEW COALITION TO UNDERCUT TEACHERS UNIONS

Hochul’s announcement came after the Department of the Treasury and the IRS issued proposed regulations Oct. 1 to implement the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit (FSTC) program, paving the way for America's first nationwide school choice framework.

The initiative, also referred to as the Education Freedom Tax Credit, allows individual taxpayers to receive up to a $1,700 dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit for donations made to non-profit scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs). However, state governors must formally opt into the program for their residents and local educational organizations to participate and receive the funds.

The IRS recently reported that more than half of U.S. states have already signed up to participate. Burke noted that "competitive pressure" will ultimately force blue states to capture the influx of private donations.

Education Secretary Linda McMahon previously noted that some Democratic leaders have resisted the federal scholarship program simply because "it’s a Trump measure."

Democratic governors who have traditionally opposed school choice initiatives will face mounting competitive pressure to join Trump's program as states weigh whether to participate and Hochul moves to formally opt in, a top Department of Education official told Fox News Digital.

Kentucky has since formally joined the federal program after the state legislature overrode Gov. Andy Beshear's veto of opt-in legislation.

Unlike traditional voucher programs that draw directly from municipal or state public education funds, tax credit scholarships allow taxpayers to redirect a portion of their federal tax liability toward non-profit funding for student scholarships. The federal framework leaves the opt-in decision to state governors, enabling local families to access federally incentivized scholarship dollars.

"I’ve been clear from the start that New York would participate in the federal scholarship tax credit program if, and only if, all schools and students, including those in our public schools, could benefit," Hochul said.

"After a careful review of the federal regulations, we believe this program has the potential to bring millions of additional dollars to New York students and families without taking a single dollar from public schools or our state or local budgets.

"I’m not going to leave money on the table when it could help our kids," she added. "That’s why I have also been directly engaging with business leaders who have committed to use this program to support public school students and their academic needs.

"I look forward to working with education leaders across the state to make sure these resources reach students in every community. My commitment to public education has not changed, and it never will."

MORE THAN 400K NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT

For decades, school choice initiatives have remained a third-rail issue for many Democrats, who contend that choice models weaken public school systems and undermine labor unions.

However, growing parent demand for alternative education options — including charter schools, private schooling and homeschooling after the COVID-19 pandemic — has pushed several prominent Democrats to reevaluate their positions.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump's landmark school choice program comes as major blue city school districts struggle to retain students since the coronavirus pandemic.

Nope.

Just him, Ditka, and a room full of cigar smoke.
