World.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on Gulf Coast
World.content:
Update: Isaias is continuing north across the Southeastern U.S. after being downgrade from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone. See the latest here, and our earlier story is below.

Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall Friday night along the northern Gulf Coast, bringing drenching rains, powerful winds and the risk of life-threatening flash flooding and storm surges to a large swath of the Southeast.

The center of Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, at around 8 p.m. Eastern Time, according to the Miami-based National Hurricane Center. It made landfall as a Category 2 storm, but quickly weakened into a Category 1.

President Trump late Friday night told reporters that White House officials were tracking the hurricane "very closely."

Isaias had earlier in the day briefly strengthened into a Category 3 storm, which is defined as a major hurricane. Tens of thousands of people have evacuated the region, officials said. More than 697,000 customers were without power across Florida, Alabama, and Georgia, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us.

Maps show hurricane's path

Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 90 miles per hour as of Friday night, according to forecasters, and life-threatening storm surge was likely along the Florida Panhandle and Alabama coasts.

The core of Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," was about 45 miles northeast of Pensacola, Florida, heading north at 20 mph late Friday night, the NHC said. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles from the storm's center, and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 160 miles.

The map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center warned "dangerous and damaging hurricane force-winds" were expected across the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, where residents who had not evacuated were advised to have a safe room to ride out the storm and prepare for the possibility of long-term power outages.

The center of the storm was forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday.

It was expected to weaken to a post-tropical storm Saturday as it moves inland, but will still produce gusty winds. The central U.S. Gulf Coast and much of the Southeast is likely to see heavy rainfall through the weekend, with flash flooding possible.

Watches and warnings in effect

A hurricane warning is in effect from the Mississippi/Alabama border to the Bay/Gulf County Line in Florida. A tropical storm warning was in place from east of the Bay/Gulf County Line to the Aucilla River in Florida.

A storm surge warning was in place from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to the mouth of the Suwannee River in Florida.

Map shows watches and warnings as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast. CBS News

The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded, forecasters warned, with heights of up to 9 feet from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, Florida. Other parts of the Florida Panhandle could see storm surge up to 6 feet.

Hurricane-force winds are expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles from the coast into southern Alabama, forecasters said.

A wind gust of 112 mph was measured at Santa Rosa Sound, Florida, according to the hurricane center. Other areas of the Southeast that were also expected to see "damaging wind gusts" included northern Georgia, the southern Appalachians and southern Middle Tennessee.

Map shows the storm forecast as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 4 to 8 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast, from southern Alabama to the Florida Panhandle, Florida's Big Bend and southwest Georgia.

Two to 5 inches of rain are expected across much of the rest of the Southeast, with up to 10 inches possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

Map shows the 3-day rain forecast for the Gulf Coast and Southeast from Hurricane Isaias. CBS News

There is also a risk of tornadoes spinning off from the storm beginning Friday and continuing through Saturday, forecasters said. The tornado threat on Saturday will extend to areas of Georgia and the Carolinas.

Florida, Georgia and Alabama declare states of emergency

"Folks who are in the path of this storm should know, this is not a random tropical system," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference Friday. "It's a major hurricane. And it's going to potentially do a lot of damage."

Evacuations were ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which are both in the Panhandle. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey has told tourists and visitors in the state's coastal areas to leave immediately.

Ivey's evacuation order "requires all non-residents, tourists and visitors in Baldwin County south of the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, including Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, and on Dauphin Island in Mobile County, to evacuate immediately," a news release said.

DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in Florida, and Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties in Alabama. Government buildings closed in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.

The Trump administration approved federal emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama.

In Orange Beach, Alabama, streets and beaches were empty during what was supposed to be a busy weekend for tourists. The gridlock on area roadways caused by fleeing residents over the past 48 hours was gone, and the evacuation window had closed, officials said, because winds were too strong.

The few residents left were trying to make the best of it. Christi Woods manages a wine store in Orange Beach, one of the only businesses that was still open Friday.

"We do take precautions, I mean, we're kind of in the flood zone," Woods said.

Three shelters were open as of Friday morning at schools in Mobile County, Alabama. At least four churches in Dothan, Alabama, are being offered as shelters Friday, and they're also providing snacks and drinks.

Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community is whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

DeSantis warned Friday of significant storm surge and likely wind damage that could put "a lot of people's lives in jeopardy if they haven't heeded evacuation orders." He said storm surge "does the most significant damage from these storms."

"Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that," he said, adding: "And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water's rising and things are happening, it's a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that."

The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday, Oct. 7, marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: Blanche, other DOJ appointees can take part in political campaigns, memo says
World.content:
The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.

A memo sent this week by Assistant Attorney General Jolene Ann Laurie relaxes ethics restrictions on Senate-confirmed presidential appointees such that they can speak at rallies, canvass for votes and even serve as delegates or officers of a national political party as long as those activities are conducted in their personal capacities.

The guidance applies to the attorney general, the deputy attorney general, assistant attorneys general, the FBI director, U.S. attorneys and others.

Former Attorney General Pam Bondi had loosened the regulations somewhat during her tenure by allowing political appointees to attend rallies and fundraisers. The new memo goes a step further.

It specifically states that presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Justice Department employees are exempt from the more stringent guidelines imposed on some other DOJ employees, such as administrative law judges and those in the Criminal Division.

Attorney General Todd Blanche addressed the Republican midterm convention in September and attended a rally for a North Carolina Republican Senate candidate, drawing criticism that he violated long-standing Justice Department norms intended to keep politics independent from the law.

"I am not in any way violating any rule or law," Blanche said about his appearances at these events, adding they were done in his personal capacity.

These moves come after the Biden-era Justice Department clamped down on appointees' political activities.

"Non-career appointees may not attend any partisan political events, even in their personal capacities," a 2024 memo said, continuing a policy instituted two years earlier.

The 2024 memo also said that appointees should "avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable."

PBS News was first to report on the new guidelines.

World.title: Pentagon's plan to livestream execution sparks backlash
World.content:
Washington — The revelation that the Pentagon plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has sparked intense pushback, with one Republican senator calling it "disgusting" and critics warning it could inspire more acts of terrorism.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed CBS News' reporting that the Dec. 3 execution will be livestreamed. Hegseth told Real America's Voice the execution would be public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth recommended, and President Trump approved, a plan to use an Army firing squad.

"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," Mr. Trump said during an unrelated White House event on Friday.

In an interview Friday night in Syracuse, New York, with WSTM-TV, President Trump said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, "but I understand that decision."

"I guess they want to have it serve as an example, and I understand that very well," the president added.

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, called the decision "beyond disgusting." Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth, but is now expressing his regret in doing so.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."

Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia wrote on X, "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."

Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth to reconsider.

"Seneca warned that Rome's bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them," he said on X. "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider."

Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said publicly executing someone is "medieval."

"That's disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions?" Murphy said on CNN. "I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval. It's frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups. And the fact that the United States is doing it — I just learned this, that is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That's what America has become?"

Ned Price, who was the State Department's spokesman during the Biden administration, said a public and livestreamed execution will create more "radicalized zealots."

"You can take it from those of us who've spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause," Price wrote on X. "Or take it from AQ and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth's proposal. Either way, it's hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America's image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable."

Alonzo Lunsford, a former U.S. Army sergeant who was shot seven times during the Fort Hood shooting but survived, said he supports the gunman's execution by firing squad. But Lunsford said this execution is "not something you should view for entertainment purposes."

"To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief," he told BBC Radio.

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement Friday morning urging the Pentagon to reconsider.

"In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" the archbishop said, citing Romans 12:17. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

Conservative talk show host Erick Erickson, who supports the death penalty, also said a public, livestreamed execution of Hasan will give him the "platform for martyrdom he wants."

"Hasan is a paraplegic, confined to a wheelchair," Erickson wrote. "The public imagery of a firing squad killing a man sitting in a chair because he cannot stand is going to undermine support for the death penalty. A society that increasingly finds ways to sympathize with the villains will do so here. This also gives Nidal Hasan the platform for martyrdom he wants. They'll be passing out the livestream video in the Middle East to inspire more terrorists to shoot up Americans to celebrate the glory of the martyrdom of Nidal Hasan."

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News that the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."

"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said.

Corn said "turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."

Despite Lunsford's concerns about the livestream, the former U.S. Army sergeant said he'll be there for the execution.

"I'm going to be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude, you failed, I'm still here,'" he told the BBC.

The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place 90 years ago in 1936. That's when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky. The execution reportedly drew a crowd of about 20,000.

Hegseth's announcement comes amid efforts from Democrats and Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach him. A vote on his impeachment was delayed by House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to cancel votes a day early ahead of the midterms.

World.title: California high-speed rail consultants billed taxpayers for late-night rides
World.content:
Well after dark one night last September, a highly paid consultant for the California High-Speed Rail Authority expensed a Lyft ride that pulled up outside the agency CEO's home in Folsom, California.

Just before midnight, another highly paid consultant expensed a Lyft ride from the same house back to his Sacramento hotel.

The first was Denver attorney Brent Butzin, who CBS California has independently confirmed is the legal-services consultant referenced in the High-Speed Rail inspector general's recent investigation. The second was Thierry Prate, a managing director at KPMG, the financial adviser examined in the same report.

Both submitted the rides as expenses associated with California's multibillion-dollar high-speed rail project.

And it wasn't the only late-night ride from the High-Speed Rail CEO's home.

Why were taxpayers billed for late-night rides from the CEO's home?

After California's independent High-Speed Rail inspector general found widespread failures in consultant travel oversight, whistleblowers provided CBS California Investigates with some of the underlying expense records.

We reviewed nearly 6,000 pages of invoices and expense claims that KPMG and the law firm Nossaman submitted to the authority for work from September 2024 through January 2026.

Among the receipts from two consultants, Prate and Butzin, we found a dozen rides to or from the small residential street in Folsom where High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri owns a home.

Another dozen rides went to or from nearby Folsom restaurants and bars.

Many rides involved late-night or early-morning pickups, including two after 1 a.m.

The receipts don't establish who attended the gatherings, what business took place, or whether Choudri was present. His wife also works for KPMG.

But the receipts reveal previously undisclosed connections between consultants' travel expenses and the CEO's private residence.

And they raise questions about who authorized those rides.

What state business justified trips to and from the CEO's private residence and nearby restaurants, sometimes after midnight?

And what influence do these highly paid consultants have over the decisions driving the project's costs and schedule?

The questions come as California's high-speed rail project continues to spend billions, nearly two decades after voters approved a bullet train connecting San Francisco and Los Angeles.

The state has spent more than $15 billion, but still hasn't laid a mile of high-speed rail track. It recently lost $4 billion in federal funding after missing key deadlines, and its independent watchdog warns it could run out of money by the end of 2027.

Meanwhile, the authority said it is paying just four consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars over two fiscal years.

Sources inside the High-Speed Rail Authority say the inspector general's findings point to something much bigger than questionable travel expenses.

Who holds influence over this multibillion-dollar public project? Who makes the decisions? And who's accountable when those decisions cost taxpayers money?

CEO declines to answer questions about late-night rides

CBS California published its investigation hours before Friday's special board meeting to discuss the Inspector General's investigation. After the meeting, investigative correspondent Julie Watts asked High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri about the late-night rides from his home.

Choudri walked away without answering. The authority's head of communications told CBS California that Choudri would not answer questions and directed reporters to email questions to his office.

CBS California had previously submitted detailed written questions to his office asking about the expense records. The authority provided a general response outlining changes to travel oversight but did not directly answer questions about the rides.

In an email, the High-Speed Rail Authority said it is tightening travel oversight, updating reimbursement rules and requiring new training for consultants and contract managers before approving additional travel expenses.

"Only travel that is pre-approved, within contract scope and consistent with state regulations will be eligible for reimbursement," the Authority said.

In a response to CBS California, KPMG said it is reviewing the travel expenses and will reimburse the Authority as appropriate.

"KPMG takes seriously its obligations regarding the accurate submission of expenses and KPMG professionals are expected to be responsible stewards of client and firm resources, said Russ Grote, Managing Director of Corporate Affairs.

CBS California also sent detailed questions to High-Speed Rail CEO Ian Choudri, Denver attorney Brent Butzin and KPMG managing director Thierry Prate.

None of the three responded to requests for comment.

Although board members had reviewed the investigation, none publicly pressed Choudri about the late-night rides or the IG's report during the meeting.

When Watts asked the board chair why he hadn't questioned Choudri about the findings, he did not directly answer. But when asked whether the CEO should speak with California reporters representing taxpayers, the chair said, "Yes," adding, "I believe in communication."

The CEO wouldn't answer our questions. The board didn't ask them.

The receipts reveal why those questions matter, and one internal email connects a late-night ride directly to work with Choudri.

'Related to work with Ian'

When the High-Speed Rail Authority questioned KPMG, the firm described one of Prate's rides to the CEO's residence as "related to work with Ian."

On that evening, Prate's Lyft arrived at the Folsom home shortly after 7:30 p.m. His next documented ride departed the same address after 1 a.m.

A late-night business meeting isn't necessarily inappropriate. Neither is visiting an executive's home.

But the records don't explain what specific work required repeated rides to the CEO's residence, who was there or how the authority determined the transportation was an appropriate business expense.

Those details matter because California's travel rules require more than a receipt. They require a legitimate business purpose.

And the inspector general found that the High-Speed Rail Authority repeatedly failed to document whether consultant travel met that standard.

A pizza delivery. Another late-night ride.

Prate's receipts also document a food delivery to the same residence.

One January evening, shortly after 9:30 p.m., an Uber Eats driver delivered a $94.39 order from a Folsom pizza restaurant to Choudri's home, charged to Prate's KPMG corporate card

The High-Speed Rail Authority disputed the food delivery, and records show the consultant accepted the dispute. Taxpayers ultimately didn't pay for the pizza. They did pay for Prate's ride home.

The receipts also don't identify who ate the food or who was at the house. But they reinforce the central question about the travel expenses.

What state business justifies repeatedly charging the project for transportation to and from the CEO's private home?

The paperwork says Sacramento. The receipts show Folsom.

The CEO's home wasn't the only Folsom destination.

Other travel records show consultants frequently taking rides between their Sacramento hotels and restaurants and bars near the CEO's home, roughly 30 minutes away.

All of the destinations were in the same shopping center as the Land Ocean Steak House that the CEO frequents, according to multiple sources.

Some rides back to Sacramento began after midnight.

Butzin's expense paperwork reveals another apparent discrepancy.

Five travel forms described the purpose of his trips as "Meetings at CHSRA in Sacramento." But attached receipts document travel to restaurants and other locations in Folsom.

The forms didn't identify those destinations. Their business-entertainment sections were blank.

None of that establishes that the restaurant visits were personal, or that every expense required a separate entertainment disclosure.

But the paperwork doesn't explain why the consultants repeatedly traveled to Folsom while billing expenses associated with meetings in Sacramento.

The discrepancies also raise questions about what the High-Speed Rail Authority reviewed before approving the payment.

If the travel forms didn't identify where the consultants actually went, how did the state determine whether the expenses were legitimate?

The Washington connection

The receipts reveal another late-night destination, this time across the country.

In May 2025, Prate and Butzin both billed travel to Washington, D.C., during the High Speed Rail 2025 conference, where Choudri was scheduled to speak on May 14, according to the conference agenda.

Just before 1 a.m. that morning, Prate expensed the first of two Lyft rides totaling roughly $60 from Shelly's Back Room, a Washington cigar lounge, to the Mayflower Hotel and back to the cigar lounge just before 1:30 a.m.

The records don't indicate who else was there.

Butzin's records raise a different question.

He billed more than $1300 for a May 13-16 trip to "Attend USHSR Annual Conference and Meetings with CHSRA/Industry Suppliers." The records include no receipts.

"Learning the hard way"

The inspector general's report revealed how requests from the CEO's office influenced travel approvals.

When a contract manager reminded a Denver-based legal consultant that he needed to explain his trips and obtain advance written approval, the consultant pushed back.

We now know the consultant was Butzin.

According to the email excerpt in the inspector general's report, Butzin argued that justifying travel wasn't his responsibility when the CEO requested his presence.

Then came a perceived warning.

Butzin added that questioning the CEO's direction was inappropriate, "as other consultants in other Authority offices are learning the hard way."

The contract manager told investigators she was directed, primarily by the acting chief counsel, to approve travel expenses because the CEO had requested the trips.

The inspector general concluded that the CEO didn't have authority to override the state contract's travel requirements.

The report documents pressure surrounding travel approvals. It doesn't establish that anyone was fired or explicitly threatened with termination.

But sources inside the High-Speed Rail Authority say the concerns extend beyond consultant travel.

They describe a workplace where some consultants are perceived as having unusual influence because of their relationships with leadership, raising questions about whether employees feel empowered to challenge spending and other decisions.

The watchdog's findings provide documented examples of the tension between executive requests and the employees responsible for enforcing contract rules.

Expensive travel. Little advance scrutiny.

The inspector general's findings are especially significant when compared with Butzin's travel records.

The High-Speed Rail Authority also paid the Denver-based consultant approximately $86,500 in hourly travel pay, totaling over a quarter of a million dollars when combined with reimbursed expenses.

Separate receipts CBS California obtained document expensive flights and hotel stays, including one airfare of nearly $937 for a flight from Denver to Sacramento and one hotel night costing $587.

The expense records include airline tickets purchased shortly before departure. The inspector general found that Butzin frequently booked flights on the day of travel, creating a risk of higher costs.

Last-minute flights aren't necessarily wasteful. Executives sometimes schedule meetings with little notice, requiring consultants to travel on short notice.

But last-minute bookings can also cost significantly more.

The watchdog's findings raise a straightforward question.

If the authority didn't document why the travel was necessary or approve it in advance, how could it ensure taxpayers weren't paying more than they needed to?

Other emails show how quickly some executive-related requests were approved.

In one exchange, Prate told the authority that Choudri had requested that he accompany him on a trip beginning the following day.

The request went to High-Speed Rail's chief financial officer.

Approval came five minutes later.

That doesn't establish that the travel was unnecessary.

But it shows how directly a request invoking the CEO could influence the approval process.

A quarter of a billion dollars in consultant payments. Who's watching?

The High-Speed Rail Authority prepared a presentation to respond to the Inspector General's investigation at Friday's board meeting.

The original version, uploaded early in the week, emphasized how little it spent on travel compared with its total consultant payments. The pie chart further highlights the scale of consultant spending.

Over just two fiscal years, the Authority paid four consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars. Only about $2 million was for travel.

The inspector general reviewed roughly half of that and found more than half was unallowable under state rules or contract terms.

According to whistleblowers, this points to a much bigger concern:

If the authority couldn't enforce basic travel-spending rules, who is overseeing the rest of the quarter-billion dollars?

But that slide was missing from the presentation the authority ultimately gave the board.

The revised version no longer discloses the total payments to those contractors.

In an email, a spokesperson said, "The information was streamlined to keep the focus clear for the Board and the public.

What are taxpayers getting for the money?

Since Ian Choudri became CEO in 2024, California's high-speed rail project has fallen further behind, even as the authority pays four major consulting contractors more than a quarter of a billion dollars over two fiscal years.

And that money isn't for laying track.

These are consultants. They're paid to provide legal advice, financial guidance, program management and engineering design. Their work helps shape the decisions about what gets built, how it gets built and what taxpayers will pay.

California created its High-Speed Rail Authority 30 years ago, in 1996. Nearly two decades have passed since voters approved billions in funding for a bullet train connecting San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Yet the state still hasn't laid a mile of high-speed rail track.

Meanwhile, a CBS California investigation found the High-Speed Rail Authority, under Choudri, repeatedly missed its own deadlines to purchase trains. Federal officials cited those failures when they withdrew $4 billion in funding.

As of October, no high-speed rail track had been laid, and the project's independent inspector general warns California could run out of money as soon as December 2027 unless it secures additional financing.

The authority says it is revising designs and changing the project's scope to reduce costs. The inspector general said much of the projected cost reduction reflected plans to build less, like reducing the plans from two tracks to one.

But in a separate review of the authority's 2026 business plan, the inspector general found that the project's schedule slipped nine months in less than a year.

Whistleblowers inside the authority question whether the promised savings account for the costs of further delays and additional consultant work.

That brings us back to the late-night rides from the CEO's home.

The receipts don't show who was present or what decisions, if any, were made or what discussions were had at the residence and nearby restaurants.

But whistleblowers warn of increasingly costly delays while California pays consultants a quarter of a billion dollars to help shape decisions, sometimes leading to more delays. They believe taxpayers deserve answers.

Who proposed the design changes? Who approved them? How much are consultants charging to revise the work? And do the projected savings outweigh the costs of delay?

The receipts reveal where the consultants went. The bigger question, say whistleblowers, is what taxpayers are getting in return.

To be continued…

Why is California paying high-speed rail consultants to fly to Sacramento when they promised they would be based in Sacramento?

In part two of our series, The Receipts, CBS California Investigates the money behind a $131 million engineering contract.

The firm promised its key personnel would relocate to Sacramento. But newly obtained receipts reveal three of the six are traveling in from out of state on the taxpayers' dime, while one senior consultant's billing rate increased nearly 23%.

The watchdog questioned more than $76,000 in travel expenses. Our investigation reveals the receipts.

[EDITORS NOTE: This story was updated to include new details following the High Speed Rail Board meeting on October 9, 2026.]

World.title: When 2 dogs went missing in a car crash, a volunteer spent weeks searching
World.content:
Christine Quaiff is a hunter of sorts, often going deep into the woods around Richmond, Virginia, to track and trap family members.

"When someone loses their dog, that's their child," Quaiff told CBS News.

Quaiff has found dozens of lost dogs over the last few years. She's part of a growing national network of lost pet recovery specialists who offer this service, often for free.

"It's about being kind to other people and doing what you wish people would do for you," Quaiff said.

Her most recent case was a desperate search for two Goldendoodles, Bailee and Tobey, who belonged to 66-year-old Annie Olup.

Olup lost her husband in August 2024, and caring for those dogs had become her purpose.

"I thought, I'm going to go back to this house and it's just going to feel so empty," Olup said of her husband's death.

In September, Olup got in a car accident. She was driving in heavy rain when she hit a guardrail, flipped her car and almost died. Her dogs were also in the car. They survived but went missing.

"Dogs typically are going to just run away as quick as possible from the commotion and look for quietness," Quaiff said.

Quaiff used drones and trail cameras to narrow the search. Then she set traps, changed the food twice a day and agreed to stay on the case indefinitely. This was all in addition to her day job as a senior technical account manager in software development.

Quaiff was constantly checking cameras and even sleeping in her car in the search area.

"The joy of seeing them be reunited is ultimately what makes us keep going," Quaiff said.

In the end, it took 10 days for Quaiff to find Tobey and 16 days to find Bailee.

And it took no time at all for the tears to flow once Olup saw her babies were back. The three are now home together again thanks to a stranger who believes it takes a village to raise a child — even the furry ones.

World.title: Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
World.content:
Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering

toggle caption i Provided by Kalshi

Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.

Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement, regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity there. The platform has exploded in growth in the past year.

According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.

Sponsor Message

In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn after his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.

"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."

The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.

Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.

At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.

Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.

Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.

Sponsor Message

Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.

The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.

During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

World.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
World.content:
Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety

toggle caption i Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.

OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

Sponsor Message

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.

In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

Sponsor Message

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."

The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.

"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.

Sponsor Message

In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."

OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.

OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.

In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.

"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

World.title: Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
World.content:
Trump says U.S. to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms

toggle caption i David Zalubowski/AP

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.

Sponsor Message

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

Trump's announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.

Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.

Sponsor Message

Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday's news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."

The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.

Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash

Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."

"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."

The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.

Sponsor Message

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months

Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.

This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.

The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.

The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.

Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine's repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.

Sponsor Message

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is "immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule." He said that Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. already in October, and that Russia's domestic market will be "fully supplied" with diesel, as well.

World.title: The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
World.content:
The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that

toggle caption i Getty Images/Hulton Archive

The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II.

The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.

Sponsor Message

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.

But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.

"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."

If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.

"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was 90 years ago

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.

Sponsor Message

Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS. People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.

"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.

The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.

He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.

"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."

He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.

In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.

"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."

Sponsor Message

Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low.

"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."

Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.

"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."

toggle caption i Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Leaders call for Hegseth to reverse course

Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President Vance told reporters, "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, similarly mused on CNN about whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.

The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."

Sponsor Message

"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.

Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., also called on the Pentagon to revoke its decision, saying, "A country cannot condone livestreaming a man's death for entertainment."

"We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square," she wrote on X. "Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing?"

World.title: U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
World.content:
U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa

toggle caption i Photo by Elizabeth Flores/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images

The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation.

A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.

The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.

Sponsor Message

Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.

Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House , a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.

Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.

"It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.

The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.

DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.

Sponsor Message

"But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.

Facilitating Soliman's return

Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.

" We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."

The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.

Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings .

Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.

That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.

The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.

" We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."

The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.

Sponsor Message

World.title: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
World.content:
Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?

toggle caption i Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/via Getty Images

A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.

The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.

toggle caption i Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/via Getty Images

Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.

But there are still far more questions than answers.

That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.

On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.

Sponsor Message

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."

Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.

Rooted in the 19th century

This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.

"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan , an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."

Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.

Sponsor Message

A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.

Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)

One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.

Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.

Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.

The situation in Russia

Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.

However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.

"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."

It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.

WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.

Sponsor Message

Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.

That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin , who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.

"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.

"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."

He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias
World.content:
How the oil industry is preparing for Hurricane Isaias

toggle caption i RONALDO SCHEMIDT/AFP via Getty Images

Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the season, is expected to make landfall on Friday evening near the Alabama Gulf Coast and Florida panhandle.

Days ago, the oil industry around the U.S. Gulf Coast started preparing. A segment of the nation's oil infrastructure — like oil rigs and platforms — operates in the region, although the majority of it is further west, towards western Louisiana and Texas.

Although oil experts are not anticipating major disruptions, oil companies have been taking precautions. Shell and BP have evacuated personnel from offshore facilities close to the storm's path, mainly deepwater platforms. Chevron has evacuated offshore drilling rigs close to the storm's path, and plans to redeploy them once the storm has passed.

Sponsor Message

In an emailed statement, Exxon told NPR they are "closely monitoring the weather. Operations are normal."

But so far, the storm seems like it will skirt most facilities. The storm's path "could be worse," said Debnil Chowdhury, head of Americas refining at S&P Global Energy. After all, the storm is heading east, and not west, toward where the bulk of oil operations — like refineries — are located.

The storm is "making a swooping turn, almost just to the east of where the most significant infrastructure is," said Bryan Domangue, the Gulf of America region director for the federal Marine Minerals Administration, who oversees offshore oil and natural gas production. "At this point, it's swept just a little south of some of our major deepwater oil and gas facilities, and then it's hugging the eastern boundary of where the infrastructure is."

He added that in addition to evacuating people who work on oil rigs and platforms, which are normal storm precautions, oil operators are doing things like shutting off safety valves below the ocean floor, and moving mobile drilling facilities when possible.

Of course, it's not unprecedented for the oil industry to face hurricanes. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita , in 2005, remain some of the most destructive in the oil and gas industry's history. Nearly 3,000 platforms were in the path of the storms and Katrina destroyed 47 platforms. Other, more recent, hurricanes have not been as destructive but have halted production or reduced capacity — such as Hurricane Francine in 2024 , Hurricane Ida in 2021 , and Hurricane Harvey in 2017 .

Sponsor Message

Another risk is what would happen if the storm became severe enough to make refineries — which are on land — go offline, analysts told NPR. If a hurricane knocks out the power, or if a refinery floods, it can take a while to get running again. It's more complicated than restarting an oil rig or mobile drilling operations.

"Restarting these things is like starting up an old car," said Carl Larry, a manager at Enverus, an energy data and research provider, even if the shutdown is short. "If you did anything in the world, anything in your life, 24/7, stop doing it for one day," he continued, "you're going to have the shakes."

He says, this is because refineries are vast and complex. They boil oil down into molecules that are turned into diesel, gasoline, or natural gas liquids like propane. Pipelines carry crude oil in and refined products out. And they have to be heated. "Every one of those little steps is built on power that's generated through the facility on a constant 24/7 basis," Larry said. If that power is switched off, the process takes time to restart.

There are two significant refineries on the hurricane's path — the Chevron Pascagoula location and the Vertex Alabama refinery. Representatives of these refineries did not return requests for comment about their storm preparations, but Ross Allen, a spokesperson for Chevron, told NPR that generally speaking, refineries prepare for storms by trying to mitigate flood risk.

Chowdhury of S&P Global Energy said these two refineries "account for about 2.5% of total U.S. refining capacity and about 5% the Gulf Coast refining capacity. And Pascagoula specifically is very important to supplying airports throughout the southeast."

While those numbers may not sound big, the global supply of diesel and gas is short, due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. So every little bit counts. American refineries are operating at 92.7% capacity, refining about 17 million barrels of crude a day.
