World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight: Maria Rita, Piaf Musical — October 10, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

Tonight, Saturday 10 October 2026, Rio de Janeiro has Maria Rita at the Vivo Rio on the Flamengo waterfront, the musical “Piaf” at the Teatro Riachuelo in Centro and the last night of the Pink Floyd candlelight concerts at the Museu do Amanhã. The evening is mild and mostly dry, around 23°C (73°F). The Festival do Rio film festival runs through Sunday. All times are Rio de Janeiro time.

Tonight at a Glance — Date Saturday, 10 October 2026. The main night of the weekend in Rio. The Festival do Rio film festival is in its last days (it runs to 11 October). All times Rio de Janeiro time (UTC-3).

— Weather Mild and mostly dry. Open-Meteo shows 23.0°C (73°F) to 23.3°C (74°F) from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m., with a 4 to 14 per cent chance of rain.

— Top pick Maria Rita, “Redescobrir Vol. 2”, at the Vivo Rio at 9 p.m. One of Brazil’s leading MPB (Brazilian popular music) singers, in a large waterfront hall.

— Neighborhood in focus Centro and Flamengo. The Teatro Riachuelo and the Museu do Amanhã are in Centro and the port area, and the Vivo Rio stands in the Parque do Flamengo.

— Entry prices Seats for “Piaf” run from R$50 (about US$10) to R$300 (about US$60). Candlelight concert tickets start at R$36.50 to R$48.50 (about US$7 to US$10), depending on the listing. Maria Rita’s ticket prices were not confirmed. Rate: US$1 = R$4.99 (RT, 9 October close).

— Safety note Use a licensed taxi or rideshare for the ride home from the waterfront and the port area, keep phones out of sight in crowds and avoid empty side streets after midnight.

Planning more nights? Read our Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Guide 2026, with neighborhoods, costs, safety and how the scene works.

If You Only Go to One Place Maria Rita, Vivo Rio MPB singer at a large waterfront hall.

Tonight’s Top 3

1. Maria Rita, “Redescobrir Vol. 2”, at the Vivo Rio Maria Rita is one of Brazil’s best-known MPB singers and the daughter of the singer Elis Regina. Tonight she brings her “Redescobrir Vol. 2” tour to the Vivo Rio, a large hall on the Flamengo waterfront. Tonight 9 p.m.

Genre MPB (Brazilian popular music) and samba.

Entry Tickets are sold through Ticketmaster Brasil. We could not confirm the price or whether the show is sold out.

Address Avenida Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo (Aterro do Flamengo).

Verdict The big-name concert of the night. For foreigners: Maria Rita sings in Portuguese, but her voice and the band carry the show without the words, and the hall has good sightlines.

2. “Piaf: Eu Não Me Arrependo” (“I Do Not Regret”) A new musical about the French singer Édith Piaf, starring the actress Laila Garin. The season opened on 10 October and runs to 1 November, with two shows today. Tonight 8 p.m. (a second Saturday show is earlier in the afternoon)

Genre Musical theatre.

Entry First-lot prices on Saturday: orchestra VIP R$300 (about US$60), orchestra R$250 (about US$50), upper box R$200 (about US$40) and balcony R$50 (about US$10). Sold-out status was not confirmed.

Address Teatro Riachuelo Rio, Rua do Passeio 38, Centro.

Verdict A polished theatre night in central Rio. For foreigners: both balcony sections are reached by stairs only, so ask the theatre about access before you buy.

3. Candlelight: Tribute to Pink Floyd A candlelit concert of Pink Floyd songs in the Museu do Amanhã, the science museum on Praça Mauá. Today is the last day of the run, which began on 8 August. Tonight Several sessions; we could not confirm the times. Choose a session on the ticket page.

Genre Progressive-rock tribute.

Entry From R$36.50 to R$48.50 (about US$7 to US$10), depending on the listing. Sold-out status was not confirmed.

Address Praça Mauá 1, Centro.

Verdict A calm, seated option that fits a first night in the city. For foreigners: pick your session on the Fever ticket page.

Also Tonight

— Festival do Rio, final weekend Film festival, screenings across the city until 11 October. Programme and times at festivaldorio.com.br; we could not confirm tonight’s sessions.

— Blue Note Rio, Copacabana Jazz club on Avenida Atlântica 1910, reopened on 5 October. Its site listed no shows for tonight when we checked, so ask the club before you go.

— Fundição Progresso, Lapa The venue on Rua dos Arcos 24 lists one event today, “Manifesto Tauã”, at 4 p.m. It is an afternoon event, not a night show.

The Night in Context

Saturday is the busiest night of the week in Rio, and this one is quieter than most for live clubs. Our checks of the main Lapa venues turned up few confirmed late shows, so tonight’s list leans towards seated concerts and theatre rather than all-night parties. That is useful information in itself: if you want a dance floor, the free street samba of Lapa and the bars along Rua do Lavradio are the usual answer on a Saturday, and they need no ticket.

Three of the picks sit in a short arc from the Aterro do Flamengo to the port. The Vivo Rio is on the waterfront, the Teatro Riachuelo is next to the Passeio Público in Centro, and the Museu do Amanhã stands on Praça Mauá. A visitor can combine an early evening show with dinner in Centro, but the area empties after the theatres close, so plan the way home before the show ends.

For a visitor from the United States, tonight is also a good test of how Rio’s ticket market works. Big concerts sell through Ticketmaster Brasil, theatre through Ingresso.com and the museum concerts through Fever. Half-price (meia) tickets are sold mainly to students, seniors and some other groups, and prices rise with each lot. Prices on this page are from ticket sellers on 9 and 10 October and can change at the door.

Practical Notes

— Transport Use Uber or 99 for the Vivo Rio and the port area, and wait inside the venue for the car. The Teatro Riachuelo is a short walk from Cinelândia station on the Metro. Lapa is best reached by rideshare after 11 p.m.

— Tickets Buy online through the venue’s ticket seller and bring a photo ID. Check the page again before you leave, because shows can sell out during the day.

— Safety Keep phones out of sight at crowded exits, avoid empty streets in Centro and the port area late at night, and use the venue’s rideshare pick-up point.

World.title: Mexico Lifts Premium Gasoline Tax Relief to 71%
World.content:

MEXICO · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Mexico, led by President Claudia Sheinbaum, is the United States’ southern neighbour and took almost half of US finished gasoline exports in July.

— What happened On Friday 9 October 2026, Mexico published fuel tax relief rates for 10 to 16 October, lifting premium relief to 71.29%.

— The numbers Relief per litre is 4.31 pesos (about US$0.24) on regular, 4.03 pesos (US$0.22) on premium and 7.36 pesos (US$0.40) on diesel.

— The US link Mexico bought 417,000 barrels a day of US finished gasoline in July 2026, 48.5% of all such US exports, US Energy Information Administration data show.

— Border zone A separate discount near the US border is unchanged, ranging from zero in Tijuana to 4.55 pesos (US$0.25) a litre in Acuña, Coahuila.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives US crude a 37% chance of touching US$100 a barrel in October (10 October, 3:19 a.m. ET).

— Still open The weekly orders do not state what the relief costs, and rates for 17 to 23 October have not been set.

Mexico raised its gasoline tax relief on premium fuel to 71.29% of the federal excise for 10 to 16 October. The order, published on Friday 9 October in the government gazette, also keeps the per-litre excise on diesel at zero.

The weekly decision matters north of the border because Mexico buys almost half of the finished gasoline the US exports. Each peso of relief is excise revenue the government gives up, so drivers pay less tax at the pump.

What the Finance Ministry Changed

The Finance Ministry, known in Mexico as Hacienda, sets gasoline tax relief every week under a decree from December 2016. It applies to the IEPS, a special tax on production and services that Mexico charges per litre of fuel.

Agreement 152/2026 lifts the premium discount to 4.03 pesos (about US$0.22) a litre, up 0.46 pesos (about US$0.025) from 3 to 9 October. That is a 12.8% rise in the relief on premium fuel.

Regular gasoline gets 4.31 pesos (about US$0.24) a litre, or 64.31% of the tax, up from 63.34% under Agreement 148/2026. Drivers still pay 2.39 pesos (US$0.13) of excise per litre of regular and 1.62 pesos (US$0.09) on premium.

Diesel keeps a 100% discount worth 7.36 pesos (about US$0.40) a litre, so the weekly excise rate on diesel is zero. A complementary diesel credit rises to 1.09 pesos (US$0.06) a litre, from 0.60 pesos (US$0.03) for 3 to 9 October.

The order, dated Thursday 8 October, was issued under Carlos Gabriel Lerma Cotera, the deputy finance minister for revenue. Gilberto Sosa Sánchez, head of the ministry’s non-tax and hydrocarbon revenue policy unit, signed it in his absence.

It took effect on Saturday 10 October, the day after publication. Amounts in this article are converted at about 18.33 pesos to the US dollar on 10 October 2026.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Oil Prices Stay High After a September Peak

West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the main US crude benchmark, sold for US$96.24 a barrel at Cushing, Oklahoma, on Tuesday 6 October. That is the latest daily price from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the statistics arm of the US Department of Energy.

WTI peaked at US$107.02 on Tuesday 15 September, up from US$84.57 on Friday 28 August. Premium gasoline tax relief rose in the latest order even though WTI traded below that mid-September peak.

Diesel relief already stood at 100% for 19 to 25 September under Agreement 141/2026, part of the same weekly system. Premium relief has climbed from 59.12% that week to 71.29% for 10 to 16 October, including an 8.1-point jump in the latest order.

The complementary diesel credit was larger in that September week, at 1.84 pesos (about US$0.10) a litre. It fell to 0.60 pesos (about US$0.03) for 3 to 9 October before rising again.

A Separate Discount Along the US Border

A second order, Agreement 153/2026, sets a separate gasoline tax discount for sales within 45 kilometres (28 miles) of the US border. The amount falls in steps from the 20-kilometre strip nearest the line, quoted below, to the outer band.

In Tijuana and Playas de Rosarito, across from San Diego, the border discount is zero for 10 to 16 October. In Mexicali, next to Calexico, California, it is 0.58 pesos (about US$0.03) a litre on regular gasoline.

Ciudad Juárez, facing El Paso, Texas, gets 3.41 pesos (about US$0.19) a litre on regular. Nuevo Laredo, across from Laredo, gets 4.12 pesos (US$0.22), and Acuña in Coahuila 4.55 pesos (US$0.25).

Every amount matches the previous week’s Agreement 149/2026, published on Friday 2 October. Along the US border, only the nationwide relief changed for 10 to 16 October.

What It Means for You

Drivers from El Paso or Laredo who fill up across the border get the same border discount as in the week to Friday 9 October. In Tijuana, across from San Diego, that discount stays at zero.

Further inland, only the nationwide gasoline tax relief applies, and it grew for premium on Saturday 10 October. The orders set tax rates, not the prices that stations post at the pump.

For US refiners, Mexico took 417,000 barrels a day of US finished gasoline in July, out of 859,000 exported, EIA figures show. Demand south of the border is a large share of their export business.

For investors in Mexican government debt, every peso of relief is excise revenue the treasury does not collect. The weekly orders list rates per litre, not the total cost.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bettors give WTI crude a 37% chance of touching US$100 a barrel in October (10 October, 3:19 a.m. ET). That is up 5 points in 24 hours, while a dip to US$85 is priced at 55.5%.

About US$1.6 million has been wagered across all price levels in that October oil market. A higher oil price would make the fuel Mexico imports more expensive.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

Hacienda has not said how much the gasoline tax relief for 10 to 16 October will cost in lost excise revenue. The two orders give amounts per litre only.

Rates for 17 to 23 October have not been set, and the ministry gives no forecast. It is also unclear how much of the larger premium discount will reach pump prices.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Mexico’s gasoline tax relief?

Mexico’s gasoline tax relief is a weekly discount on the IEPS, the federal excise charged per litre of fuel. The Finance Ministry publishes the rates in the government gazette, and each set applies for seven days.

How much is the relief from 10 to 16 October?

Regular gasoline gets 4.31 pesos (about US$0.24) a litre, premium 4.03 pesos (US$0.22) and diesel 7.36 pesos (US$0.40). The weekly excise rate on diesel is therefore zero.

Does the US border region get a different rate?

Yes, stations within 45 kilometres (28 miles) of the US line get a separate gasoline tax discount that varies by town. It ranges from zero in Tijuana to 4.55 pesos (US$0.25) a litre in Acuña, unchanged from the week before.

Why does it matter to Americans?

Mexico bought almost half of US finished gasoline exports in July 2026, according to the EIA. Its gasoline tax relief lowers the fuel tax in a major market for US refiners, including towns along the US border.

World.title: Peru Quechua Lion King Film Wins Boston Vote in October
World.content:

PERU · CULTURE

Key Facts — The country Peru is an Andean nation on South America’s Pacific coast, home to Cusco, the old Inca capital, and the ruins of Machu Picchu.

— What happened Peru’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday, 9 October, that Runa Simi won the best-feature audience award at CineFest Latino in Boston.

— The story on screen Fernando Valencia, a radio host from Cusco, sets out to dub Disney’s animated The Lion King into Quechua with help from his young son.

— The US link The film had its world premiere at New York’s Tribeca Festival in 2025, and its Boston screening was on Saturday, 3 October.

— The language Quechua, which became the shared language of the Andes in the Inca period, is the mother tongue of about 3.8 million people in Peru.

— Still open The ministry gave no vote count and did not say when or where the film will next screen in the United States.

A Peruvian documentary about a Cusco father’s bid to make a Quechua Lion King has won over a US audience. Runa Simi took the audience award for best feature at CineFest Latino in Boston, Peru’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday, 9 October.

Quechua became the shared language of the Andes under the Incas, and the project began as a hobby in Cusco, their old capital. For US viewers, the prize puts an Indigenous language from Peru’s tourist heartland on an American festival stage.

What Peru’s Foreign Ministry Announced

Director Augusto Zegarra’s film won the audience prize for best feature, the Foreign Ministry said in an information note. The festival ran in Boston from Wednesday, 30 September, to Sunday, 4 October.

Runa Simi was shown on Saturday, 3 October, at the Emerson Paramount Center, an arts venue in central Boston. More than 150 people attended, including members of the Peruvian community, the ministry said.

CineFest Latino presents films each year about Latin America, Spain and the Latino community in the United States. Its founder and executive director, Sabrina Avilés, introduced the screening.

She stressed the importance of giving visibility to the language, identity and culture of “our countries” and preserving them, the ministry said. After the film, Zegarra and its lead, Fernando Valencia, joined a virtual talk with the audience.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Cusco Father, His Son and The Lion King

Valencia is a single father and radio host in his native Cusco who makes content in Quechua, the Tribeca Festival’s film page says. He records voices with his young son, Dylan, turning Spanish dialogue into Quechua.

His online clips of animated films dubbed into Quechua went viral. That pushed him toward his biggest goal yet: a full Quechua version of Disney’s animated The Lion King.

“Our language Quechua,” Valencia says, “is like life itself,” according to Tribeca’s synopsis. He tackles the Quechua Lion King project from a home studio, Peru’s Foreign Ministry said.

The ministry said the film puts Andean language, identity and culture in the spotlight. Tribeca lists the documentary at 81 minutes, in Quechua, Spanish and English, with English subtitles.

From Tribeca in New York to Boston

Runa Simi had its world premiere in the documentary competition of the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York, the festival’s page shows. It is Zegarra’s first feature film.

In January, it won the Ibero-American award at the Palm Springs International Film Festival in California, the Lima daily El Comercio reported. Sabrina Avilés, the founder of CineFest Latino Boston, sat on that three-member jury.

El Comercio reported in August that the film had collected 27 awards at more than 60 festivals in over 30 countries. The paper said it was booked for a one-week run at the Firehouse Cinema in Manhattan from 28 August.

Its executive producers include the actor Benjamin Bratt and Peter Bratt, according to the Tribeca credits. Zegarra filmed Valencia’s Quechua Lion King effort over nine years, El Comercio reported.

The Boston prize was an audience award, decided by festival-goers rather than by a jury of critics. It gives the Quechua Lion King story, rooted in the southern Andes, a fresh hearing in the United States.

Why Quechua Matters in Peru

In all, 3,805,531 people in Peru learned to speak in Quechua as their first language, according to Peru’s Ministry of Culture. The ministry says Quechua took hold across the Andes in the Inca period, as a language of government and trade.

About 60% of Peruvians spoke Quechua at the start of the 20th century, the ministry says. By the start of the 21st, the share had fallen to about 15%, though Peru had more Quechua speakers in 2014 than in 1876.

Quechua has had an official alphabet since a 1985 resolution of the Education Ministry. An Education Ministry table cited by the Culture Ministry rates the Quechua of Cusco and Puno as a vital language.

What It Means for You

For US travelers, Cusco is the gateway to Machu Picchu, and Quechua is part of daily life there. See What to Do in Cusco in October 2026 for this month’s events.

For US film fans, Runa Simi, the Quechua Lion King documentary, has already screened in New York, Palm Springs and Boston. In Boston, members of the Peruvian community were in the audience, the ministry said.

What Is Not Known

Peru’s Foreign Ministry did not say how many votes the film received or which other films competed. It also did not say whether the award carries prize money.

The ministry did not say when Runa Simi will be shown again in the United States, or where. Its note also does not say whether Valencia has finished the full Quechua Lion King dub.

Neither the ministry’s note nor Tribeca’s synopsis says whether Disney has authorized a Quechua Lion King.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Runa Simi about?

It follows Fernando Valencia, a radio host and single father from Cusco, who dubs films into Quechua with his young son. His big goal is a full Quechua Lion King, a dub of the Disney animated film.

What award did Runa Simi win in Boston?

It won the audience award for best feature at CineFest Latino, which ran in Boston from 30 September to 4 October. Peru’s Foreign Ministry announced the prize on 9 October.

What is Quechua?

Quechua is a family of Andean languages that spread widely in the Inca period and is still spoken in seven South American countries. About 3.8 million people in Peru learned it as their first language, the Culture Ministry says.

Where has Runa Simi been shown in the United States?

It premiered at New York’s Tribeca Festival in 2025 and won the Ibero-American award at Palm Springs, California, in January. On 3 October it screened at CineFest Latino in Boston, where it won the audience award.

World.content:

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Runoff · Sunday, 25 October Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula: what happens next First-round results, how the runoff works, the key dates and who backs whom, in one guide. Read the runoff guide →

Key Facts — The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country and economy, chooses its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between Flávio Bolsonaro and President Lula.

— What happened A Brazil poll by AtlasIntel, released on Friday 9 October, gives Flávio 52.8% of valid votes and Lula 47.2%.

— The swing AtlasIntel’s last round before the first vote, with interviews ending on Friday 2 October, had Lula ahead by 0.2 points.

— The survey AtlasIntel interviewed 5,026 voters online from 3 to 8 October, with a margin of error of one percentage point.

— The other polls Three polls published since the first round, including this one, put Flávio ahead, while a fourth, Vox Brasil, shows Lula narrowly in front.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro an 88.4% chance of winning the 25 October runoff (10 October, 3:22 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 88% and Kalshi at 88% (Lula: 12% and 12% ), as of 10 October, 3:20 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

A new Brazil poll released on Friday 9 October puts Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva before the 25 October runoff. The AtlasIntel survey gives Flávio, the conservative eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, 52.8% of valid votes to 47.2%.

For Americans, the race decides who runs Latin America’s largest economy and how Brazil deals with Washington and Beijing. Investors in Brazilian stocks and the real follow each Brazil poll for signs of a change of government.

What the AtlasIntel Poll Shows

Counting all answers, Flávio has 51.1% and Lula 45.7%, a gap of 5.4 points, according to AtlasIntel’s published report. Another 3.2% said they would vote blank, spoil the ballot or had not decided.

Valid votes leave out blank and spoiled ballots, the way Brazil’s electoral court counts the result. On that basis, the gap in this Brazil poll is 5.6 points.

The movement since AtlasIntel’s previous round is large. That round, with interviews ending on Friday 2 October, had Lula at 47.6% and Flávio at 47.4%.

Since then Flávio has gained 3.7 points and Lula has lost 1.9, the financial news site InfoMoney reported. The shift followed the first round on Sunday 4 October, in which Flávio finished first.

Flávio, a senator for Rio de Janeiro, runs for the conservative Liberal Party (PL), his father’s party. Lula, 80, of the left-wing Workers’ Party (PT), which he co-founded, is seeking a fourth term.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil Elections 2026 Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Poll Was Done

AtlasIntel, a polling firm that recruits respondents online at random, interviewed 5,026 voters across Brazil from Saturday 3 to Thursday 8 October. The results carry a margin of error of one percentage point either way, at a 95% confidence level.

The survey is registered with the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Brazil’s election authority, under number BR-03663/2026. Brazilian law requires every published election poll to be registered there first.

AtlasIntel publishes the survey jointly with Bloomberg, the US financial news group. It cost R$75,000 (about US$15,000), paid from the pollster’s own funds, according to the news site Poder360.

Conversions here use about 5.01 reais to the US dollar on 10 October 2026.

Fieldwork began on the day before the first-round vote, Poder360 noted. The other recent surveys started only after the vote.

Who Voters Trust on Crime and the Economy

The Brazil poll also asked which candidate voters trust more on key issues. Flávio leads on crime and drug trafficking by 53% to 43%, and on fiscal balance and spending control by 52% to 42%.

On the economy and inflation he leads by 52% to 45%, AtlasIntel’s figures show, as InfoMoney also reported. Lula ties him on poverty and inequality at 48% each, and on the environment at 47% each.

On foreign policy, the area closest to relations with Washington, Flávio leads by only 49% to 47%. The split is the same on promoting democracy and on health.

The survey also measured Lula’s standing as president. In it, 44.7% approve of his performance and 53.4% disapprove, while 51.9% rate his government bad or terrible.

How It Compares With Other Polls

AtlasIntel’s figures are close to two other polls published since the first round. Datafolha, the polling arm of the Folha de S.Paulo newspaper group, gave Flávio 52% of valid votes and Lula 48% on Thursday 8 October.

PoderData/Aya, a poll released by Poder360 on the same day, gave Flávio 53% and Lula 47%. Both surveys are registered with the electoral court, with margins of error of 2 and 1.8 points.

One Brazil poll disagrees. Vox Brasil, with 2,100 interviews, shows Lula at 44.2% and Flávio at 42.7% of all answers, according to Poder360.

The official count gives the polls context. In the first round, Flávio received 56.1 million votes and Lula 53.8 million, according to the electoral court.

AtlasIntel’s own final round before that vote had shown Lula slightly ahead. The miss led to calls for an inquiry into pollsters, as The Rio Times reported.

Details of the Datafolha survey are in this earlier report.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, an online prediction market, bettors give Flávio Bolsonaro an 88.4% chance of winning the runoff. Lula stands at 11.5% (10 October, 3:22 a.m. ET), and Flávio’s price rose 2.2 points in 24 hours.

The “Brazil Presidential Election” market has drawn about US$179.6 million in total bets, with about US$1.3 million traded in the last day. These are bets, not polls.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 88.4% · Lula 11.5% (US$180 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 88% · Lula 12% As of 10 October, 3:20 am ET (08:20 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US investors, three of the four latest polls and the betting markets point the same way, toward a Flávio win. A late Lula recovery would upset that view, so each new Brazil poll can move Brazilian stocks and the real.

Brazilians registered to vote in the United States and elsewhere abroad vote only for president, according to the electoral court. Brazil’s constitution makes voting compulsory for literate citizens aged 18 to 70.

More than 158.7 million voters are called to the polls on 25 October, according to the electoral court.

Campaign advertising on free radio and television restarted on Friday 9 October and runs until Friday 23 October. Each candidate gets equal airtime, so the race can still move.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how voters who backed other first-round candidates will split, or how many will vote at all. Turnout could decide whether a 5.6-point lead holds.

The Record network cancelled the runoff debate it had set for Sunday 11 October. The first one is now due on Thursday 15 October on the SBT network.

The Band TV network, with the São Paulo newspaper Estadão, holds one on Sunday 18 October and Globo on Friday 23 October, according to Poder360. Both candidates have said they intend to take part in runoff debates.

No Brazil poll is a forecast, and a lead can shrink in the 15 days left.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is leading Brazil’s presidential runoff?

Flávio Bolsonaro leads the latest Brazil poll by AtlasIntel, with 52.8% of valid votes to 47.2% for President Lula. Datafolha and PoderData/Aya show similar leads, while Vox Brasil shows Lula narrowly ahead.

When is Brazil’s runoff election?

The runoff is on Sunday 25 October 2026, three weeks after the 4 October first round. Brazilians registered abroad, including in the United States, vote only for president.

How reliable is this survey?

This Brazil poll interviewed 5,026 voters, a large sample with a margin of error of one point. AtlasIntel’s last round before the first vote showed Lula ahead, yet Flávio finished first, so treat any single survey with caution.

Who is Flávio Bolsonaro?

He is a senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. He runs for the conservative Liberal Party (PL) and finished first in the 4 October first round.

World.content:

BOLIVIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Bolivia is a landlocked Andean nation led since November 2025 by President Rodrigo Paz, who has renewed security cooperation with Washington.

— What happened On Friday 9 October, the US Embassy gave Bolivia’s police protective gear, tear gas and crowd-control equipment at a ceremony in La Paz.

— Who paid The State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs funded it; no value or quantities were published.

— Who gets it UTOP, the police tactical operations unit that faced the 53-day blockades, which marked its 50th anniversary at the same ceremony.

— Why now The government says UTOP held the line through 53 days of road blockades; supporters of ex-president Evo Morales now threaten new ones.

— For travellers The US rates Bolivia Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, and tells visitors never to cross roadblocks.

Bolivia police have received riot gear, tear gas and protective equipment from the United States, a sign of renewed security ties. The handover took place in La Paz on Friday 9 October, as the police tactical unit known as UTOP marked its 50th anniversary.

US taxpayers paid for it, a reversal for a country that once expelled the US ambassador and US law enforcement agencies. On Friday, supporters of ex-president Evo Morales warned they could encircle the eastern city of Santa Cruz if lawmakers pass an anti-blockade bill.

What the US Gave Bolivia’s Police

The equipment came from the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL), the State Department bureau that funds police and anti-drug programmes abroad. Matthew Zamary, INL’s director at the US Embassy in Bolivia, led the ceremony at the National Police Academy.

“The United States is proud to donate protective equipment, tear gas and crowd-control equipment,” Zamary said, according to the state news agency ABI. No value, quantities or number of Bolivia police officers equipped were published.

Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo and Police Commander General Adrián Álvarez received the material. “We receive this valuable donation of riot-control equipment with deep gratitude,” Álvarez said, according to the radio network Erbol.

Oviedo addressed the diplomats directly. “Gentlemen of the Embassy, thank you very much for the donation,” he said, according to his ministry.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Washington Is Backing Bolivia’s Police

Zamary described the gift as part of an alliance between two democracies that have chosen to face common threats together. He cited Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has described the relationship as a truly renewed partnership.

Zamary said a new chapter opened in November, when Rodrigo Paz became president. Paz replaced Luis Arce of the Movement for Socialism (MAS), the leftist party Evo Morales led as president from 2006 to 2019.

The embassy called the gift part of a wider agenda: police professionalisation, anti-corruption work and joint action against drug trafficking and transnational crime networks. The State Department lists Bolivia as the world’s third-largest cocaine producer.

Paz praised the Bolivia police at a decoration ceremony on Thursday 8 October. He said seizures of drug-trafficking aircraft rose from about nine a year to between 50 and 60.

He also credited the force with capturing Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset.

The relationship still has friction points, as Washington’s latest human trafficking grade for Bolivia shows.

The Blockades Behind the Donation

Oviedo said UTOP was decisive during 53 days of road blockades and handled them without a single death caused by the police. He said those blockades were “financed by narco-terrorism”, according to the ministry’s statement.

Zamary spoke of “more than seven weeks of violent blockades.” He said legitimate protest must be told apart from actions that deny others free movement and access to food, medicine and basic services.

He added that the equipment must come with training, discipline, proportionality and full respect for human rights. On Thursday, Paz said police and soldiers kept humanitarian corridors open for oxygen and food during the 53 days.

The security climate stayed tense on Friday. In the La Paz district of San Antonio, Bolivia police found four handmade dynamite devices ready to detonate and 20 firecrackers, the ministry said.

Officers also seized three phones, a passport and a jacket with the letters DEA, the initials of the US Drug Enforcement Administration. Oviedo linked the devices to Aristóteles Calle, whom he called a key figure in a “terrorist and drug-trafficking structure”.

Calle is a former ministry official under Eduardo Del Castillo, Arce’s government minister, whom prosecutors now seek over alleged links to Marset. Police commander Álvarez said the evidence suggests the devices were meant for announced protests; no arrests were reported.

What It Means for You

For US travellers, the most direct effect is on road travel. The State Department rates Bolivia at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, in an advisory updated on 18 August 2026.

It warns that “roadblocks are a common form of protest throughout the country” and tells visitors: “Do not cross roadblocks.” The new threat against Santa Cruz makes that advice current again.

The anti-blockade bill would let prosecutors pursue ministers, governors, mayors and other officials who fail to resolve conflicts in time. A committee of the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, reportedly approved it, but one deputy told Visión 360 it is being reconsidered.

Vicente Choque, a pro-Morales leader, said that if the law is approved, “we have to call to encircle Santa Cruz”, according to Opinión.

Adriana Jiménez, a deputy for Libre, the conservative alliance of ex-president Jorge Quiroga, said his claims lacked political basis.

For US taxpayers and investors, the gift to Bolivia police shows Washington backing the Paz government with practical security help. It is equipment, not personnel: neither government announced US officers or troops on the ground.

What Is Not Known

Neither government has said what the equipment cost, how much tear gas was delivered or how many Bolivia police officers will use it. It is also unclear whether more INL deliveries are planned.

No date for a full Chamber of Deputies vote on the anti-blockade bill has been announced. Morales supporters have not said when, or whether, they would act on the Santa Cruz threat.

In the explosives case, the ministry named no one charged. The link between the devices and protest plans remains a police hypothesis.

More: Bolivia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US give Bolivia police?

Protective equipment, tear gas and crowd-control gear, according to Bolivia’s Ministry of Government. It was handed over in La Paz on Friday 9 October 2026 and funded by the US State Department.

Which Bolivia police unit will use the gear?

UTOP, the tactical operations unit of the Bolivia police, which was marking its 50th anniversary at the handover ceremony. The government says the unit handled 53 days of road blockades.

Is it safe to travel to Bolivia now?

The US rates Bolivia Level 2, “exercise increased caution”. Roadblocks are common, and the State Department tells visitors never to cross them.

Why does this matter for US–Bolivia relations?

Bolivia once expelled the US ambassador and US law enforcement agencies. The donation shows security cooperation has returned since Rodrigo Paz became president in November 2025.

EL SALVADOR · CLIMATE

Key Facts — The country El Salvador is Central America’s smallest and most densely populated country, led by President Nayib Bukele, a close ally of US President Donald Trump.

— What happened On Friday, 9 October, the US Embassy said Washington is providing up to US$55 million in drought aid to El Salvador.

— The money Up to US$25 million goes through the United Nations to the worst-hit areas, and US$30 million more is coming for preventive action.

— Why now On Wednesday, 7 October, the Legislative Assembly declared a six-month national emergency over the El Niño drought, with 59 votes.

— The damage A farmers’ group reports losing about 20% of the first basic-grain harvest, and authorities expect a 40% shortfall in hydropower.

— Prediction markets Polymarket bets give an 80% chance that this El Niño peaks above 2.5 on a NOAA warming index (10 October, 3:20 a.m. ET).

— Still open The US Embassy has not named the UN agency that will handle the money or set a timetable for spending it.

The United States is providing up to US$55 million in drought aid to El Salvador, its embassy in San Salvador said on Friday, 9 October. The money targets the areas hardest hit by a drought linked to El Niño, a Pacific warming pattern.

The pledge came two days after Salvadoran lawmakers declared a six-month national emergency over the drought. For Americans, it is US taxpayer money aimed at a region that Washington watches closely for hunger, rural hardship and migration.

What the US Drought Aid Covers

Up to US$25 million of the drought aid is being channelled through the United Nations to the worst-hit areas, El Diario de Hoy reported. Another US$30 million is on its way for anticipatory, or preventive, action with the Salvadoran government and the UN, according to La Página.

The embassy said the money aims to protect the most vulnerable families in areas short of rain. The Salvadoran government and international organisations are to share in the work.

The embassy did not say which UN agency will handle the money, which areas will be served or how many families will receive help.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on El Salvador Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why El Salvador Declared a Drought Emergency

The Legislative Assembly, El Salvador’s single-chamber parliament, approved the six-month emergency with 59 votes on Wednesday, 7 October, according to Diario Co Latino. Bukele’s Nuevas Ideas party holds a large majority there, and the President requested the decree.

The decree can be extended at the President’s request and lets state bodies move funds to prevent and soften the damage. According to Diario Co Latino, the Foreign Ministry coordinates international cooperation, while the Defence Ministry handles aid logistics.

The Ministry of Governance declared a drought red alert on 25 August for the most exposed areas, especially the dry corridor, a drought-prone farm belt. The dry conditions put at risk about 6.9 million quintals of basic grains, roughly 313,000 metric tons, Diario El Mundo reported.

Opposition lawmakers questioned the timing. Claudia Ortiz of the small opposition party Vamos said it was known since April that a “Super Niño” would hit.

Ortiz called the decree “a blank cheque” for state purchases. Francisco Lira of ARENA, the conservative party that ruled from 1989 to 2009, said his August call for a drought plan was rejected.

Luis Treminio of CAMPO, an association of small and medium farmers, said the emergency came five months late, El Diario de Hoy reported. CAMPO puts losses in the first basic-grain harvest of May and June at about 20%.

What the IMF Expects From El Niño

The International Monetary Fund (IMF), which runs a loan programme with El Salvador, expects higher costs ahead. Its latest programme review expects El Niño to lift power generation costs by 0.6% of GDP this year, Diario El Mundo reported.

Salvadoran authorities expect hydropower output to fall about 40% short and demand to rise about 5%, according to the IMF report. Most of the gap will be filled by oil-fired plants, which raises fuel imports and exposure to crude prices.

The IMF also estimates that food prices can rise by up to 2.5% six months after a moderate or stronger episode. Farming is about 5% of the economy, but subsistence farmers could be hit hard, the fund warned.

Using government data, the IMF expects only a limited hit to the grain harvest, because the drought mainly affects the smaller second planting. That August to September crop makes up less than a third of output, the fund said.

The outlook from NOAA, the US weather and oceans agency, is not easing. On 8 October, its Climate Prediction Center gave an 83% chance of a record El Niño, the strongest since 1950, in October to December.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bets on how strong this El Niño gets have drawn about US$79,600. Traders gave an 80% chance that it peaks above 2.5 on the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), a NOAA warming gauge.

That price, taken at 3:20 a.m. ET on 10 October, slipped 2.5 points in 24 hours. A peak between 2.25 and 2.5 stood at 16%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US taxpayers, the drought aid will be spent through the United Nations and alongside the Bukele government. For Salvadoran families in the United States, money sent home may buy less food if the IMF’s price forecast proves right.

The Environment Ministry (MARN) expects the shift to the dry season to begin in the second half of October, after a shorter rainy season.

What Is Not Known

The embassy has not said when the drought aid will arrive or which UN agency will run it. Nor has it said how the money will be shared out among El Salvador’s 14 departments, or provinces.

It is also unclear whether the US$30 million for preventive action is new money or comes from earlier programmes. Nor is it clear how much of its own money the government will spend under the emergency decree.

More: El Salvador news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much drought aid is the United States giving El Salvador?

Up to US$55 million in drought aid, according to the US Embassy in San Salvador. Up to US$25 million goes through the United Nations, and another US$30 million is on its way for preventive action.

Why does El Salvador need drought aid now?

El Salvador has gone through four meteorological droughts this year, Diario El Mundo reported. A farmers’ group reports losing about 20% of the first grain harvest, and lawmakers declared a six-month national emergency on 7 October.

What is El Niño?

El Niño is a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean that shifts rainfall around the world. In Central America it usually brings drought, weaker harvests and lower hydropower output.

Does the drought affect travel to El Salvador?

The drought aid targets the communities hit hardest by the lack of rain. Visitors may see food prices rise over time, and the Environment Ministry expects the dry season to set in from late October.

HONDURAS · SOCIETY

Key Facts — The country Honduras is a Central American country between Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua, long marked by violent crime, poverty and migration toward the United States.

— What happened Pope Leo XIV received the Honduran bishops at the Vatican on the morning of Friday, 9 October, the Holy See Press Office said.

— The message He urged them to answer violence with peace education in families, schools, neighbourhoods and villages, and to defend every person’s dignity, one bishop said.

— The meeting Planned for one hour, the private audience with the nine bishops of the Honduran Episcopal Conference ran past two hours, Vatican News reported.

— Why it matters in the US Leo XIV was born in Chicago, and Honduras says deportations of Hondurans could reach 50,000 in 2026, mostly from the US.

— Still open The Vatican has not released a text of the pope’s words; they reach the public through the account of Bishop Jenry Ruiz of Trujillo.

Pope Leo XIV, the first US-born pope, met nine Honduran bishops privately at the Vatican on Friday, 9 October, for more than two hours. He urged them to answer their country’s violence with education for peace, one of the bishops said.

The stakes reach the United States. Honduras’ National Migration Institute says deportations of Hondurans could reach 50,000 by the end of 2026, mostly from the US, El Heraldo reported.

What Pope Leo Told the Honduran Bishops

The Holy See Press Office, the Vatican’s official news office, listed the audience among the pope’s meetings on Friday morning. It named the guests simply as “bishops of Honduras” on their ad limina visit.

Bishop Jenry Orlando Ruiz of Trujillo, a diocese on Honduras’ Caribbean coast, described the talk to Vatican News, the Holy See’s media service. He said the pope asked for a culture of peace that starts in families and spreads to schools, neighbourhoods and villages.

“Every Honduran needs to become an educator for peace,” Ruiz said, summing up the pope’s request. He called the encounter “very relaxed, very family-like” and full of closeness.

According to Ruiz, the pope also asked for values education in Catholic schools, public schools and universities. He tied that to respect for the dignity of every person and to Catholic social teaching on justice and the common good.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Honduras Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Came to Rome and Why

An ad limina visit is a trip that Catholic bishops ordinarily make every five years to report to the pope on their dioceses. Under the church’s Code of Canon Law, they also pray at the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul in Rome.

The Honduran bishops belong to the Honduran Episcopal Conference, known by its Spanish initials CEH, the body that groups the country’s Catholic bishops.

They met the pope in the Apostolic Palace, El Heraldo reported. Vatican News said the visit ended that day.

One bishop was missing. Bishop Teodoro Gómez of Choluteca, the conference’s vice-president, died on 28 September at Madrid’s Barajas airport while travelling to Rome, Vatican News reported.

The pope offered his condolences to the Honduran church. Gómez, 63, was buried on Thursday, 8 October, in a crypt of Choluteca’s cathedral in southern Honduras, La Prensa reported.

Gómez also chaired Cáritas Honduras, the church’s charity network, the paper said. During the visit, the bishops sang to the Virgin of Suyapa, patron of Honduras, in the Vatican Gardens, La Prensa reported.

Why Violence Is the Theme

Vatican News named violence, poverty and migration among the hardships Honduras is going through. Leo XIV, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, has led the church since May 2025, the Vatican says.

The US State Department rates Honduras at Level 3, “Reconsider travel”, citing crime. Its advisory says violent crime such as homicide, armed robbery and kidnapping is common.

The same advisory rates Gracias a Dios, a department on the eastern Caribbean coast, at Level 4, “Do not travel”. For the latest numbers, see the September homicide count for Honduras.

According to Ruiz, the pope listened as the Honduran bishops laid out the joys, hopes and worries of Hondurans. The pope also asked that the church’s national mission lead to a personal encounter with Christ, not just a calendar of events.

What It Means for You

For Americans with family, business or church ties in Honduras, the message changes no law or policy. Ruiz said he would carry the pope’s greeting and blessing home to his diocese and to all Hondurans, Proceso Digital reported.

Migration remains the closest link to the United States. The US Embassy in Tegucigalpa again warned Hondurans on social media that caravans will fail, El Heraldo reported on Friday.

Its post told people not to waste their money or risk their lives, saying smugglers lie. A caravan of hundreds of Hondurans left San Pedro Sula for the US on 20 September, the paper said.

Travellers should read the State Department advisory before any trip. The pope’s appeal does not change the security picture on the ground.

What Is Not Known

By Saturday morning, the Vatican had not published a speech or transcript of the audience. The pope’s words reach the public mainly through Ruiz’s account to Vatican News.

It is not known whether President Nasry Asfura’s government will take up the Honduran bishops’ call for peace education in public schools. It is also not known whether the pope plans to visit Honduras.

More: Honduras news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Pope Leo XIV tell the Honduran bishops?

According to Bishop Jenry Ruiz of Trujillo, the pope asked the Honduran bishops to answer violence with peace education in families, schools and communities. He also stressed the dignity of every person and Catholic social teaching on justice.

When and where did the meeting take place?

The pope received the Honduran bishops at the Vatican on the morning of Friday, 9 October, according to the Holy See Press Office. The private audience in the Apostolic Palace ran past two hours.

What is an ad limina visit?

It is a visit that Catholic bishops ordinarily make every five years under church law. They pray at the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul and report to the pope on their dioceses.

Why does this matter to people in the United States?

Leo XIV is the first pope born in the United States, and Honduras is closely tied to the US through migration. Honduras’ migration institute says deportations of Hondurans could reach 50,000 by the end of 2026, mostly from the US.
