World.title: Water Upgrades for Jacó, Quepos and Manuel Antonio Stall After Seven Years
World.content:
A loan-funded program to upgrade water systems in Jacó, Quepos, Manuel Antonio, Limón and Guácimo has reached just 25% completion after seven years, according to a Ministry of Finance report on externally financed public projects. The program is one of five projects the ministry singled out in its review of the first half of 2026. They have been in execution for between seven and nearly 12 years, and several will not meet their current deadlines.

The delays carry a direct cost as Costa Rica has paid $43.7 million in commitment fees, the charges lenders apply to approved loan money that has not yet been disbursed, according to the report. The Coastal Cities Water and Sewer Program, run by the Costa Rican Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (AyA) with financing from the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (BCIE), was designed to last six years. A 38-month extension pushed its end date to June 2029.

Its six components include upgrades and expansions of the water systems in the five towns and a new building for the National Water Laboratory. The ministry attributed the delays to recurring problems with contracting, design approvals and expropriations. The longest-running project on the list is the Transportation Infrastructure Program of the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT), financed by a $450 million loan from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB). It has been in execution for 11.6 years.

By the end of June, $439.83 million of the loan had been committed and $348 million disbursed. The current disbursement deadline is November 2026 under a third extension, and the ministry expects a fourth. The program’s goals hinge on the new highway to San Carlos, where work stalled for six years after the original construction contract was terminated. Work resumed last year on the southern section, which is just over 15% complete, in a sector where Costa Rica’s highway projects have repeatedly run over budget and behind schedule.

MOPT will finance the central section with its own funds after the IDB declined to approve the only bidder. Public Works Minister Efraím Zeledón told the Legislative Assembly’s Treasury Affairs Committee that 17 properties in the central section and four in the southern section still have to be acquired, though he said those parcels are not needed to complete the highway’s main trunk.

Two other AyA projects also made the list. A program to reduce non-revenue water, meaning water that is produced but never billed because of leaks, illegal connections or metering errors, has been underway for 10.8 years and stands at 66% progress, with about $50 million of a $130 million plan executed.

The report cited low bidder participation, tenders declared void, limited capacity to manage several contracts at once and high turnover among specialized staff. AyA President Lourdes Saúrez said in August that the project had accelerated considerably, adding that non-revenue water had fallen four percentage points to about 49% of production and that the target once the work is finished is 38%.

A separate AyA program to expand water supply in the San José metropolitan area, along with urban aqueducts and the Juanito Mora sanitary sewer system, is 55% complete after 8.1 years. Of its 11 works, divided into 18 stages, 10 are finished, three are under construction and five remain in tendering or technical preparation.

The ministry downgraded that program’s condition to critical. It concluded that even a 42-month extension, which moved the disbursement deadline to Oct. 30, 2027, would not give it enough time. The fifth project is the Costa Rican Electricity Institute’s (ICE) Borinquen I geothermal plant near Liberia, Guanacaste, financed by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). It was originally due for completion in September 2026 and is just over 56% complete after nine years.

As of June, ICE was seeking an extension of at least four years on the loan, and the institute has said the plant will be finished in early 2030. The ministry described the project’s progress as limited. Of the $43.7 million in commitment fees, $23 million went to the IDB, with 67% of that amount tied to the transportation program. Fees to the BCIE totaled $13.5 million across several institutions, and delays at Borinquen I have cost $4.6 million in fees to JICA.

The ministry said disbursement extensions are legitimate tools for managing delays but should be exceptional and technically and financially justified, and should not become a recurring practice. The findings arrive as a national El Niño plan warns of major risks to water supply in the months ahead. MOPT, AyA and ICE had not publicly explained the causes of the delays or the status of their extension requests as of Friday.

World.title: Costa Rica Raids 80 Locations in Major Fuel Theft and Organized Crime Investigation
World.content:
Costa Rica carried out 80 raids before dawn today against an alleged criminal organization. The group is suspected of hijacking cargo containers, siphoning hundreds of thousands of liters of fuel, selling drugs and taking part in two homicides. The operation, known as Portus, began at 4 a.m. this morning. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) in Limón led it, together with the Deputy Prosecutor’s Office Against Money Laundering and Asset Forfeiture and the Deputy Prosecutor’s Office Against Drug Trafficking and Related Crimes.

Michael Soto, interim director of the OIJ, said 22 people had been detained in the first hours of the operation. He said further arrests were pending. The investigation began in 2024, and Soto said the case name refers to a port. The raids centered on the Limón province, including the Liverpool, Moín and Limón 2000 areas. They also reached Heredia, Upala, Puntarenas, Desamparados, Puriscal, Escazú, Guápiles, Siquirres and Batán. The deployment involved 1,275 judicial personnel: 1,100 OIJ agents, 85 judges and 90 prosecutors.

Soto said two of the detainees are alleged leaders of the organization. They are a man surnamed Delgado, known by the alias “Chon,” and a man surnamed Vargas, known as “Salchichón.” According to Soto, the organization is linked to 11 container robberies in Limón, Puntarenas, Liberia and San Ramón. The stolen cargo included tuna, seafood, meat and cleaning products, with an estimated value of about $1.5 million.

Investigators believe the group used the Finance Ministry’s customs information system (TICA), to pick its targets, Soto said. Members allegedly entered container numbers and the license plates of the trucks carrying them. That showed them what each shipment held and its declared customs value before they decided which loads to attack. Soto said the stolen goods were then allegedly sold back into the legitimate market.

A second line of the investigation concerns fuel theft, mainly in Alajuela and Siquirres. Soto said investigators identified five permanent illegal taps used to extract fuel. Authorities attribute about 654,000 liters (roughly 172,800 gallons) to that activity, valued at approximately ₡400 million, or about $875,000.

Soto said members of the structure had distinct roles. Some allegedly extracted the fuel, others sold it, and others received or placed the stolen products on the market. Karla Montero, executive president of Recope, described the groups as dangerous. She said the cost of fuel theft is ultimately passed on to fuel prices paid by every consumer.

She added that each illegal tap carries the risk of a spill that could cause a serious accident or significant environmental damage. Authorities also link the organization to two homicides in Limón. A woman named Aráuz was killed on Dec. 27, 2025, in Limón 2000, in a case Soto said appears to be connected to the fuel theft. A man surnamed Morrison was killed on Aug. 2, 2026, in Liverpool, in what Soto described as an apparent score-settling linked to drug trafficking.

The group is also under investigation for the retail sale of marijuana and cocaine in Liverpool and Limón 2000. Investigators are also looking at illicit association and money laundering. Early in the operation, two people fled through the back of a house as agents arrived. Soto said officers reported hearing a gunshot and reacted, and the suspects were detained a short distance away. He said it did not appear to be a direct confrontation and that the shot may have been fired to intimidate the officers. Two agents suffered minor injuries during the raids.

Authorities reported seizing five firearms, including an AR-15 rifle, as well as cash and high-end vehicles. Notations will be placed on two properties linked to the case. At one property, agents found a swimming pool decorated with an image of Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar, according to authorities.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said the detainees will give their statements to prosecutors, who will request preventive detention. Díaz said the case will remain in Costa Rican courts because the structure appears to operate locally. He said there is currently no evidence of ties to international drug trafficking or terrorism that would open the door to extradition. None of those detained has been charged. The Public Ministry will determine their legal situation in the coming days.

Operation Portus is the latest in a series of large-scale OIJ operations in Limón this year. They include the Caso Riverside raids in June against a drug trafficking structure, and a July operation targeting an alleged cocaine smuggling network at the Moín container terminal. Recope has reported years of heavy losses from illegal fuel taps on its pipeline network.

World.title: Tropical Wave 50 Reaches Costa Rica Saturday Night With More Heavy Rain
World.content:
Plan for yet another wet weekend of rainy weather as Tropical Wave No. 50 is expected to reach Costa Rica late Saturday night, adding even more moisture in places that have already had days of steady rain. The heaviest rain is likely in the Northern Zone and the Caribbean, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). The Central Valley and the Pacific should expect scattered showers.

For those non weather experts, a tropical wave is a band of low pressure that drifts west across the Caribbean during the rainy season. It doesn’t spin like a hurricane, but it pulls in moisture and fuels showers and thunderstorms as it passes. The bigger risk, as with every one of these tropical waves, is the ground, not the rain. Soil that has been soaking for days can’t absorb much more water. That means even a moderate downpour can loosen a hillside or push a river over its banks.

Make sure to watch mountain roads most closely and that includes Route 32 through Braulio Carrillo National Park, the main highway between San José and the Caribbean, which is prone (see our earlier article) to landslides in heavy rain. Check conditions before you leave and give yourself extra time. Don’t drive or walk through flooded roads or rivers. Fifteen centimeters (6 inches) of moving water can knock you off your feet, and 30 centimeters (1 foot) can float many cars. You often can’t tell how deep or fast the water is from the edge.

For those of you visiting us, if you have river tours, waterfall hikes or rafting booked in the north or on the Caribbean side, confirm with your operator before you go and have a backup plan. Low-lying neighborhoods that flood easily should keep an eye on nearby rivers and drains through Sunday. This rainy season has been unusually busy. Of the first 48 tropical waves recorded in 2026, 41 influenced Costa Rica’s weather whereas in all of 2025, 34 tropical waves affected us.

Each new wave arrives before the ground has had time to dry out from the last one. That repeated soaking is why landslide and flood risk keeps building even when a single wave isn’t especially strong. The IMN and the National Emergency Commission (CNE) post updates on their official channels as conditions change. Check them before you go anywhere this weekend and follow local instructions if alerts are raised.

World.title: Juan Manuel Cerúndolo Beats Nicolás Mejía to Set Up Carlos Alcaraz Clash in Shanghai
World.content:
Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerúndolo advanced to the second round of the Shanghai Masters on Thursday with a 6-4, 6-4 victory over Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía, setting up a meeting with world No. 3 Carlos Alcaraz. The 24-year-old Argentine needed just one hour and 22 minutes to get past Mejía, a qualifier ranked No. 119 in the world. Cerúndolo, ranked 55th, recovered from an early deficit and took control of the match with his left-handed serve and consistent baseline play.

He finished with five aces, committed no double faults and won 84% of the points behind his first serve. Cerúndolo converted four of seven break-point opportunities while dropping his own serve twice. The victory was Cerúndolo’s first at the Shanghai Masters after losing in the opening round of his tournament debut last year.

His reward is a considerably tougher assignment against Alcaraz, who enters the tournament as the No. 2 seed and one of the favorites for the title. The Spaniard arrives in Shanghai fresh off winning the Japan Open in Tokyo on Tuesday, defeating Czech player Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4), 6-4 in the final.

That victory marked Alcaraz’s first title since returning from a lengthy absence caused by a wrist injury. The 23-year-old has steadily regained his form in recent months and is looking to win the Shanghai Masters for the first time. His best previous result at the tournament was a quarterfinal appearance in 2024.

Saturday’s second-round meeting will be the first official tour-level match between Alcaraz and Cerúndolo, although the two players have faced each other before. They met at the 2021 Next Gen ATP Finals in Milan, where Alcaraz defeated the Argentine 4-0, 4-1, 2-4, 4-3 (7-3) during the group stage. Alcaraz went on to win that tournament, which featured some of the leading young players in men’s tennis.

Cerúndolo has since developed into an established presence on the ATP Tour, with several notable performances against higher-ranked opponents. His biggest victory came at this year’s French Open, where he stunned then-world No. 1 Jannik Sinner in the second round. The Argentine rallied from two sets down to win 3-6, 2-6, 7-5, 6-1, 6-1 after Sinner began struggling with physical problems while leading in the third set. The result ended the Italian’s 30-match winning streak.

Cerúndolo followed that victory with a nearly six-hour win over Spain’s Martín Landaluce to reach the fourth round of a Grand Slam for the first time. Those results added to a career that began attracting international attention in 2021, when Cerúndolo won the Córdoba Open in Argentina as a 19-year-old qualifier making his ATP Tour debut.

Thursday was also a productive day for Argentine tennis in Shanghai. Sebastián Báez recovered from a slow start to defeat American Marcos Giron 1-6, 6-3, 6-4. Thiago Tirante advanced with a 6-4, 6-2 victory over Serbia’s Hamad Medjedovic, while Camilo Ugo Carabelli rallied past qualifier Ilya Simakin 2-6, 6-2, 7-5.

The four victories gave Argentina a strong opening to the ATP Masters 1000 tournament, although Cerúndolo now faces the highest-profile challenge of the group. For Alcaraz, Saturday’s match offers an opportunity to extend his recent winning run. For Cerúndolo, it is another chance to test himself against one of the world’s best players just over four months after producing one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 season.

World.title: ‘Brother Where Art Thou?’ Salvadoran man accused of burglarizing his own brother’s home and stealing $540 granted bail
World.content:
‘Brother Where Art Thou?’ Salvadoran man accused of burglarizing his own brother’s home and stealing $540 granted bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old Salvadoran national accused of breaking into his own brother’s home in Lords Bank Village and stealing $540 in cash has been granted bail after pleading not guilty to burglary.

Gerson Rodrigo Ceren Preza appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in Court #6 on Friday, where he was charged in connection with the alleged burglary of his brother’s home.

According to police, the incident occurred on Monday, October 5, when the brother left his Lords Bank residence secured around 5:21 p.m. Upon returning later that evening, he noticed that his front door appeared to have been tampered with.

A review of surveillance footage allegedly showed his younger brother, who lives nearby, entering the house while holding a knife and searching through a wallet. The brother subsequently discovered that $540 in cash was missing.

Police investigators later examined the residence and determined that entry had allegedly been gained by prying open the deadbolt lock on the wooden front door.

During a recorded police interview conducted in the presence of a Justice of the Peace, Gerson reportedly admitted to entering his brother’s home with a knife but denied stealing any money.

At Friday’s arraignment, Gerson attempted to explain his version of events, but Senior Magistrate Dennison advised him against making potentially incriminating statements after entering a not-guilty plea.

With no objection from the prosecution, bail was granted in the sum of $3,000 with one surety, which he met.

As conditions of bail, Gerson must provide a Belizean surety, refrain from contacting or interfering with his brother, and remain within Belize unless granted permission by the court. He must also report to the Ladyville Police Station every Friday between 7:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.

His next court appearance is scheduled for December 4, 2026.

World.title: Martin Lopez fined $1,500 for attacking 64-year-old uncle with machete
World.content:
Martin Lopez fined $1,500 for attacking 64-year-old uncle with machete

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 22-year-old Belize City construction worker has been fined a total of $1,500 after pleading guilty to attacking his 64-year-old uncle with a machete during a family dispute at their Buttonwood Bay residence.

Martin Lopez appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in Court #6 on Friday, where he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument and harm against his uncle, a retired teacher.

The incident occurred around 11:30 a.m. on Tuesday, October 6, at a residence on Buttonwood Bay in Belize City. According to the prosecution’s facts, the uncle had visited his mother’s home when his nephew began verbally abusing him. As the uncle attempted to leave, Lopez struck him twice in the back with a machete and once more on his right upper arm.

The injured man subsequently sought medical attention at the Cleopatra White Polyclinic, where a doctor observed swelling to his upper right arm and complaints of pain to his back and neck. His injuries were classified as harm.

In court, Lopez admitted to the attack but claimed he had been defending his grandmother, alleging that his uncle had been verbally abusing her when he arrived home for lunch. He described his uncle as a troublesome individual who was not supposed to be at the family residence.

However, Senior Magistrate Dennison rejected the explanation as a mitigating factor, noting that nothing in the prosecution’s facts supported Lopez’s claim that he had acted in defense of his grandmother. The court considered this an aggravating factor in determining his sentence.

Taking into account that Lopez had no previous convictions, Dennison imposed a $500 fine for aggravated assault, payable by November 30, 2026, or three months’ imprisonment in default. For the harm conviction, he was fined an additional $1,000, payable by January 31, 2027, or four months’ imprisonment in default.

Lopez was also ordered to pay $5 in court costs for each offense, bringing his total financial penalty to $1,510.

World.title: Accused killer of Edward ‘Scrubby’ Saldano, Paul Sambula receives full disclosure
World.content:
Accused killer of Edward ‘Scrubby’ Saldano, Paul Sambula receives full disclosure

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-one-year-old Paul Elver Sambula, accused of the March 2026 murder of well-known Belize City street figure Edward Saldano Jr., also known as “Scrubby,” has been provided with full disclosure of the prosecution’s evidence ahead of his preliminary inquiry.

Sambula, a former call center employee, appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Court #3 on Friday afternoon, where he received 162 pages of documents, 16 photographs and 11 DVDs containing evidence that prosecutors intend to rely upon in the murder case.

The Magistrate explained the disclosure process to Sambula and advised him to review the material before returning to court on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, for his preliminary inquiry. At that hearing, Sambula will have an opportunity to challenge the evidence before the matter proceeds toward committal to the High Court.

Sambula was initially arraigned on March 10, 2026, for the murder of 26-year-old Saldano, who was gunned down in broad daylight on March 5 near the intersection of Amara Avenue and Dean Street in Belize City. He was remanded to the Belize Central Prison, where he has remained in custody.

The killing, which was captured on surveillance footage, occurred around 12:30 p.m. as Saldano was riding his bicycle toward Dean Street. Footage showed him confronting and struggling with an armed attacker before being shot. After Saldano collapsed, the gunman allegedly stood over him and fired additional shots. Saldano was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he died.

Police subsequently indicated that the shooting may have stemmed from internal tensions involving individuals from the George Street area. Investigators reported that threats had allegedly been exchanged before the fatal confrontation.

Sambula, who turned 31 while incarcerated in April, remains on remand and has yet to secure legal representation.

World.title: Four BMW tires and rims valued at $1,500 stolen from Belize City garage
World.content:
Four BMW tires and rims valued at $1,500 stolen from Belize City garage

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the disappearance of four BMW tires and rims valued at $1,500 from a mechanic’s garage on Amandala Drive.

The owner reported that he discovered the tires missing from St. Martins One Stop garage on Tuesday, October 6.

He told police that the four 16-inch tires, mounted on silver rims, had been stored beside a container inside the garage compound.

He said he last saw the tires approximately one week earlier and discovered them missing when he visited the premises around 7:30 p.m.

He reportedly searched the property and questioned employees and neighboring residents, but nobody could account for the missing items.

Police are investigating the theft.

World.title: Belize expresses solidarity with Panama
World.content:
Belize expresses solidarity with Panama

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement saying that Belize stands in solidarity with the Government and people of the Republic of Panama following the recent earthquakes and the damage sustained by affected communities.

“We extend our solidarity to all those affected during this difficult time. Belize reaffirms its friendship with Panama and joins in the hope for the safety and resilience of its people and the restoration of homes and livelihoods,” the Ministry said.

Panama was shaken by a powerful 7.7 quake around 12:56 pm today.

World.title: Watchman charged after US$3,000 stolen from doctor’s Ladyville residence
World.content:
Watchman charged after US$3,000 stolen from doctor’s Ladyville residence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A watchman from Patchakan Village, Corozal District, has been arrested and charged with burglary after allegedly stealing US$3,000 from the home of a doctor along the Philip Goldson Highway.

Eloy Cawich was formally charged on Wednesday, October 7, following an investigation into a burglary at the residence of a 71-year-old doctor near Mile 10¼ of the highway.

The doctor reported that his home was burglarized sometime between 1:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. on Sunday, October 4.

He discovered that US$3,000 in various denominations had disappeared from an attaché case kept inside his bedroom.

According to the police report, the doctor identified Cawich, his employee, as the only other person who knew where the money was stored. Nothing else appeared to have been disturbed or stolen.

Investigators determined that entry had been gained by breaking glass louvers on a bathroom window. Crime scene technicians also recovered a fingerprint.

Police subsequently detained Cawich, who allegedly admitted to stealing the money during questioning.

The report further states that investigators conducted a video-recorded interview under caution in the presence of a justice of the peace, during which Cawich allegedly acknowledged entering the residence without permission and taking the money.

He was subsequently charged with burglary.

World.title: Construction worker investigate for attempted murder after allegedly chopping coworker with machete who made a joke about him
World.content:
Construction worker investigate for attempted murder after allegedly chopping coworker with machete who made a joke about him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an alleged attempted murder at a worksite along the Coastal Road, where a 19-year-old construction worker was attacked with a machete after making a joking remark about a colleague.

A resident of the Bullet Tree Road area, was injured during an incident at Coconut Point Company near La Democracia on Sunday, October 4.

According to his statement, the man said he was socializing with coworkers and their employer at their living quarters around 7:30 p.m. when he made a joking remark about a colleague known as “Dumbotas”.

The main claimed that the coworkerresponded by threatening to kill him with a machete, but he initially dismissed the threat because everyone had been laughing.

Moments later, while he was smoking a cigarette, he was reportedly struck in the back by a rock.

When he turned around, he allegedly saw his coworker standing a short distance away, swinging a machete toward his face.

The man raised his arm to protect himself and sustained a chop wound to his forearm. He claimed the attacker attempted another blow, but he managed to escape and lock himself inside his room.

The complainant was transported to the Western Regional Hospital, where he remained admitted in stable condition when police compiled their report.

Police detained the attacker, a Guatemalan national residing in Armenia Village, in connection with the attempted murder investigation. He is awaiting charges.

World.title: Department of the Environment assesses Economic impact of Sargassum on Coastal Communities
World.content:
Department of the Environment assesses Economic impact of Sargassum on Coastal Communities

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE), under the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, has hosted a closing workshop on the “Economic Assessment of Sargassum Impacts in Belize.”

The assessment was conducted by Rapid Environmental Assessment (2003) Ltd. (REAL), under the auspices of the DOE and the Central American Commission on Environment and Development (CCAD).

The study aims to establish baseline data on the economic and social effects of Sargassum influxes on Belize’s coastal communities, marine resources, and economic activities. Stakeholders in Placencia, Seine Bight, Hopkins, San Pedro, Ambergris Caye, and Caye Caulker were engaged to assess the impacts on tourism, fisheries, and local livelihoods.

The assessment examined changes in hotel occupancy, bookings, and tourist spending, as well as variations in fish catches, income losses, and increased operating costs for fishers. It also considered disruptions to coastal livelihoods, the costs of adaptation measures, government preparedness, policy gaps, and public spending on Sargassum management.

Representatives from the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, the DOE, CCAD, the Taiwan Cooperation, and the Belize Sargassum Task Force participated in the workshop to review the findings and discuss strategies to strengthen Belize’s response.

The DOE emphasized that collaboration among government agencies, coastal communities, and private-sector stakeholders is essential to protecting coastal and marine resources while supporting affected livelihoods.

World.title: Market Bag: Sorrel scarce, lettuce reaches $2,000
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaicans may have to dig deeper into their pockets for one of Christmas’ most beloved staples, as vendors at the Coronation Market warn that sorrel could be both scarce and expensive this year.

The festive favourite, traditionally used to make the popular Christmas drink, would normally be making its way into the market by now. However, sorrel was nowhere in sight when Market Bag visited this week, raising concerns about its availability ahead of the holiday season.

With drought conditions continuing to affect agricultural production, vendors say shoppers could face higher prices this year.

“You might search the whole market and you don’t find it. If you do find it, it’s still gonna have a price,” one vendor warned. “Anytime things get scarce, the less it is, the more the price goes up so I won’t put a fixed price because I’m not sure as yet. But the point still remains: if you pay $1,500 last year, now we have the drought, it would be maybe about $2,000.”

Meanwhile, prices for other produce remain high at Coronation Market this week, with lettuce climbing to as much as $2,000 per pound and plantains selling for $3,000 per dozen. Ripe bananas were going for $1,000 per dozen, while tomatoes were priced at $500 per pound.

Sweet peppers were selling for $400 per pound and Scotch bonnet peppers for $600 per pound. Onions and Irish potatoes dipped to $250 per pound, while sweet potatoes increased slightly to $450 per pound.

World.title: US announces sanctions on ICC, hours after Nobel award to former judge
World.content:
The Hague; Exterior of International Criminal Court or ICC in the Netherlands

WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — The United States (US) on Friday announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal’s operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a “rogue court,” escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump’s administration against the Hague-based tribunal.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement.

But the immediate impact of the sanctions was softened by a series of exemptions that offer a de facto six-month grace period.

The State Department said that was meant to give the court’s member states time to show “meaningful progress” toward addressing US concerns.

The grace period could be adjusted depending on the “success or failure” of those efforts, the department added.

The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that “history will judge this moment.”

Countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement that they “strongly disagree” with the announcement.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the US decision “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar.”

The European Union called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work.”

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, said it hoped the six-month delay meant “there is room for dialogue.”

Rights group Amnesty International urged countries to “resist” the move, saying the sanctions were “designed to isolate and ultimately destroy” the court.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant over alleged crimes in Gaza, praised the US action.

“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” his office posted on X.

The move came on the same day the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the peace prize to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal, served on the ICC and later led a UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.

Rubio’s statement did not mention Pillay or the Nobel award.

He said the sanctions were needed to protect security personnel and elected officials from prosecution by a court the United States has never joined.

“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said, adding that the measures would cut off the court’s resources and cripple “its ability to operate.”

The top US diplomat said Washington had for more than a year spelled out “basic gestures of good faith” it expected from the court, and had held off on the designation in hopes that the ICC or its member states would change course.

He said no “meaningful steps” had been taken to address US concerns.

Rubio also called on US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defense” to rein it in, warning that otherwise Washington would keep working to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.”

The Trump administration had already sanctioned 17 people linked to the court, including its prosecutor and several judges, over the ICC’s investigations involving the United States and Israel, which is also not a member.

Trump last month called on all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as “out of control” and a “rogue institution.”

World.title: Hope, Rutherford fire West Indies to record T20 chase of 250
World.content:
West Indies Romario Shepherd (left) and captain Shai Hope celebrate after winning the second T20 international cricket match between India and West Indies at the JSCA International Stadium Complex in Ranchi on October 9, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

RANCHI, India (AFP) — Skipper Shai Hope and Sherfane Rutherford struck blazing knocks as the West Indies recorded the second-highest T20 chase of all time on Friday to beat India by six wickets.

After India posted 249-5 batting first, the West Indies rode on a 120-run fourth-wicket partnership between Hope, who hit an unbeaten 102, and Rutherford (84) to achieve the target with nine balls to spare in Ranchi.

Hope completed the win with the ninth six of his innings and one that brought up his century off 45 balls, as the West Indies bounced back to level the five-match series at 1-1.

“When you chase here in India, you always give yourself a chance,” said Hope.

“You always think you’re in the game, regardless of what score is on the board. But (from) 5-2 was always going to be challenging.”

South Africa hold the record for the highest successful run chase in men’s T20 cricket, scoring 259-4 against the West Indies in Centurion in 2023.

West Indies’ previous best chase was when they overhauled 231 by South Africa in Johannesburg in 2015.

Hope and the left-handed Rutherford led an aggressive counter-attack after joining forces with the West Indies 58-3.

Rutherford reached his fifty off 24 balls and kept up the charge before falling to left-arm wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav.

He hit seven fours and seven sixes in his 37-ball blitz.

Hope, who struck his second T20 ton, stood firm and put on an unbeaten stand of 74 with Romario Shepherd, who hit 34.

Rutherford later called Hope a “phenomenal player” and one who “inspires” him.

Indian speedster Mayank Yadav struck in the opening over with two successive wickets, including removing Shimron Hetmyer for a first-ball duck.

Yadav also bowled Rovman Powell for 24 with a delivery that clocked 150 km/h (93 mph), but Hope and Rutherford turned the match in the West Indies’ favour.

Earlier, Sanju Samson made 82 off 41 balls before skipper Shreyas Iyer and Tilak Varma powered India to an imposing total after being asked to bat first.

Iyer said dew played a major part in the West Indies chase.

“The margin of error on this wicket was very minor. Any minor error was going into the stands,” he said.

Samson and Ishan Kishan (43) put on 97 runs for the second wicket after swashbuckling opener Abhishek Sharma departed for 20.

Spinner Roston Chase struck the first blow and then delivered two more — bowling Kishan and Shivam Dube — to check India’s surge.

Pace bowler Shamar Springer dismissed Samson but Iyer and Varma bludgeoned 83 runs off 33 balls for the fifth wicket.

Iyer fell to the penultimate ball of the innings after a rapid 40 off 18 balls while Varma finished unbeaten with 44 in equally quick time.

The third match is on Sunday in Indore.

World.title: JPS says power restored after outage impacts several parishes
World.content:
A Jamaica Public Service (JPS) technician on the job. (File photo)

Jamaica Public Service Company (JPS) is advising that all customers have been restored with electricity following service disruption across several parishes on Friday morning.

The electricity provider said the outage was due to transient trips on the transmission network which also impacted generating units. Adverse weather conditions were being experienced at the time of the trips, JPS said in a release.

All customers were restored by 11:34am following the system disturbance at 10:14am. The cause of the event is being further investigated, JPS said.

Among the parishes impacted, based on reports reaching Observer Online, were Kingston, St Andrew, Manchester, Clarendon and St James.

World.title: WATCH: Tile City launches $290m showroom on Constant Spring Road
World.content:
Tile City and Home Centre launched its state-of-the-art Signature Showroom on Constant Spring Road in St Andrew on Thursday, bringing an immersive experience that the company says opens the door to a fresh approach to building, renovating and designing spaces.

The company invested approximately $290 million in the 10,000 square foot showroom, including $40 million in a 240 kilowatt solar energy system.

Among the guests at the launch were Minister of Industry, Investment and Commerce Senator Aubyn Hill, as well as Minister of State in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce, Delano Seiveright.

Seiveright praised Tile City’s growth and the impact the initiative will have on the Jamaican economy.

“I am very proud of Tile City and Home Centre, they have been around for 27 years, they started off with two containers and here there are now with this massive showroom,” Seiveright said. “We are excited about it, they have created jobs, they have created opportunities and their reach spreads throughout the entire Jamaican economy.”

According to the company, the grand opening celebrates more than a new space, noting that it represents a renewed commitment to inspiring creativity, making quality design more accessible and helping Jamaicans bring their visions for their homes and projects to life.

(Video by Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: ‘Just know it wasn’t me’: Cardi B addresses cancelled BZR WKND performance
World.content:
Cardi B performs during halftime during Game Three of the 2026 NBA Finals between the San Antonio Spurs and the New York Knicks on June 8, 2026 at Madison Square Garden in New York, New York. (Photo: AFP)

American rapper Cardi B has broken her silence following the cancellation of her highly anticipated performance at BZR WKND in Jamaica, apologising to disappointed fans while insisting that the circumstances surrounding her withdrawal were beyond her control.

In a video message shared on Friday morning, the Bodak Yellow hitmaker said she had initially intended to let the official cancellation statement speak for itself but felt compelled to address the situation amid speculation about the reason for her withdrawal.

“Good morning, I wasn’t really gonna address this because I felt like the statement was enough, but clearly it wasn’t. First things first, I want to really, really apologise to Jamaica and to my Jamaican fans. The reason why I cancelled so late is because when I say I tried my best and I waited and I waited and I waited for things to get in place and together, but it didn’t,” she said.

The Grammy-winning artiste explained that she had been looking forward to visiting the island, particularly as the trip coincided with her birthday celebrations. She revealed that she had made arrangements to extend her stay in Jamaica for a vacation with friends and family following the performance.

“I’m actually sad that I’m not able to go to Jamaica because this weekend is my birthday weekend. So I made plans for next weekend cause after my performance, I was planning to vacation with my friends and my family members for a couple of more days after my performance, which clearly that’s not happening,” she continued.

Cardi B also dismissed speculation that poor ticket sales had prompted the cancellation, claiming that more than 18,000 tickets had been sold for the event.

“For the haters, not the Jamaicans, but for the haters talking about due to low ticket sales, it was never that because I heard there was over 18,000 tickets sold and not only that, but it’s like be for real I’m Cardi B. I’ve done sold out in Saudi Arabia, in Thailand, everywhere around the world and not only was Jamaica was going to pop out for Cardi B, you have people from different Caribbean islands that were going, from The Bahamas to the Dominican Republic to St Lucia…Everybody was going to come see me.”

While the rapper stopped short of revealing the specific issues that led to her withdrawal, she suggested that contractual restrictions prevented her from disclosing further details.

“However, I can’t talk. I can’t talk…contracts, but just know it wasn’t me. Just know. And I’m sorry. I tried my best. I waited this long because I was trying to give chances over and over and over and over and over and over and over again and things didn’t meet to the point that it’s like, it would have just, it’s just, oh, I don’t want to say much,” she said.

Despite the setback, Cardi B expressed hope that she would eventually get the opportunity to perform for her Jamaican fans.

“Just know that I’m sorry. And I really, really, really wish that I could come and perform in Jamaica one day because I really love you guys. I have an amazing fan base out there and I’m sorry. And I love you and sh*t is beyond my hands. I promise y’all,” she ended the video saying.

News of the American rapper’s withdrawal broke on Thursday afternoon, just over a week before her scheduled October 18 performance at the National Stadium in Kingston.

Cardi B had been announced as the headline act for BZR WKND, which is scheduled to run from October 16 to 18.

World.title: MELISSA FRAUD SHIELD
World.content:
One of a number of houses in Unions Acres, St James, still waiting for repair to the damage caused by last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

LASCO Financial Services has revealed that it began holding back 30 per cent of donations made through the Government’s Hurricane Melissa relief platform after its system flagged as suspicious, a number of transactions linked to the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

LASCO said it remitted 70 per cent of the money received to ODPEM daily while the reserve was being held, with more than 95 per cent of all donated amounts having been paid over to the agency by the end of March, before the 30 per cent withholding was discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account returned to normal.

The disclosure provides a new explanation for the arrangement, which came under scrutiny after the Auditor General’s Department found that 30 per cent of online donations had been retained for up to 45 days by a financial services institution, without a formal written agreement governing the retention.

The audit found that $15.7 million and US$298,429 in donations withheld between October 28 and December 31, 2025 were due to be transferred to ODPEM by February 15, 2026.

However, the financial services institution told auditors on March 9 that none of the withheld funds had yet been transferred.

Four days later, ODPEM provided a transfer receipt showing that $16.1 million and US$305,292 had been sent on March 9, but the auditor general said she could not independently confirm that the money had reached ODPEM’s accounts because the agency had not provided the relevant bank statements.

LASCO Financial, in a July 31 letter to Public Accounts Committee (PAC) Chairman Julian Robinson, said the decision to retain the money followed a review of the risk associated with the account after its payment system detected suspicious activity.

According to the company, the 30 per cent was not treated as money belonging to it, but as a refundable security reserve intended to protect against possible losses arising from disputed or fraudulent card transactions.

The company said a July 8, 2024 agreement with ODPEM expressly provided for a refundable security reserve, but no reserve was instituted at the time, based on the risk assessment then in place.

LASCO Financial said the 45-day period was based on guidance from its banking partners, who advised that this was the period within which a customer could challenge a transaction.

“If a charge-back occurred due to ODPEM transactions, without reserve, LASCO would have to absorb full loss,” the company said, adding that the arrangement was “standard practice by financial institutions in these types of transactions”.

A charge-back occurs when a card transaction is challenged and the money is reversed through the banking system.

LASCO said the reserve was therefore intended to ensure that money would be available if a transaction processed through the donation platform was later disputed and reversed.

The company said the donation button remained active on the Government’s Support Jamaica website and continued to receive contributions, while the withholding arrangement was eventually discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account had returned to normal levels.

The latest explanation comes after the issue was raised during a meeting of the PAC on July 28 at which questions were asked about why a financial institution had been allowed to retain a portion of disaster donations and whether there was a formal agreement authorising the arrangement.

At that meeting, ODPEM Director General Commander Alvin Gayle told the PAC that the funds, which had prompted the auditor general’s concern, had since been received by the agency.

Gayle also acknowledged that there had been no formal arrangement specifically governing the retention of Hurricane Melissa funds, even though there was an existing agreement covering the processing of donations.

In a subsequent August 31 response from the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) to questions from the committee, the Government said the legal teams of ODPEM and LASCO were still discussing the terms of the agreement.

The OPM also told the PAC that ODPEM selected LASCO after assessing the available payment-processing options.

It said LASCO is currently the only financial services provider with which Amber Innovations Inc — the company behind the relevant licensed payment products — has granted a non-exclusive licence for a payment-based solution to merchants.

World.title: ‘I don’t shy away from court’
World.content:
Attorney Hugh Wildman speaking at a news conference on Thursday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Attorney Hugh Wildman on Thursday insisted that he would never deliberately stay way from the fraud trial of his client Fritz Pinnock in the St Andrew Parish Court, but said his involvement in the murder case of six cops in the Home Circuit Court, downtown Kingston, has been creating unavoidable scheduling clashes due to the latter matter being dragged out by the prosecution.

Wildman was defending himself at a news conference he called a day after Justice Sanchia Burrell told Pinnock that he may have to cross-examine a witness himself if no legal representation is present for him when the delay- plagued Ruel Reid and company fraud trial resumes next Monday.

“Today’s press conference is called to respond to the media reports and various comments concerning the Pinnock and Reid matter, where the judge made certain comments in my absence and gave the impression that I deliberately stayed away from the court.

I wish to make it abundantly clear that everybody in Jamaica knows my position; I don’t shy away from court,” Wildman said.

“In fact, I am known to appear in all courts and take a certain stand to defend my clients vigorously,” he said.

“The situation is this: It is a known fact that we are engaged in the trial of the six police in downtown since the 7th of January of this year.

When the case commenced, the trial judge [Sonia Bertram- Linton] made it abundantly clear that she got instructions from the chief justice that that case must be a priority case; that’s what she told us,” Wildman said.

He said that in all his years of practising law he has never seen a situation in which a murder trial is dragged out by the prosecution the way that the policemen’s matter has been.

“The case has been going on unnecessarily long because of the conduct of the prosecutor in recalling and recalling witnesses, evidence to adduce new evidence, and it goes on and on, uncontrolled.

It amounts to an abuse of process.

The case continues and continues, and nobody knows when this case will come to an end,” he said.

“Everybody in the justice system knows about this.

In fact, we have had cases in court where Supreme Court judges have said they know Mr Wildman is engaged in other matters, and they put off the case.

Up to this week…

The point is this, I explained to Ms Burrell the challenge we are having with the downtown case, which is a priority.

It’s a murder case with six policemen.

I’m representing four of the accused persons,” he said, emphasising that, “It is impossible for me to be at two places at the same time.” On Wednesday in the Parish Court, fellow defence attorney Carolyn Chuck told Justice Burrell that Wildman had advised that he would ask another attorney to hold in his stead; but no one turned up.

Chuck went on to share that Wildman had indicated that he could also have challenges with being present next week as he was given time off from the Supreme Court to deal with the arrangements for his mother’s funeral.

Justice Burrell acknowledged the sensitivity of the matter and extended condolence to Wildman’s family.

However, she queried why this had not been communicated before.

“I don’t take lightly that Mr Wildman is making funeral arrangements for his mother, and my condolence goes out to him and his family, but early information- sharing makes a huge difference,” she said.

“I have to be very sensitive because all of us who are here either have a mother or had a mother at some point…

but I am not understanding the lack of communication; the lack of communication is very unhelpful,” the judge said.

Emphasising that the case impacts four other accused, Burrell said Wildman and Pinnock are not entitled to an infinite supply of the court’s resources.

Her comments came on the one-year anniversary of the official start of the trial, which has been plagued with scheduling challenges.

“It cannot be that Mr Wildman avoids appropriate and adequate communication and expects to get what he asks for,” she said.

“How can the rights of four other people be expected to continuously and infinitely, at this point in time, … be expected to yield to Mr Wildman’s failure — I am using the word failure — to organise himself?” Justice Burrell said.

Pinnock, the former Caribbean Maritime University head; former education minister Ruel Reid; his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle; as well as Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence (Jamaica Labour Party, Brown’s Town Division) are defendants in the high-profile $25-million fraud trial in the parish court.

In the matter being heard in the Home Circuit Court, the six policemen are on trial for murder in relation to the January 12, 2013 shooting deaths of Matthew Lee, Ucliffe Dyer, and Mark Allen on Acadia Drive in St Andrew, during an alleged shoot-out.

On Thursday, Wildman said he was trying to find a solution to his problem, telling the news conference that he has written a letter to Chief Justice Bryan Sykes urging his intervention.

“I was shocked when I heard that the judge was behaving like that, as if I deliberately stayed away from court.

Everybody knows that that is not my style.

I want to be there to defend my client, Mr Pinnock, and defend him vigorously, because we maintain that there is no case against him.

But the point is that I am locked in that trial downtown.

What do I do?” he said.

“Should I have walked away from the criminal case downtown with the six policemen? I don’t know why this is taking so long.

Every day, up to yesterday, I made serious submissions in law based on the constitution, that the trial is an abuse of process with what is going on downtown,” he said.

World.title: EU budget slashed by €159B in new Irish proposal
World.content:
The bloc is split between frugal countries demanding cuts of several hundred billions to the nearly €2 trillion proposal on the table and a rival camp of southern and eastern states, known as the Friends of Cohesion, opposing reductions.

In a concession to the Friends of Cohesion, Ireland shielded farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, that account for half of the total budget and are politically sensitive, from any cuts.

Instead, the bulk of the reductions came from foreign aid which was cut by €38 billion; competitiveness which was axed by €75 billion and the EU’s administrative costs which were reduced by €10 billion.

Dublin also scrapped a rainy day fund, known as the "EU Facility cushion," that allowed the European Commission to deploy cash to tackle unforeseen emergencies throughout the seven-year budget cycle.

However, Ireland’s proposal is unlikely to satisfy the frugals, who have warned against disproportionate cuts to new EU-wide priorities such as competitiveness, defense and development funding.

Germany and its allies criticized the previous Cyprus Council presidency for cutting only €32 billion in the last negobox in June.

World.title: UK bans Protestant march from Catholic area in Northern Ireland
World.content:
“I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions,” Bryant appealed in a statement explaining why he was reversing the original decision by the Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body for managing the region’s chronic conflicts over Orange Order demonstrations.

Street fighting over those traditional marches helped to trigger the onset of Northern Ireland’s three-decade conflict, known as “The Troubles,” which left nearly 3,700 dead before a 1998 peace accord.

Hundreds of Catholic locals backed by Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party that leads Northern Ireland’s fraying cross-community government, gathered along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown to cheer the reversal.

First Minister Michelle O’Neill, who has been accused of breaking the law while helping locals block the Orangemen’s intended path since Sept. 27, went on Ireland’s flagship TV talk show, the Late Late Show, to express relief on behalf of the residents of Garvaghy Road.

“For the last 13 days they’ve been living with this constant fear and a cloud hanging over them that this unwanted sectarian march was going to be forced down that road,” she said.

But the main pro-British party in the coalition, the Democratic Unionists, denounced Bryant’s move as a capitulation to mob rule. Some DUP lawmakers called for Northern Ireland’s police chief, who had recommended the policy reversal, to be fired.

Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson said the U.K. government had sent a dangerous message that Northern Ireland “should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest.”

Northern Ireland’s nearly three-decade system for managing conflict over parades “now lies in tatters,” he said, “and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”

World.title: Ryanair lashes out at Air France and Lufthansa over ownership probe
World.content:
The association confirmed to POLITICO that it has spent months urging EU and Irish aviation authorities to investigate whether Ryanair complies with the bloc’s ownership and control rules.

Under those rules, airlines must be majority-owned and effectively controlled by EU nationals or entities to hold an EU operating license. ENAA argues that Ryanair no longer meets those requirements, pointing to the airline’s March announcement that only 30% of its shares are held by EU nationals. O'Leary, an Irish citizen, holds 4% of the stock.

When the Irish Aviation Authority seemed “reluctant to engage on the matter,” ENAA took the matter to court. If Ryanair loses the case, it could be forced to change its ownership structure. The carrier's operating license would only be suspended if it does not comply with the verdict.

An aircraft operated by Irish low cost airline Ryanair makes its way past BER airport's control tower in Schoenefeld on June 29, 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images

Ryanair has rejected the allegations, arguing that its non-EU shareholders do not have voting rights, which means the airline is under EU control.

In an emailed statement, Ryanair accused its rivals of attempting “to restrict competition and choice for EU air travel” by challenging its operating license.

Grounding risk seen as remote

Augusto Viansson Ponte, a London-based director at Alton Aviation Consultancy, doubted that the legal case would be easily dismissed, but also said it was unlikely that Ryanair would lose its operating license.

World.title: Arrested German spy chief lashed out at his old agency over allegations he spied for Russia
World.content:
Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest.

Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany.

The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties.

While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.”

Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.

Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.

Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin.

World.title: Dutch PM slams ‘absurd’ US decision to livestream execution
World.content:
“As far as I’m concerned, it is really up to the social media platforms in Europe to prevent this from being circulated and broadcast on their channels. But I fear it will be impossible to prevent,” he said.

Jetten added that if the execution does appear on European social media, there will be “a great number of reports filed,” as violent content must be moderated by social media platforms under European law.

“Video-sharing platforms that allow video content displaying scenes of gratuitous violence must use effective age assurance so that children cannot normally see this content,” a spokesperson for the Irish Media Commission told POLITICO. This means platforms can show violent content as long as they ensure it doesn’t reach minors.

The media regulator is currently investigating X over possible breaches in online safety rules for failing to carry out proper age checks.

The UN has said livestreaming an execution would amount to torture. “The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights told AFP.

The body said its statement is in line with previous ones it has released about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran.

The European Commission did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

This is a developing story.

World.title: France, Germany try to save face on joint tank project
World.content:
France’s chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, told lawmakers Thursday that Germany had pulled out of the project. His comments landed especially awkwardly as German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is currently on a state visit to France.

Later in the evening, Mandon tried to backpedal in a written statement, arguing the project was only delayed to the late 2040s.

In recent years, Franco-German defense industrial projects have repeatedly failed. MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that France and Germany would most likely build separate tanks.

Now, Pistorius has said the two countries will still work together on “unmanned systems and automated processing.”

The German minister pledged that the project wouldn’t meet the same fate as the Future Combat Air System, the joint next-generation fighter jet program that collapsed before the summer. “The crucial point is that we learn from our mistakes. That is why MGCS is in no way at risk and remains an important future project for our two nations and our two armed forces,” he said.

But the imbroglio highlights strains in the defense relationship between Paris and Berlin, and an increasing number of French lawmakers are now calling for Paris to look for other partners.

“Defense cooperation with Germany is at an all-time low, since Germany is going it alone,” a French lawmaker working on defense policy told POLITICO on condition of anonymity.

Rixa Fürsen contributed to this article from Bordeaux, France.

World.title: Silent killer: study finds most with high blood pressure unaware
World.content:
A recent British study involving around 1.4 million people in England has found that more than a third of adults have high blood pressure.

 

Worryingly, the study shows that around 6 in every 10 people affected, 59%, do not know they are living with this "silent killer" and have not received any treatment.

These figures highlight a persistent failure to detect one of the main risk factors leading to heart and vascular disease and strokes, amid growing calls from health experts to step up early screening campaigns and save millions of people at risk of deadly complications.

A marked rise with age

Researchers from the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford analysed blood pressure readings taken in clinics as part of the "Our Future Health" programme, the largest health research initiative in the United Kingdom. The data covered participants who joined the programme between 2022 and 2025.

The study used World Health Organization criteria to define high blood pressure, classifying someone as hypertensive if their systolic reading is 140 millimetres of mercury or above, their diastolic reading is 90 millimetres of mercury or above, or if they are already taking blood-pressure-lowering medication.

The data showed a large variation in prevalence by age: 15% among adults aged 18 to 39, rising gradually to 71% in people aged 80 and over.

Men were more likely than women to have the condition, with rates of 42% for men compared with 29% for women, after adjusting for age groups.

Half of those on treatment do not reach the target level

The problem does not only concern undiagnosed cases. The study found that 50% of participants taking one or more medicines to lower blood pressure still had readings of 140/90 millimetres of mercury or above, the threshold used in the research to define high blood pressure.

According to the researchers, these findings show that difficulties in diagnosing and controlling the condition in England persist, despite clinical guidelines that have been in place for years.

They pointed out that current guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) requires several measurements before confirming a diagnosis and, in some cases, recommends starting with lifestyle changes before prescribing medication. They believe this approach may be leaving some cases without detection or effective treatment.

Calls for a more proactive approach

Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician in the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on the study, said high blood pressure is often described as a "silent killer", arguing that the current methods of detecting and treating the condition need to be reconsidered.

Liu stressed that the "silent killer" crisis is not confined to older people, noting that more than 15% of younger adults aged 18 to 39 were found to have high blood pressure.

She noted that this younger group currently falls outside routine medical monitoring, as they do not meet the age criteria for the National Health Service (NHS) regular health check programme, which starts at 40. This, she said, makes an urgent update of early detection policies necessary.

Liu called for stronger population-wide prevention strategies, alongside directing treatment towards those most at risk of heart disease and other cardiovascular conditions.

For his part, Ian Turnbull, deputy chief medical officer for the "Our Future Health" programme, clinical researcher in Oxford University's Population Health Department and a general practitioner, said the results are in line with what doctors see in general practice, where many cases of high blood pressure remain undetected or are not treated optimally.

He highlighted the need for a more active approach to finding people with the condition, including examining whether treatment should start on the basis of an individual's predicted risk of heart and vascular disease, rather than relying solely on blood pressure levels.

British Heart Foundation warns of missed chances for prevention

Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, described the study's findings as worrying, saying they reveal the scale of undiagnosed high blood pressure and the difficulties in controlling it among people who are already receiving treatment.

Williams said high blood pressure remains the main modifiable risk factor associated with cardiovascular disease, noting that it is linked to around half of all heart attacks and strokes in the United Kingdom.

He added that millions of people are living with the condition without knowing it, which means important opportunities for diagnosis and early intervention are being missed.

According to Williams, improving the detection and treatment of high blood pressure could help tens of thousands of people avoid preventable heart attacks and strokes. However, he believes this will require a rethink of how people at risk are identified, treated and followed up, to ensure blood pressure checks and effective therapy reach all groups.
