World.title: As Russia escalates its war, the EU realises its support for Ukraine won't be enough
World.content:
The European Union is rapidly coming to terms with the limitations of its multibillion-euro support for Ukraine, as Russia's all-out escalation wrecks the country's finances, depletes its air defences and deepens its reliance on cash-strapped donors.

 

"This war will last longer than we thought," a European diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "There's a realisation that needs will continue to present themselves, but it's not yet clear how this will be addressed."

"We must send a clear message that the EU won't change its position and will double down on its support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia," another diplomat said.

Railways, bridges, cargo vessels, power stations, data centres, warehouses, medical centres, schools and kindergartens have all come under Russian airstrikes in recent days. Even the National Academy of Sciences has been targeted.

The relentless bombardment, a calculated mix of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, has killed scores of civilians, including over 30 people in Kramatorsk after a glide bomb attack set two public buses ablaze.

On Thursday, Russia plunged Kyiv into darkness, offering a grim preview of a winter that is likely to be the harshest, cruellest yet of the war.

This is "terror against people and life. And it is important that leaders do not ignore what is happening", Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

"Pure and simple: these are war crimes," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, expressing her solidarity.

The escalation has hit the country's war-battered economy particularly hard, as the endless waves of drones disrupt ordinary activity, force businesses to close, raise material costs and eat away at profits.

Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has added further strain, preventing Ukrainian farmers from selling tonnes of grain to their global clients and depriving the state of an essential source of revenue.

The deterioration raises serious questions about the viability and durability of the EU's multiple support programmes, notably the €90 billion loan that leaders agreed last year to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's needs for 2026 and 2027.

The loan, it must be noted, was designed under the premise that the war would end sometime this year. Russia's escalation all but guarantees this will not be the case.

Russia has wrecked destruction on Ukraine. AP Photo

Ukraine's Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has warned that the 2027 budget will be the most complicated since the start of the full-scale invasion. He has urged international donors to fill a staggering $78 billion (€70 billion) gap.

The Commission has refrained from endorsing the headline figure, which vastly exceeds the €45 billion it plans to provide next year under the support loan. Instead, it has promised to speed up disbursements, contingent on internal reforms.

"For 2027, the picture is indeed more challenging," Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said on Friday after a meeting of finance ministers.

"It's clear that we are facing a sizeable funding gap. The exact quantification is still a work in progress."

Brussels has not formally reopened the debate on new support for Ukraine, as member states are currently embroiled in bitter negotiations over the next EU budget.

Officials and diplomats, however, privately admit it is only a matter of time before leaders are compelled to address the matter, which has become increasingly contentious amid rising debt, stagnant growth and far-right opposition.

The total absence of US aid, once a key provider of weapons, compounds the equation.

A group of EU countries has attempted to revive the debate on the immobilised Russian assets, arguing the €90 billion loan "will not be enough".

But Belgium, the main custodian of the assets, has pushed back. France and Italy, two key votes, remain reluctant to go down the uncharted avenue.

"On the assets, there's still some interest, but we still remember very clearly what happened in December," a senior diplomat said, referring to the dramatic summit where an asset-backed proposal fell apart. The loan was then set up as Plan B.

"As of now, there's nothing new or substantial on the table."

The option of issuing more joint debt to support Ukraine, as done with the €90 billion, has become politically unattractive amid spiralling borrowing costs.

Meanwhile, the option of ramping up bilateral contributions, which is much more straightforward, risks placing the burden on a few wealthy countries, namely Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordics.

With no easy solutions, Brussels is asking other allies, such as the UK, Canada and Japan, to step up to the plate as it figures out what to do next.

"We are assessing other possibilities in any case," Dombrovskis said. "We are committed to ensuring that Ukraine has the necessary funding for as long as it's necessary."

World.title: 'Crashout', 'Ragebait' or 'Peak': Want to know which word is favoured by Germany's youth?
World.content:
For weeks, young Germans have been able to vote on which word best reflects their generation. The favourites are "Crashout", "Ragebait" and "Peak". Together, they attracted votes in the mid six-figure range. The poll was open to 11- to 20-year-olds.

 

On Saturday, Langenscheidt, the publishing house behind the vote, will announce this year's winning term at the Frankfurt Book Fair. These are the favourites.

Crashout

If you "crashout", you've lost control. "Completely losing your composure, freaking out or emotionally exploding," is how the Langenscheidt jury defines the term, which has already made it into the top three.

The twist: it does not always mean that someone is genuinely overreacting. The word can also be used ironically, especially when an emotional outburst is triggered by something trivial.

Ragebait

This term refers to digital posts on social media: content deliberately designed to provoke a reaction. "With provocative takes, blatant false claims or completely wild opinions, people try to stir up anger," explains the Langenscheidt jury.

For responses are the currency on platforms such as Instagram or TikTok. Reactions bring clicks, comments, shares and reach. The more outrage there is, the more often a post is shown: the algorithm boosts it.

Peak

This originally English word can in fact be translated literally in German: it is about peak values, highlights and summits. "If something is peak, it is the best of the best – the absolute high point, maximum quality or simply 10/10," is how the Langenscheidt jury puts it.

The other most voted words of 2026:

Altogether, 43 percent of all votes cast went to the top three terms, according to an analysis by the publisher. Since 2008 it has been choosing the Youth Word of the Year.

For Langenscheidt's spokesperson there was a surprise. The popular 67 (Six Seven), which comes with a hand gesture, only made it into the top ten and not into the three most popular terms. It is less about a fixed meaning than about belonging. The trend went viral thanks to TikTok, basketball memes and above all the song "Doot Doot (6 7)" by US rapper Skirlla.

"We were actually sure that 67 would end up in the top three," said the publishing house's spokesperson. "Once again, it shows how unpredictable and fast youth language evolves." The fact that many of the words are Anglicisms, on the other hand, came as little surprise to the publisher – that was already the case back in 2023.

Another absolute classic, "Digga", was among the submissions once more, but the term has never yet taken first place.

The Youth Word of the Year clearly shows just how much language use is shaped by social media. AP Photo

In addition, the line "Du bist gut genug" ('You are good enough') from a song by KitschKrieg, Shirin David and Blumengarten made it into the top ten. The short sentence went viral on TikTok and other platforms and has also delighted audiences abroad. According to the Langenscheidt jury, there are now countless memes, remixes and parodies of it.

Another term, "Gute Käse", does not have a literal meaning but roughly stands for "really good" and "solid", and ranks among the ten most popular expressions. "Macker" can mean boyfriend, crush, mate or simply a guy, depending on the context. "Schere" comes from gaming and is used in the sense of "Sorry, my bad".

Yet another language made it into the top ten: the Turkish version of the word "super". The term became widely known through a viral video of an ultramarathon runner who, when asked "How are you?" after his race, simply replied "Süper".

"Mehrzweckeier" ruled out by jury

The jury also excluded a term this year that had been submitted many times: "Mehrzweckeier". The expression first appeared at a demonstration against the reintroduction of conscription. The placard originally carried the slogan "Merz leck Eier", which was confiscated by the police. The protester then faced an investigation for slander and defamation.

Afterwards, a campaign on Reddit called on people to submit the altered term "Mehrzweckeier" as a candidate for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year. The jury vetoed it "because the term stems from a campaign and at the same time is based on a personal insult", as the reasoning puts it. It therefore meets two key exclusion criteria, the jury said.

Gammelfleischparty: The very first Youth Word of the Year

In 2008, "Gammelfleischparty" was chosen as the very first Youth Word of the Year. It refers to an over-30s party and is a cynical comment on how young people see older generations.

As the years went by, terms such as "hartzen", "swag" and the acronym "Yolo" ('you only live once') were voted winners.

More votes than ever before

Thanks not least to social media and Susanne Daubner reading out the shortlist on the main German news programme Tagesschau, the vote on the Youth Word of the Year has attracted huge attention.

World.title: When will El Niño peak and end? A full timeline of the weather phenomenon taking the world by storm
World.content:
2026 will go down in history for what could become the largest El Niño in living memory, as the world scrambles to prepare for an onslaught of extreme weather.

 

The natural weather phenomenon (Spanish for ‘the boy’) occurs irregularly – roughly every two to seven years – when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. Experts first started warning that a strong El Niño could form at the beginning of this year, supported by large amounts of heat in the subsurface ocean and the expected weakening of low-level trade winds.

In the first week of June, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed that El Niño conditions were officially underway. Towards the end of summer, experts warned that the “unprecedented” El Niño could become the largest event since the 19th century – gaining the nickname of a ‘Godzilla’ or ‘Super’ El Niño.

Is El Niño getting stronger – and what are the impacts?

According to the WMO, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October, November and December.

Sea-surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of El Niño, are measured by the widely used Niño 3.4 index. This increased markedly from an average +1.6 °C above normal in June 2026 to +2.5 °C above normal in August.

For October-November-December, the seasonal average Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly is forecast to reach approximately +3.7°C. This would be the highest since observations began and is stronger than the previous record of +2.6°C in November 2015-January 2016.

Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe.

El Niño’s weather impacts are mainly felt in the tropics, but Europe can experience milder, wetter winters. An El Niño peak can also weaken the polar vortex, increasing the likelihood of a cold snap.

South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.

Extreme weather overseas will still have a knock-on effect for Europe. The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands has been working in areas that are directly impacted by El Niño and warn that many staple foods that Europe imports could be at risk.

For example, in Nicaragua, crops such as maize and beans may fail in already fragile areas, leading to food insecurity and income loss in the country. A lack of rain and low flows in rivers also mean that irrigated crops in Colombia, Northeast Brazil and India will face severe restrictions or will need to rely more on groundwater, potentially causing overexploitation in the area – and export shortages.

A timeline of El Niño: When will it peak and end?

The WMO’s latest statement says that El Niño is forecast to peak in December, and will continue into next year.

“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” warns WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 per cent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”

Related El Niño transforms Atacama desert as thousands of hectares burst into bloom

The almost-certain figure isn’t from one climate model. The WMO has coordinated ocean buoy, satellite and radiosonde data from 13 national and international centres to make the prediction.

El Niño isn’t expected to end until spring 2027, but its impacts will likely stretch further. It’s why experts warn that next year could become the hottest on record.

El Niño clashes with climate change

Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.

Human-caused global warming from the burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. It is this that paved the way for Europe’s scorching summer, long-standing drought and deadly wildfires.

Nowadays, El Niño’s impacts are compounded by an already warming world – one that has a much stronger influence on the extreme weather we’re witnessing. 2025, for example, was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally-forming cool drag of El Niño’s counterpart, La Niña.

Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño events too, by making them 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era.

“El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok in October.

“The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

World.title: Which Europeans post the most holiday selfies? Study reveals travellers’ social media habits
World.content:
Are the reels, snapshots and vlogs in cyberspace impacting how we travel in real life? Well, if you’re a Portuguese traveller, you’re probably more likely to upload selfies and personal photos from your trips than tourists from elsewhere.

 

This was a finding in the latest study by online travel agency Opodo, which looked into the way social media is shaping travel choices. The research drew on responses from 9,000 travellers from the UK, US, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Germany and France.

Portuguese travellers upload selfies and personal photos from their trips the most (50%), according to the research. They are followed by Spanish travellers, who rank second in the survey (40%), then Italian (35%), German (30%) and French (22%).

Opodo’s survey also asked respondents whether or not social media has inspired them to travel to somewhere they had never previously considered.

This especially rang true among travellers aged 25 to 35, with 52% saying that it does inspire their holiday choices. This figure is up from 32% in a similar poll in 2024.

This trend is amplified even further among Gen Z travellers at 59%. While, in comparison, for respondents aged 65 and above, just 5% get their inspiration from social media.

Social media as a travel influencer

On the other side of the Atlantic, however, American travellers lead the way in being most likely to venture abroad after being influenced by social media (49%). The US is followed by travellers from Spain (48%) and Italy (44%), while Brits are apparently the least interested market surveyed with only 25% saying it holds influence over them.

"Social media has become a powerful window to the world, making travel discovery more accessible, visual, and personal than ever before," Pablo Caspers, Chief Travel Officer at eDreams ODIGEO, said.

“Whether it's finding an off-the-beaten-track spot or capturing memories with loved ones, online platforms allow travellers to celebrate the best parts of their journeys and inspire others to explore."

But just how else is social media impacting our travel habits?

Fact versus digital fiction

Travellers were also asked how likely they would post a positive image of their travels on social media even if the trip fell flat.

Opodo found that Portuguese travellers once again ranked top (54%) and were most likely to keep up a positive social media presence regardless of the quality of the trip. Travellers from the US and Spain follow behind at 46% and 36%, respectively.

Further, most Brits remain “relatively authentic”, with 27% saying they would be “very unlikely to post positively”, according to the research. While German travellers were among the least likely to put a positive spin on a disappointing trip, with just 23% saying they would post positively.

Europe’s foodies

As it turns out, the Portuguese are also massive foodies, with 66% of respondents saying they share content of their feasts online. Travellers from Spain rank next (57%), followed by German travellers (51%).

What else do Europeans share from their trips?

When it comes to admiring hotels and accommodation, Germans ranked the highest for sharing online images of their stay at 51%, followed by the Portuguese, French and Spanish – with the former respondents being 41% likely to do so and the latter two at 38%.

Portuguese travellers are also the most fascinated by landscapes and landmarks during their getaways, with 88% saying that’s what they post online. The Spanish are also fond of capturing the scenery around them (82%) followed by French and German travellers, both at 76%.

Aside from being the most likely to share selfies, food pictures and being fascinated by their surroundings, Opodo also found that the Portuguese were the most adventure-seeking travellers, too.

As many as 66% of Portuguese respondents said they share their experiences and activities during their trips, followed by Spanish and German travellers (57%), with the top three rounded off by Italian travellers at 53%.

Who cares most about social media while travelling?

Overwhelmingly, Opodo’s research points to travellers caring about what is said on social media when it comes to travel.

As many as 90% of Portuguese travellers are mindful of this, followed by Italians and Spanish (87%). French and German respondents both ranked at 82%.

When it comes to checking social media regularly, even while on holiday, German and US travellers are most likely to do so (both at 34%). Portugal and Spain came next (33% and 27% respectively). On the other hand, Italian travellers are the least concerned with social media developments while away (20%).

How else is social media influencing European travellers?

Which travellers are most likely to use social media to help them picture their holiday before booking?

1. Portuguese: 22%

2. Italian: 20%

3. German: 19%

World.title: Teacher salaries in Europe: Which countries offer the best pay?
World.content:
Higher pay for teachers is among the demands of unions behind recent protests in France, alongside more staff and better working conditions.

 

Their concerns reflect a wider challenge across Europe: making teaching financially attractive. Teachers are generally paid less than similarly educated workers, according to the OECD, and experts warn that salaries are not competitive enough to attract and retain staff.

So, which countries pay the highest teacher salaries? And how do teacher salaries rank when purchasing power is taken into account?

Teacher salaries vary widely across Europe, according to the OECD’s Education at a Glance 2026 report. Among the 28 education systems compared, actual salaries for primary school teachers in 2025 ranged from €18,669 in Turkey to €74,086 in Denmark.

Actual salaries refer to the annual average earnings received by full-time teachers aged 25-64 before taxes. They include all work-related payments, such as the base salary, performance-related bonuses, extra pay for holidays, and other payments.

Iceland (€73,752), Ireland (€69,747), Germany (€69,453) and Austria (€65,851) complete the top five, all above €65,000.

Teachers in Norway (€59,453), Belgium’s Flemish Community (€59,105), Northern Ireland (€57,838), Scotland (€57,619), Belgium’s French Community (€55,689), Wales (€52,894), Finland (€52,272) and England (€50,727) also earn more than €50,000.

Major economies: Germany highest, Italy lowest

Among the major European economies, Germany pays teachers the most. The four UK nations follow Germany, all with salaries above €50,000. Teachers earn €41,968 in France, while Italy has the lowest salaries at €32,100.

A figure for Spain is not available.

Several countries below €25,000

Actual teacher salaries are below €25,000 in seven countries: Czechia (€24,457), Hungary (€23,181), Slovakia (€22,936), Romania (€20,805), Latvia (€20,516), Greece (€18,746) and Turkey (€18,669).

“Large differences in European teacher salaries reflect differences in national income levels, salary structures, qualifications and career progression, rather than one single factor,” Daniel Wisniewski, secretary general of the European Federation of Education Employers, told Euronews Business.

“Differences in taxation, social benefits and allowances also complicate comparisons between countries.”

Teachers at upper secondary schools generally earn more than those at primary schools, except in Turkey and Northern Ireland. Salaries are the same at both levels in Scotland, Lithuania and Estonia.

Upper secondary teacher salaries range from €17,615 in Turkey to €93,938 in Iceland. They are also above €80,000 in Denmark (€85,999) and Germany (€80,163).

The largest gaps in favour of upper secondary teachers are seen in Iceland, Finland, Belgium, Denmark, Austria and Germany, where they are paid at least €10,000 more than primary school teachers.

What can teachers buy with their salaries?

Salary figures alone don't tell the whole story. If prices are high in a country, even relatively high teacher salaries could buy less than in another country.

To account for differences in living costs, Euronews Business adjusted the OECD’s salary figures in national currencies using Eurostat’s purchasing power parities for household final consumption expenditure.

The results are expressed in purchasing power standards (PPS), a common unit that can buy the same amount of goods and services in each country. The PPS measure uses average EU prices as a benchmark, while the OECD expresses its purchasing power comparisons in purchasing-power-adjusted US dollars.

On this basis, teachers in Germany have the highest purchasing power — meaning their gross salaries can buy the most goods and services — among the education systems compared.

Primary school teachers’ average annual pay after adjusting for price differences is lowest at 21,456 PPS in Greece and highest at 64,143 PPS in Germany.

Wisniewski noted that sizeable differences remain after adjusting for purchasing power, showing that living costs cannot by themselves explain the salary variation.

“National pay policies, qualification requirements, career scales, experience and the earnings available in alternative graduate professions also contribute significantly to the remaining gap,” he said.

Germany is followed by Austria (58,265 PPS), Denmark (53,036 PPS), Ireland (51,226 PPS) and Belgium’s Flemish Community (50,846 PPS), completing the top five education systems where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the most.

At the other end of the ranking, Greece is joined by Latvia (24,670 PPS), Slovakia (26,916 PPS), Czechia (27,349 PPS) and Estonia (28,197 PPS), where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the least among the education systems compared.

For upper secondary school teachers, Germany also tops the overall purchasing power ranking at 74,034 PPS, while Greece ranks lowest at 23,289 PPS.

Among Europe’s largest economies compared, Italy comes last at 36,964 PPS.

Three UK nations follow Germany, while England (43,091 PPS) ranks below France (46,058 PPS).

Professor Mihails Hazans of the University of Latvia noted that countries at the top of the teacher salary rankings in PPS also have GDP per capita well above the EU average.

“The factors behind these differences include traditions and social norms, strength of teachers’ trade unions, as well as actual workload covered by the statutory salaries,” he told Euronews Business.

Significant changes in PPS rankings

When nominal salary and PPS rankings are compared, some countries change position significantly. For primary school teachers, the biggest risers are Turkey, up six places, and Poland (up five). Belgium’s French Community and Romania both move up four places.

This means that these countries rank higher once differences in price levels are taken into account.

Iceland records the biggest fall, dropping from second place to 12th. Sweden and Estonia also fall by three places.

The OECD’s purchasing power rankings, which are based on US international dollars, differ from Euronews Business’s calculations using Eurostat conversion rates.

Turkey ranks significantly higher in the OECD rankings. It is 11th for primary school teachers and 17th for upper secondary school teachers.

Pay is not competitive enough to attract and retain teachers

Daniel Wisniewski pointed out that across OECD countries, teachers’ actual salaries at primary and general secondary levels average only 87–95% of the earnings of tertiary-educated workers, meaning that similarly qualified people can often earn more outside teaching.

“Teacher pay is not consistently competitive enough to attract and retain teachers across Europe,” he said.

Jelmer Evers, European director at the European Trade Union Committee for Education, suggested that teachers should be paid at least as much as other workers with comparable qualifications and responsibilities, reflecting the complexity and societal importance of their profession.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan's cultural presence?
World.content:
From coffee competitions to literature awards, Beijing appears to be working to limit Taiwan's international cultural and political impact.

When Taiwaneseauthor Yang Shuang-zi's "Taiwan Travelogue" won the 2026 International Booker Prize, it marked a historic breakthrough on the global stage. But behind the triumph lay a sharp geopolitical reality.

On stage, Lin King, who translated the book into English, gave voice to the anxiety looming over Taiwan, where she spent a large part of her childhood.

"In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, I made the explicit decision that rather than translating Sinophone works indiscriminately, I would only translate writing from Taiwan for the foreseeable future," she said in her acceptance speech. "I will continue to do so until the day comes that my homeland's sovereignty is no longer a provocation or a punchline — until no English speaker feels comfortable saying to me, 'I really should come visit you in Taiwan while it still exists.'"

Literature and politics

"Taiwan Travelogue" follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tour. As she and her Taiwanese interpreter explore local street food together, a subtle intimacy unfolds between them. The narrative centers Taiwan's history rather than Beijing's preferred "Greater China" framework.

"Literature and politics are directly connected," Yang told DW. "Politics determines the allocation of resources, and the allocation of resources determines which works get pulled out, held up high and defined as 'good literature.' The idea that politics can just be kept out of it doesn't exist."

A few days after the 2026 International Booker Prize was announced, China's Taiwan Affairs Office reacted by saying: "Writers from both sides of the Taiwan Strait should firmly uphold a national standpoint, respect historical facts, and squarely face the immense suffering inflicted upon the Chinese people ... by Japan's war of aggression and fascism."

"From China's perspective, they do not want to see Taiwan's voice gain prominence." Yang said.

Her book demonstrates that Taiwanese culture is shaped by multiple historical strands — including indigenous, Japanese colonial and local Han influences, rather than being merely a "branch of Chinese culture."

During Yang's German book tour this October, an event at the Literaturhaus in Munich sparked controversy when the writer's interpreter significantly shortened certain statements concerning Taiwan, China, history, and politics. The interpreter later admitted that there had been oversights and shortcomings in the translation but denied deliberately deleting content due to their political stance or the situation in Taiwan.

Taiwan and China

Beijing claims Taiwan as a Chinese province and has long threatened to use force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan's democratically elected president has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan.

Since 1949, Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence, maintaining its own government, military, and legal systems while facing ongoing military pressure from Beijing.

Taiwan's democratically elected president, Lai Ching-te, rejects China's assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan Image: Taiwan Presidential Office/AP Photo/Picture alliance

China's international overreach?

China's monitoring of Taiwanese international engagement reaches far further than words over a literature prize.

"The target of suppression and harassment primarily include outspoken individuals, exiled activists, diaspora community organizers, alongside their family members and close affiliates back home," said Dr. Yan-ho Lai, senior fellow of Georgetown Center for Asian Law. "From the PRC's (People's Republic of China) eyes, these groups are a threat to regime security, as they are able to amplify the dissenting voices and alternative stories of China to the West."

In April this year, Taiwanese barista Lin Shao-hsing, also known as Bala, won the 2026 World Latte Art Championship in the United States. Soon after, all mention of Taiwan as it related to Bala's win was removed from the official World Coffee Championships website.

It now says that Bala was representing "the competition body of Chinese Taipei," a term often used in international contests, such as the Olympics, to refer to Taiwan, but almost never used in Taiwan itself.

According to a 2026 poll by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center, the vast majority of people in Taiwan identify as "Taiwanese," while only 2.5% identify as Chinese.

In 2024, China allegedly planned to stage a "car collision" during Taiwanese Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim's visit to the Czech capital Prague. Czech intelligence officials told local media that the incident had been part of a much larger and escalatory plan by Chinese diplomats and intelligence officers working out of the Chinese embassy in Prague.

In early October this year, the FBI said authorities arrested a woman in California for allegedly spying on the son of Taiwan's president.

According to the US Department of Justice, the woman had traveled to Seattle in 2025 under instructions from Beijing to monitor the Taiwanese president's son and his family, capturing photos, video footage, and license plate information.

During a press conference on October 6, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it "consistently opposes the hype surrounding so-called 'Chinese spies' and the smearing and vilification of China."

"It reflects the ambiguity and limitation of international law, that the PRC using soft power to restrict the visibility of Taiwan may not directly fall into international law arena, as Taiwan is not recognized by international bodies as a sovereign state party." said Dr. Lai.

Edited by: Kate Martyr

World.title: How the Houthi-Saudi conflict is affecting countries on Africa's Red Sea coast — and beyond
World.content:
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which Yemeni government forces are trying to take back from the Houthis, is located not far from Djibouti and other African states.

In September, one of the major conflicts in the Middle East came within sight of Africa, as Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Yemen's Perim Island.

The island forms the narrowest point of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the southern entrance of the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It is roughly 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Djibouti and 20-minutes by air from Ethiopia.

In early October, Yemen's armed forces and their Saudi allies launched a counteroffensive. The Iran-backed Houthis have been firing on merchant ships since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.

Economic consequences are coupled with higher number of refugees

African economies are already suffering from crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, which is making fuel and fertilizer scarce and more expensive.

If the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also becomes impassable, the situation could deteriorate further. Shipping companies would have to make detours via the Suez Canal, which is controlled by Egypt, or the southern tip of Africa, as some already do. The additional costs would be passed on to consumers.

Bab el-Mandeb trade disruption: What it means for Djibouti To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The human cost of the escalation in Yemen hit Djibouti almost immediately. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), at least 3,700 refugees have crossed from Yemen into Djibouti since September. Most of those who made it to the country's northern Obock region are women and children.

The UNHCR is preparing to assist another 10,000 people who have not yet crossed into Djibouti. But Obock, which is on the border with Eritrea, is extremely dry and this is causing other issues.

"We don't have much water here. There's no groundwater at all," Alessandra Roccasalvo, the UN Development Program (UNDP) representative for Djibouti, told DW. "Everything has to be desalinated."

Thousands flee to Djibouti from Yemen's war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Djibouti is a strategic military hub

Despite its small size, Djibouti — a Muslim-majority country at the Horn of Africa with a population of just over a million — is a major player in the region. Its position at the entrance to the Red Sea makes it an attractive commercial and military shipping hub.

The United States, China, France, Italy, and Japan all operate military bases in Djibouti. The German Bundeswehr was also present until 2021, as part of a naval mission to combat maritime piracy.

The country's civilian ports serve as transshipment, or intermediate hubs for global shipping cargo, goods and containers. So far, the Houthi advance has not led to empty docks in Djibouti.

But there are still potential consequences, said Roccasalvo: "Basically, there's an economic upswing here — which means, as in any country experiencing an upswing, building materials are needed: cement, raw materials, and other things."

Less of that money is now coming in because ships have to pay nearly twice as much for insurance and reinsurance as they used to. "Many ships no longer want to pass through the Suez Canal. Many no longer want to pass through the Red Sea."

Knock-on effects for landlocked neighboring Ethiopia

Ethiopia — the world's most populous landlocked country — handles about 95% of its imports and exports through Djibouti's ports. Price hikes resulting from higher shipping insurance premiums to cover for potential war-related loss are affecting the country greatly.

Shortly after the Houthis seized Perim, Ethiopia's economy faced another, even more immediate threat: On September 23, fighting broke out in the country's northern Tigray region.

Since then, the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) have reportedly made gains against the Tigray-led rebel coalition that aims to overthrow the national government. The rebels briefly advanced toward the main corridor used for transporting goods between Djibouti's ports and the Ethiopian hinterland.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to certain experts, the ENDF's advances have since reduced the threat of yet another trade blockade — but as long as the conflict remains unresolved, the situation could potentially deteriorate again.

For months now, Ethiopia has suffered more than almost any other African country from the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and has already had to ration fuel at times. In the long term, the country aims to reduce its dependence on imports, for example by powering vehicles with domestically generated electricity instead of imported gasoline.

In early 2024, Ethiopia became the first country in the world to impose a ban on the import of internal combustion engine vehicles Image: Shewangizaw Wegayehu/DW

Can the conflict in Ethiopia affect Bab el-Mandeb access?

Ethiopia and its northern neighbor, Eritrea, have severed diplomatic ties; other regional powers such as Sudan, Egypt, and Somalia may find themselves siding with Eritrea rather than with Ethiopia.

Eritrea sees itself as facing a threat that Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has reiterated on several occasions: With Ethiopia deprived of access to the sea since Eritrea's independence, Abiy has often alluded to rectifying this perceived injustice — either through a political agreement, as was once sought with Somalia's breakaway region of Somaliland, or by force.

The port of Assab is located on the edge of Eritrea's panhandle — and is often described as the most likely target should Abiy choose the path of aggression. If the fighting within Ethiopia further escalates into a full-blown regional war, this could also lead to additional restrictions on safe passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the surrounding waters.

Experts have also raised concerns about the Shiite Houthis increasingly collaborating with the Sunni terrorist group Al-Shabab, which is based in Somalia. Although their ideologies are fundamentally different, they are particularly united by their hostility toward Israel and the US.

Inside Somalia's arms smuggling network To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What tools are at the disposal of African countries to help remedy the situation?

The three African non-permanent members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and Somalia — held an emergency meeting in mid-September, jointly calling for free shipping lanes and endorsing the demand that the crisis in Yemen be resolved under the auspices of the UN.

Liberia's UN Ambassador Lews Garseedah Brown formulated joint principles with his counterparts from Somalia and the Congo: the African nations are hoping for a UN-led diplomatic solution for Yemen Image: Bianca Otero/ZUMA/picture alliance

The situation at Bab el-Mandeb and in northern Ethiopia once again demands flexibility from Africa. In fact, some African economies could also benefit from relocation activities: Ports inKenya and Tanzania, for example, are becoming increasingly attractive for transshipment.

And while many countries are suffering from high oil prices, Nigeria's Dangote Group has announced an initial public offering and a new refinery in Kenya.

This article was originally published in German. It has been updated.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

World.title: Indian police detain 'Cockroach' movement founder and dozens of protesters in New Delhi. Follow live.
World.content:
Skip next section How have India's opposition politicians reacted to the Delhi protest crackdown?

Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has slammed the measures taken by Indian authorities to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party's protest from going ahead.

He called out a "war-like deployment" of security personnel and said that the suspension of the internet in a key part of Delhi was among the "most regressive" and "repressive" measures.

"A government confident in the fairness of its elections would welcome questions about them, whereas one that turns its capital into a fortress to avoid them only deepens the very suspicions it seeks to suppress. The government should provide answers, not lathis (sticks); expression, not repression," Tharoor wrote on X.

He also called for the release of the protesters who had been detained.

Tharoor said India's Gen Z "deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ," in a play on words.

Leaders of the CJP on Friday likened the clampdown on their planned protest to a "state of emergency."

A state of emergency was declared in India by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were invoked by the Congress leader for 21 months, during which civil liberties were suspended, much of the opposition was jailed and media was censored.

Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) National Convenor and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also mounted an emergency-related attack against Modi's government.

"This is worse than the Emergency. It's official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear," he said, referring to the arrests of CJP's three main leaders.

World.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
World.content:
US weather authorities are warning of "life-threatening" storm surges on the Gulf Coast due to the Category 2 hurricane. Extreme winds, rising water levels and possible tornadoes are also on the radar.

Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a Category 2 storm near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening.

The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.

What do we know about Hurricane Isaias?

The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland."

The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia.

Isaias is packing sustained winds of up to 105 miles per hour Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP

Isaias was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall. It later weakened to a Category 1 storm.

After the storm made landfall, the Florida Division of Emergency Management said the tornado watch for parts of North Florida has been extended until at least 6 a.m. local time Saturday (10 a.m. UTC).

The NHC said the hurricane has maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometers per hour).

The storm has downed trees in Pensacola in the Florida panhandle Image: Joe Raedle/Getty Images/AFP

Evacuations took place in coastal communities as the hurricane approached.

All flights at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport have been canceled due to the storm. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida.

Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to #Isaias."

Florida Governor DeSantis urges residents to 'buckle down'

In a press conference, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to "buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned those "thinking about using this storm's power outages and evacuations to break in, loot, or steal: don't even try it."

"During an emergency, these crimes become first-degree felonies, punishable by up to 30 years in prison," Uthmeier said.

People boarded up businesses ahead of the storm's landfall Image: Marco Bello/REUTERS

According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama.

Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said Uber, Comcast and Home Depot have offered to help Alabamians during the storm. Uber, for example, is offering free round-trip rides to state-approved evacuation shelters in Mobile and Baldwin counties.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
World.content:
The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.

A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

What was said in court?

The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.

The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

The brothers' parents were in court to hear the guilty verdict Image: Guillermo Arias/AFP

Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.

Victim begged for mercy

Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.

She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.

The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.

Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.

World.title: Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash
World.content:
Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan "absolutely" deserves the death penalty by firing squad but told reporters he has yet "to make a determination" on whether it will be livestreamed.

"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.

What did Hegseth and the Pentagon say about Hasan's execution?

Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."

Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.

He is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after he was shot by an officer responding to the Fort Hood shooting.

JD Vance says he would not watch livestream of execution

US Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Friday, also said he doesn't know whether the livestream is "actually going to happen."

"If it is shown publicly," Vance added, "I'm not going to be watching it." Vance is a devout member of the Catholic Church, which opposes the death penalty.

"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the US vice president said.

Hasan is incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks [FILE: September 16, 2026] Image: Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/IMAGO

Livestream plan faces bipartisan backlash

The Pentagon's plan to broadcast the execution has been met with a fierce backlash from within Trump's own Republican Party and the opposition Democrats.

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.

Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.

Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."

"The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment," he said in a statement posted on X. "Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."

Democratic Congressman Eugene Vindman of Virginia, who said he oversaw legal proceedings following the Fort Hood attack, said livestreaming Hasan's execution "is what terrorists and authoritarian regimes do. It's un-American."

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the idea of a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plan a "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Trump names new press secretary to succeed Karoline Leavitt
World.content:
Trump has appointed Katie Zacharia to take over the White House press secretary role vacated by Karoline Leavitt. She assumes the role with Trump struggling with low approval ratings driven by the US war with Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.

Zacharia is a 'loyal and brilliant supporter,' Trump says

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said it was a "great honor" to appoint Zacharia to the role, calling her a "loyal and brilliant supporter" and member of the Make America Great Again movement.

Zacharia, a 42-year-old native of California, had been serving as Senior Communications Advisor to Truth Social. She had also earlier worked as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.

Zacharia, in a post on X, thanked Trump and said "his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our country and communicating to the American people the major wins that the administration is making every single day," Zacharia said. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out."

Zacharia said her predecessor Leavitt was "fabulous" and that she set a "high standard" to meet for the press secretary job.

Karoline Leavitt to quit as White House press secretary To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will Zacharia follow Leavitt's combative approach?

Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.

Earlier this week, conservative-leaning broadcaster Fox News announced that Leavitt would provide commentary on the network starting from November 1.

Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.

In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis. She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.

Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president. During Trump's first term from 2017 to 2021, he had four press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.

Zacharia's tenure comes as Trump faces low approval ratings due to high energy prices amid the Iran war and the looming midterms on November 3, where the opposition Democrats are expected to make major congressional gains.

World.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
World.content:
For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.

Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.

Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.

The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end.

France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Problems of centralization

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.

Dilapidated infrastructure

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.

France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Macron tried in vain to address problem

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created.

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

Schoolchildren and students all over France have joined in on the protests Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

Increasing deficiencies

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

Pupils and students in Bron, a suburb of Lyon, called for better learning conditions and investment in the education system Image: Pittore/NEIRDAPROD/SIPA/picture alliance

Cancelled lessons

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.

Broken promises of equality

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

Students also protested against the media coverage of the problems in the education system Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

Protests in the run-up to the presidential election

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

Saint-Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko, tried to shield student protesters from riot police Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP

Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.

With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Las cajas de ahorro islámicas están de moda en Turquía
World.content:
Sus sucursales se han multiplicado en los últimos años, especialmente en las capitales de provincia del interior de Turquía, donde ocupan los puestos de honor de las principales avenidas. Sus lustrosos y modernos escaparates prometen hacer realidad los sueños de sus clientes: adquirir una casa, un automóvil o una tienda “sin necesidad de créditos” o “sin pagar intereses”. Son las Empresas de Financiación mediante Ahorro (TFS, en turco), una suerte de cajas de ahorro islámicas basadas en los principios de las finanzas islámicas, como el rechazo a los intereses —aunque esto, como mucho en las finanzas islámicas, tiene truco— y la mutualización del riesgo: un grupo de ahorradores aporta cuotas mensuales a un fondo común y, por turnos o por sorteo, cada miembro recibe el capital solicitado para adquirir la propiedad elegida.

Algunas, como Eminevim o Fuzul, se han convertido en grandes grupos empresariales. Comenzaron su existencia como sociedades de ahorro colectivo creadas durante los años noventa por empresarios del entorno del islamismo político deseosos de financiarse fuera de unos bancos controlados por la —entonces dominante— élite laica del país. Otras quebraron o fueron liquidadas, pues operaban en un vacío legal. Su historia cambió en 2021, cuando el Gobierno del conservador Recep Tayyip Erdogan endureció los requisitos de solvencia, profesionalizándolas y poniéndolas bajo el control de la Agencia de Regulación y Supervisión Bancaria. Pero sobre todo, su verdadera explosión se ha dado desde que, en 2023, Mehmet Simsek fue nombrado ministro de Finanzas con el mandato de reducir una tasa de inflación que había llegado a superar el 100% interanual. Aplicó el manual más ortodoxo e instó al Banco Central a elevar el precio del dinero, lo que ha supuesto que los bancos restrinjan los créditos y eleven los intereses de sus préstamos hipotecarios por encima del 40% anual (la inflación sigue sin bajar del 30%). “Debido a las medidas de macroprudencia financiera, se ha hecho muy difícil acceder a créditos bancarios. Aunque, al inicio, las TFS se dirigían a personas de bajos ingresos, ahora les interesan a trabajadores de cuello blanco e incluso a gente de ingresos altos que no puede acceder a créditos bancarios”, explica Ahmet Büyükduman, analista financiero.

Una comisión fija por adelantado

Frente a los elevados intereses que demandan los bancos —y que implican que se termine pagando casi cuatro veces el capital inicial en préstamos a diez años—, las TFS cobran una comisión fija por adelantado, equivalente a entre el 7% y el 10% del capital solicitado. La pega es que solo se puede acceder a la casa, el automóvil o el negocio que se va a adquirir cuando se ha aportado al fondo el 45% de su valor, lo cual puede ocurrir pronto —si se adelanta parte del capital o se eligen cuotas de pago mensuales elevadas— o tardar varios años. La TFS, luego, hipoteca el bien hasta que el cliente ha terminado de pagar los plazos, pero entretanto puede hacer uso de él. Otro de los problemas es la protección de los ahorros contra la inflación galopante, ya que la cantidad solicitada por un cliente al inicio del programa puede haberse convertido en insignificante cuando llega a ejecutarla. Así que las TFS han tenido que establecer programas de inversión de estos ahorros en oro, bonos del Estado acordes con las finanzas islámicas (sukuk) o fondos.

De los apenas 370.000 usuarios que las TFS tenían hace tres años en Turquía se ha pasado a más de 1,5 millones en la actualidad, y su tamaño en activos se ha multiplicado por diez hasta superar los 9.000 millones de euros. Aun así, apenas suponen una fracción de la banca tradicional, y es que muchos turcos mantienen cierta suspicacia: por el carácter islámico de este sistema y porque algunos lo acusan de ser un esquema piramidal, debido a la necesidad de que lleguen nuevos ahorradores para mantenerse. Pero Büyükduman atribuye estas críticas a falta de información: “También los bancos pueden quebrar si los depositantes se retiran”. Para este experto, lo más importante es que estas entidades “promueven el ahorro antes de ofrecer un préstamo” y permiten a personas que trabajan en sectores informales acceder a financiación.

World.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

World.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
World.content:
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

World.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Most recently, the 85-year-old chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide.

Announcing the prize in Oslo, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said it was going to someone who “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict”.

Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay said “if you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The award comes as the system of international justice is under attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick, if necessary”, and the US has sanctioned several of its staff.

Pillay played a significant role in the anti-apartheid movement in her homeland as a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and other activists. She went on to serve as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, spending the last four of her eight years there as its president.

She was one of the ICC’s first judges, sitting in the appeals chamber from 2003 until 2008, when she stepped down to become UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

In 2019, she was appointed as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice by the Gambia, which had filed genocide proceedings against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingya minority.

Last year, as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, she said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

In a post on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” she said.

The prize is administered by the Nobel Foundation and comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (around €1.07 million).

World.title: Museums, festivals and clubs in Groningen ban smart glasses
World.content:
