World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

World.title: ‘Light rosè’, or why claim that Abkhazia has no good wine is outdated. VIDEO
World.content:
Wine in Abkhazia

For a long time, Abkhazia was known mainly for its basic range of wines. The region’s unpredictable climate, with annual rainfall of up to 2,000 mm, was seen as a challenge, as was the popularity of mass-produced semi-sweet wines.

However, modern winemaking practices have challenged this perception. Today, Abkhaz wine producers are shifting their focus towards premium wines.

The Association of Winemakers is actively reviving local indigenous grape varieties. It says fermentation control and modern scientific methods now make it possible to produce delicate, dry and fresh rosé wines.

World.title: European Parliament resolution on banning opposition parties in Georgia: what it says
World.content:
On 8 October, the European Parliament adopted its latest — and seventh — critical resolution on Georgia. This time, it focuses on the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban five opposition parties and political groups.

In the resolution, the European Parliament strongly condemns the attempts to outlaw these opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them.

The draft resolution also once again calls for the release of political prisoners and sanctions against those responsible for Georgia’s democratic backsliding. It specifically names Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, party secretary-general Kakha Kaladze, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili.

The document says that the actions of Georgian Dream have caused the situation in Georgia to deteriorate further. Democracy and media freedom have declined, while human rights and the rule of law face growing violations. The document says this increasingly conflicts with Georgia’s international obligations and responsibilities, including the Copenhagen criteria.

The draft resolution also notes that two German foundations — the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation — had to close their offices in Tbilisi after the authorities rejected their funding applications under the grants law.

The draft resolution also again refers to the persecution of journalists in Georgia who covered the authorities’ repression of the opposition and civil society.

According to the draft resolution, the European Parliament:

Strongly condemns the attempt to outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them. It stresses that a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that using judicial mechanisms to eliminate legitimate political opposition is incompatible with democracy. It notes that banning the only opposition party represented in the Georgian parliament undermines the government’s previous narrative that it targeted only parties “under boycott”;

World.title: Eni completes installing offshore CO₂ storage platform in Liverpool Bay
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. Eni has completed the installation of an offshore CO₂ storage platform in the UK’s Liverpool Bay, the company said on October 9.

“Eni CCUS Holding, jointly owned by Italian energy company Eni and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP), part of BlackRock, has completed the installation of a new carbon capture and storage (CCS) platform in Liverpool Bay, the UK, marking a major milestone in the development of infrastructure for the HyNet industrial decarbonization cluster,” said Eni.

The Douglas CCS platform will serve as the offshore hub of the Liverpool Bay carbon dioxide transportation and storage system, receiving CO₂ captured from industrial facilities across northwest England and North Wales before transporting it through existing offshore pipelines, repurposed for CO₂ transport, to depleted natural gas reservoirs for permanent storage.

According to Eni, the facility is the world's first purpose-built offshore platform dedicated to carbon capture and storage for industrial decarbonization.

The platform was delivered in less than 18 months after the contract was awarded, following an accelerated engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning programme.

The installation comprises topside facilities weighing 1,885 tonnes, a supporting jacket structure weighing 1,755 tonnes and eight foundation piles with a combined weight of 730 tonnes.

The project combines newly built infrastructure with the reuse of existing offshore assets, including pipelines and depleted gas reservoirs, to support the transportation and long-term storage of captured carbon dioxide.

Construction is progressing across the wider Liverpool Bay CCS network, which is approximately 50% complete, according to the company.

Around 60% of the project's investment expenditure is being delivered through UK-based supply chains. The development is expected to support more than 2,000 jobs during construction and create approximately 200–300 long-term positions over more than 25 years of operation.

Liverpool Bay CCS is part of Eni CCUS Holding's portfolio of carbon capture, utilization and storage projects and forms a key component of efforts to develop CO₂ transportation and storage infrastructure for industrial decarbonization.

The Liverpool Bay CCS project will operate as the backbone of the HyNet Cluster to transport carbon dioxide from capture plants across the North West of England and North Wales through new and repurposed infrastructure to safe and permanent storage in Eni’s depleted natural gas reservoirs, located under the seabed in Liverpool Bay. The project itself foresees the efficient repurposing of part of the offshore platforms as well as 149km of onshore and offshore pipelines, and the construction of 35km of new pipelines to connect industrial emitters to the Liverpool Bay CCS network.

HyNet is one of the world’s most advanced CCS Clusters that will significantly contribute to the reduction of emissions from a wide range of industries across the North West of England and North Wales. This includes companies involved in cement manufacturing, energy from waste plants, low-carbon hydrogen production, as well as additional industrial players who will connect to Eni’s infrastructure. With a storage capacity of 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year in the first phase, and the potential to increase to 10 million tonnes of CO2 per year in the 2030s, Eni’s CO2 T&S system will make a significant contribution towards achieving the UK’s CCS ambitions. Construction of the project is expected to commence this year, ready for planned start-up in 2028, in line with industrial emitters in the HyNet Cluster.

World.title: Indonesia launches official Pencak Silat community in Azerbaijan (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. An event was held at the Indonesian Embassy in Azerbaijan to mark the launch and strengthening of the presence of the Pencak Silat community, a traditional Indonesian martial art, today, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Pencak Silat, an indigenous martial art and intangible cultural heritage recognized by UNESCO, contributes to strengthening diplomatic relations and cross-cultural understanding between Indonesia and Azerbaijan.

Berlian Helmy, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Indonesia to Azerbaijan, officially inaugurated the Azerbaijan Pencak Silat Community (APSC).

The Embassy of Indonesia in Baku officially recognizes and supports the Community as the sole body authorized to organize and oversee all Pencak Silat activities in Azerbaijan.

This step is expected to attract the full attention and support of the relevant Azerbaijani authorities and Ministries, with the aim of strengthening the sport’s legal status and developing its domestic ecosystem.

The official signing ceremony took place in Baku, attended by members of Indonesia diplomat, representatives of the sports community, and local Azerbaijani journalists.

The agenda commenced with national anthems of both countries, followed by remarks from the President of the Azerbaijan Pencak Silat Community, Magami Bayramov, and an address by the Ambassador of the Republic of Indonesia.

In his remarks, Helmy emphasized that Pencak Silat has long been practiced as a global martial art and is regularly contested by numerous countries at international competitions.

In light of its growing international recognition, he expressed his strong hope that the Azerbaijan Pencak Silat Community would soon prepare and send its best athletes to compete and achieve success at the prestigious 21st World Pencak Silat Championship, scheduled to take place in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, on December 5–12.

President of APSC, Magami Bayramov, expressed his highest appreciation to the Indonesian Embassy for this important recognition. According to him, this recognition would further motivate Azerbaijani athletes to strengthen the sport’s recognition and development in Azerbaijan, while also preparing themselves to compete at the World Championship in Uzbekistan.

The ceremony concluded with the reading of the official inauguration document by the organizing committee, followed by the signing of the document by the Ambassador of the Republic of Indonesia and a group photo with the Community’s board members.

World.title: Equinor to sell 30% stake in Canada's Bay du Nord project to Shell
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. Norwegian energy company Equinor has agreed to sell a 30% stake in the Bay du Nord offshore oil project in Canada to Shell, while retaining a 70% interest and operatorship, Equinor said on October 9.

The transaction is intended to support the project's development as the companies work towards a final investment decision, currently targeted for early 2027.

"We are pleased to welcome Shell as a partner in Bay du Nord. This is a strategic project for Equinor, with a high-quality resource base and the potential to create significant long-term value," said Philippe Mathieu, Equinor's executive vice president for Exploration and Production International.

He added that Shell's participation would strengthen the project as it advances towards the investment decision.

Equinor said the transaction was in line with its approach to portfolio management, capital allocation and risk-sharing in large-scale developments.

Bay du Nord is located in the Flemish Pass Basin, approximately 500 kilometers offshore Newfoundland and Labrador, about 500 kilometers northeast of St. John's. Discovered in 2013, the project comprises a series of oil discoveries and is considered a potential entry point for developing the region's deepwater resources.

The development concept envisages a floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) vessel connected to subsea infrastructure. The project could also provide opportunities for additional subsea tiebacks and further development across the basin.

The project is in the final stages of front-end engineering and design (FEED), with work focused on improving capital efficiency, execution planning and overall project readiness.

Equinor and Shell will continue to advance the project towards an investment decision, subject to market conditions, regulatory approvals and the companies' internal decision-making processes.

Bay du Nord represents a major potential investment in Canada's offshore oil industry. According to project estimates, the initial investment could reach approximately 14 billion Canadian dollars, while government revenues could total around CAD 20 billion and the project's contribution to gross domestic product could reach approximately CAD 50 billion.

The development is also expected to support thousands of jobs across construction, subsea fabrication, drilling, logistics, marine operations and maintenance.

If developed, Bay du Nord could establish infrastructure for future subsea tiebacks, supporting continued offshore activity and expanding industrial capabilities in Newfoundland and Labrador.

World.title: SLB signs 15-year deal with TotalEnergies for digital well planning
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. Global energy technology company SLB has signed a 15-year agreement with TotalEnergies to deploy its DrillPlan well planning and engineering solutions, SLB said on October 8.

The agreement aims to connect subsurface data with well planning and engineering workflows, enabling multidisciplinary teams to collaborate using a common set of data, designs and assumptions throughout the well construction process.

SLB's DrillPlan solutions will integrate offset well data, trajectory designs, casing and completion inputs, and other engineering parameters to streamline well design and planning activities. The platform is intended to help teams identify design conflicts earlier, reduce manual work and rework, and improve consistency in drilling programs.

The cloud-native application enables engineers to design, validate, and document wells from the conceptual stage through execution. Its capabilities include trajectory and casing design, hydraulics, torque and drag analysis, well control, risk assessment, time and cost estimation, emissions tracking and reporting.

The platform also supports integration with other digital systems, including SLB's Petrel subsurface software and Techlog wellbore software, as well as the OSDU Data Platform and other well delivery and operational solutions. These integrations are designed to facilitate data exchange between subsurface, engineering, planning and operational teams.

"Operators are increasingly looking for scalable technologies that can support more consistent planning decisions across large and diverse portfolios," said Rakesh Jaggi, president of SLB's Digital business.

According to SLB, the agreement reflects a broader industry shift toward scalable and interoperable digital platforms that combine specialist engineering expertise with enterprise-wide digital capabilities.

The companies will draw on their respective technical expertise to connect workflows, integrate customized processes and support the continued deployment of digital technologies across TotalEnergies' operations.

SLB is a global technology company providing products and services to the energy industry, with operations in more than 100 countries. Its business includes digital solutions, oil and gas technologies, industrial decarbonization, and the development of new energy systems.

World.title: Turkmen commodity exchange records cotton, yarn deals
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. In the October 5 trading session on SCRMET, foreign and domestic deals were concluded in the textile sector.

This was reflected in a press release published by the State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET).

According to the report, entrepreneurs from Türkiye reached agreements with local business representatives for the purchase of cotton fiber.

On the domestic market, local entrepreneurs reached agreements with the Ministry of Textile Industry of Turkmenistan for the purchase of cotton yarn.

SCRMET reported that a total of two transactions were finalized during the session, amounting to 7 million manat ($2 million) and $99,000.

The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered, and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities.

SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade.

World.title: Azerbaijan seeks to expand non-oil trade with Turkmenistan - сommentary
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 10. Azerbaijan attaches particular importance to developing economic ties with Turkmenistan, specifically to strengthening trade cooperation in non-oil and gas products and increasing trade volume, the member of the Azerbaijani Parliament’s Committee on Economic Policy, Industry, and Entrepreneurship, Vugar Bayramov, told Trend.

The MP noted that in his speech at the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Azerbaijan and Central Asia, the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, highlighted the development of our country’s economic relations with Central Asian states, including Turkmenistan.

According to him, in 2025, trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan amounted to $208 million. During this period, Azerbaijan imported $114.5 million worth of goods from Turkmenistan, while exports to that brotherly country totaled $63.8 million.

Bayramov noted that last year, Azerbaijan conducted trade with Turkmenistan involving 518 types of products.

According to the MP, energy resources account for the bulk of imports from Turkmenistan. For example, in 2025, Azerbaijan imported $36.4 million worth of natural gas, $12.5 million worth of jet fuel, and $7.7 million worth of heavy distillates or gas oils for other purposes from its sister country.

In addition, Azerbaijan imported $7.4 million worth of liquid fuel for specific technological processes and chemical transformations, $2.3 million worth of mineral or chemical nitrogen fertilizers, and $1.4 million worth of lubricants for specific technological processes and chemical transformations. Other goods were also imported from Turkmenistan.

V. Bayramov noted that processed agricultural products predominate among the goods exported from Azerbaijan to Turkmenistan.

Thus, last year, Azerbaijan exported to Turkmenistan white sugar and other chemically pure sucrose worth $22.4 million, products made of iron or non-alloy steel worth $7.8 million, cotton fiber worth $3.9 million, ferrous metal structures worth $1.8 million, as well as oil and other products worth $931,000.

The MP stressed that, as in other brotherly Turkic states, the top priority is to further increase trade with Turkmenistan.

“The main goal is to strengthen trade cooperation in the non-oil and gas sector,” V. Bayramov added.

World.title: Zach Bates qualifies on pole for Bathurst 1000
World.content:
Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.

Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.

Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.

But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.

Bates denied Kostecki with a scorching lap of Mt Panorama. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.

Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.

In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.

Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.

But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.

Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.

Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.

Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.

But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.

Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.

Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.

Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

2. Brodie Kostecki/Todd Hazelwood (No.17 Dick Johnson Racing)

World.title: Police investigating unexplained infant death at Adelaide motel
World.content:
South Australian Police have attended the Tollgate Motel in Glen Osmond on Saturday morning to investigate a reported infant death.

ABC News understands police and ambulances were called to the Tollgate Motel, adjacent to the South Eastern Freeway, five kilometres south-east of the Adelaide CBD, from 9am.

Some witnesses estimated around 20 officers were present.

Police vehicles attended the scene throughout the morning. (Supplied)

"There were at least four or five police cars here," a nearby resident told the ABC.

"It's a bit concerning that we've got police cars down the end of our quiet cul-de-sac."

Police left the scene by mid-afternoon, after establishing a cordon.

Police have cordoned off a room at the Tollgate Motel. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The cause of the child's death is currently undetermined.

Police have confirmed that an investigation is ongoing with the assistance of crime scene investigators and Eastern District Detectives, and a report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Two 'very lucky' men survive light aircraft crash in field
World.content:
A light aircraft plunged into a field north of Perth on Saturday, with the two men on board surviving the crash with non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said the pilot of the single-engine aircraft crashed near the Greenside private airfield, off Brand Highway in Muchea, north-east of Perth, this morning.

Emergency services responded to the incident, during which the aircraft sustained "significant damage", police said.

A man in his 60s and another man in his 30s were treated at the scene.

The two men on board survived the crash with non-life-threatening injuries. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Department of Fire and Emergency Services (DFES) district officer Gareth Deeg attended the scene and said one occupant extracted himself from the aircraft, while the other person was assisted out.

"Without knowing the investigation and seeing the speed and the reasons behind it, any aircraft that comes on an abnormal landing is obviously critical," he said.

" The two gentleman are very lucky today to be able to walk away and be safe. "

'Complex' crash site

The men were transported to Royal Perth Hospital at priority one, and St John Ambulance said they are believed to have non-life-threatening injuries.

Mr Deeg said several people at the airfield at the time of the crash quickly came to the aid of the two men.

He described the crash scene as "complex".

"It's complex for a number of natures: the location, the information that's provided, the fuel, the aircraft, what it's made out of," he said.

The Greenside Recreational Flyers Club, one of the state's largest, operates at the airfield, according to its website.

The aircraft crashed around 250 metres from the airfield's runway. Its fuselage, wings and tail were badly damaged.

Police said their inquiries are ongoing.

World.title: St Kilda end the drought to send Dal Santo out a winner
World.content:
St Kilda gave departing AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo the perfect send-off with a drought-breaking two-point home win over Collingwood.

With the bottom-of-the-table Saints holding a 0-8 record, Dal Santo announced on Friday he was standing down and took charge of the team for the final time in Saturday's game at Moorabbin Oval.

After scoring just one point last week and tallying five behinds in the first half on Saturday, the Saints kicked five second-half goals on their way to a 5.9 (39 ) to 5.7 (37) win.

Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw kicked two goals and Tyanna Smith bagged 25 touches and 12 clearances for the Saints, who ended an 11-match losing streak stretching back almost a full year.

Collingwood (1-8) kicked the only two goals of the first half, the first to captain Ruby Schleicher, who later came off the ground with an injury to her right shoulder.

The other major went to Sabrina Frederick in her 100th AFLW game, as Collingwood stretched a two-point lead after a goalless first quarter to 12 at half-time.

The victory was St Kilda's first of the AFLW season. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

With the wind at their backs, the Saints rallied In the third quarter, kicking three straight goals and four for the term to lead by 10 points at the last change.

Ashley Centra, who gathered 25 touches for the Pies, kicked a goal in the final 30 seconds to cut the gap to two points, but the Saints held on.

"I understand this is my last game, but that was a really good game by the girls. I thought we fought really hard," Dal Santo told Fox and Kayo.

"I'm really proud of this group. It's been a delight and I'm really grateful for being a part of their journeys.

"I've loved it. Five years and the time is right," added Dal Santo, who finished with a 23-39 win-loss record.

AAP

World.title: Outback Dolly Parton Festival bigger than ever after star's death
World.content:
An outback town has traded its 9 to 5 farm tools and workwear for a day of bedazzled country glam and platinum-blonde bouffants inspired by megastar Dolly Parton.

The 3,500-resident town of Narromine in western NSW transformed into "Dollymine" for its annual October festival, which celebrates the country music icon, who died in August at the age of 80.

"So this is Dollymine — not Narromine — for the weekend," attendee Juanita Peardon said.

Narromine has tuned into "Dollymine" for the annual festival this weekend. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

A record number of visitors were urged to leave their frown at the updated town sign for this year's event.

Along the streets of "Dollymine", a sea of pink and bejewelled coats of many colours, sweet lovin' friends and wayfaring strangers gathered to say in their own way "I Will Always Love You" to the Queen of Country.

Many went to great lengths to do their "more is more" idol proud, like Natasha Kelly from Dubbo who stayed up until 4am sewing rhinestones into her Dolly-inspired outfit.

Natasha Kelly sewed rhinestones and sequins into her family's Dolly-inspired outfits. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

Labour of love

Festival organiser Skye Rush said she has been blown away by the support this year.

"It's been great; locals have come out in force, and all the visitors have come out in force as well," she said.

"Our shops are being used, our accommodation is being used, [the event] fills the town with people."

Skye Rush said the event is the largest it has ever been. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

The festival began in 2022, run by a volunteer committee of die-hard Dolly fans.

It faced funding challenges and was cancelled in 2024, before being rescued by a $150,000 state government grant and a boost from the local council.

Ms Rush said the event has always been about celebrating Parton's legacy, even before she died in August.

"It's her attitude to people, attitude to small towns, attitude to not forgetting where she's from," she said.

"We're a small town, and we support our locals."

Aunty Ruth said Dolly Parton had a strong connection to country. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

Narromine Elder Aunty Ruth said Dolly Parton represented a lot to the town.

"Why wouldn't you celebrate such a beautiful person?" she said.

"To me country is country, and to be on the land; if country music's part of the land, that's where we are going to be."

Gathering from far and wide

The town is five and a half hours' drive north-west of Sydney, but the remote location has not stopped people from all over the country from coming to celebrate.

Best-dressed judge Dolly Delicious travelled to the event from Canberra and has attended all five festivals.

He said Dolly Parton's death in August has not put a dampener on celebrations.

"I'm a bit sad, but I'm actually really excited to celebrate her … all her music, all her looks," he said.

" It makes me really fuzzy inside — it's incredible. "

Dolly Delicious and Juanita Peardon have been attending the event for many years. (ABC Western Plains: Lucy Thackray)

Sam and Amber Bloem got married last week and sang Parton's 1982 duet Islands in the Stream at their reception instead of a first dance.

"We love Dolly, so we had to stop in," Amber said.

"[There's] lots of pink and sparkles … fantastic music; it' s just lovely."

Sam (left) and Amber Bloem signed their two children Archie and Jack up to Parton's Imagination Library when they were born. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

The Bourke locals said it was especially important to celebrate Dolly's legacy this year, including her efforts to promote literacy in children.

"Our kids were part of her Imagination Library, so they've been getting books sent from her every month since they've been born," Amber said.

"Our kids call her aunty Dolly because she sends something in the post each month," Sam said.

Johnny Gilmore says he has loved the community spirit in Narromine. (ABC Western Plains: Catherine James)

For Johnny Gilmore, supporting regional towns like Narromine has also been a motivator.

"We always like to support country towns, and we love the music, so we always come out and try to support the town and have some fun," he said.

"I love her music; everything from the 70s and 80s is always wonderful."

World.title: Samoa looks for power from pain in World Cup tilt
World.content:
Junior Paulo knows what it feels like to pull yourself from the depths of grand final misery and glowingly represent your country at a Rugby League World Cup weeks later.

So he is happy to lend a helping hand to his Samoa teammates who are suffering similar heartache.

Parramatta's Paulo had big dreams of winning the NRL grand final in 2022, but they shattered when the forward's side suffered a 28-12 loss to Penrith in the decider.

He had to forge on, and weeks later found himself leading Samoa in a historic World Cup final against Australia.

Paulo will lead Samoa for the second tournament in a row. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Paulo will be looking to repeat the dose this time around after the tournament was officially launched at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday.

Samoa are one of 10 men's teams vying for glory, beginning when Australia face New Zealand on Thursday night, while eight teams will make up the women's tournament that starts with the Jillaroos taking on Samoa in Parramatta the following evening.

This year, four of Samoa's players — Newcastle winger Greg Marzhew, prop Pasami Saulo, and second-rowers Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen — will be feeling a similar pain to Paulo's back in 2022.

The Knights quartet lost to the Sydney Roosters in the grand final last Sunday.

"I was in the same shoes, losing to Penrith and then [having to play in the] World Cup," Samoa co-captain Paulo said.

"All you want to do is … be able to turn it around.

"So for them [Manuleleua and McEwen], they're eager to get back out and play some footy. Hopefully it means they bring the physicality that they do.

"It's time for us to bring them up to being ready to represent Samoa, but also making it enjoyable for them."

Regardless, Paulo cannot wait to lead a star-studded Samoan side when they begin their campaign next Friday against France before facing Papua New Guinea and Tonga.

The men's and women's tournaments will kick off next week. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

All eyes are sure to be fixed on star half Jarome Luai after a headline-riddled season where he was announced as the first official signing for the PNG Chiefs from 2028 before later being released by Wests Tigers to join Parramatta for 2027.

"He's [been] just a bit misunderstood by many towards the back end of the year. People were very opinionated about him," said Paulo of his co-captain.

"He's locked in, putting his best foot forward and representing Samoa. He enjoys being in these camps, and you can just tell how locked in he is by the first day we got into camp.

"[I] just want to see him evolve as a leader, and grow into the leader he is now. All the boys will be backing him, and luckily, nothing fazes Romey [Luai] too much."

In the lead-up to the tournament, some members of the team also spent some time in Samoa, which Paulo said was an "indescribable" feeling as it reminded the players they are embarking on something for more than themselves.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Indian police detain 'cockroach' movement founder Abhijeet Dipke
World.content:
The founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has been arrested ahead of a protest against India's electoral commission on Saturday.

TV channels reported earlier that police officers met founder Abhijeet Dipke at the Delhi airport after he arrived from the financial capital, Mumbai, and asked him to call off the protest as authorities had banned it.

"I have come to be arrested, arrest me … I am not afraid of you guys," Mr Dipke told police officers who spoke to three men on board the aircraft, television images showed.

"No, this is not an arrest," one police officer replied.

"Please cooperate."

Protesters demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. (AP: Aijaz Rahi)

Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight upon landing, the movement said in a statement.

CJP condemned the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, which it called a "pre-planned interception" aimed at crippling the leadership of Saturday's rally, and demanded their immediate release.

Thousands of demonstrators are expected at Delhi's designated protest site, Jantar Mantar, where authorities have imposed sweeping restrictions, including suspension of mobile internet.

Police said on Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

Police detain some demonstrators heading to protest site

The demonstration site has been cordoned off with yellow metal barricades and thousands of police have been deployed in and around the area.

The police intercepted protesters before they could reach the protest site, chasing some away and detaining others.

Police officers stopped buses, cars and other vehicles heading to the protest area. (Reuters: Priyanshu Singh)

The preparations signal the authorities' determination to contain a fast-growing protest campaign that has drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

India's 'Cockroach' protests intensify Delhi police say three female journalists are making sexual harassment allegations against officers.

Those detained were bundled into police vehicles and driven away.

At entry points to central New Delhi, officers stopped buses, cars and other vehicles, boarding them to search for people headed to the demonstrations.

Anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers stood along key routes.

Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas while trying to cover the demonstration.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights?" said Tanya Negi, a college student who travelled from Mumbai.

Restrictions on train services were expected to disrupt travel across the capital and make it harder for protesters to reach the venue.

India's young return to streets

The protests centre on the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters.

Protesters are demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.

The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.

Demonstrators participate in a protest organised by opposition parties demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner. (Reuters: Sharafat Ali)

The dispute has also become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Inside the 'Cockroach' party A student who started a youth uprising across India is fast becoming the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12-year reign.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition politicians stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Mr Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Mr Modi's party.

The commission and the government deny the allegations.

For the Cockroach Janta Party, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The protests come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.

World.title: History was there for the taking… until Wallabies bombed under a high-ball blitz
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion History was there for the taking… until Wallabies bombed under a high-ball blitz Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author October 10, 2026 — 7:37pm

October 10, 2026 — 7:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was going to be such a clever opener. “Let that be a lesson to world rugby,” I would exult, with echoes of Vitas Gerulaitis, “NO-ONE beats the Wallabies at the one ground 41 years in a row! 23 years and counting: The All Blacks retain the Bledisloe Cup. Getty Images Or maybe ... “Anyone can have a bad four decades, but that’s where the Wallabies really draw the line.”



It all turned, see, on the fact that our blokes had not won against the All Backs at Auckland’s Eden Park since 1986, and for the first part of this Bledisloe Cup Test match it really looked as if – hold my coat, Captain Cook – history was at hand. The Wallabies swept all before them. They carved them up in the backs, and stopped the hosts’ attack cold. They picked them off in the lineouts. The green and gold so dominated territory and possession that when our fullback Tom Wright sliced the defence wide open just seven minutes in to score, I was morally certain that for the next 40 years, I’d be able to boast: “I was there the night it all turned around, the beginning of the Green and Golden Age, after decades of All Blackness!” Tom Wright on his way to the tryline against the All Blacks. Getty Images But then those All Black boogers struck back, as they are ever wont to do, and one thing in particular did us real damage. The All Blacks kept putting up the high ball, and not only did none of the Wallabies appear to even call for it, many of them they didn’t even look particularly interested in claiming it.



It is a mystery to this despondent correspondent how a team so outstanding at so many other things continues to get this most basic of all required skills wrong. It is particularly confusing when Max Jorgensen and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii had been so great at it a fortnight ago against the Springboks. For the damage done by not swallowing whole the pills put up towards them was considerable, as the All Blacks quickly scored two converted tries and a penalty to lead 17-7. At least the fact our captain Harry Wilson restored a little order with a try just before halftime allowed us to hope, with the All Baddies only holding a 17-14 lead at the break. The Wallabies celebrate after Harry Wilson’s try before halftime. Getty Images Who would come out for the Wallabies in the second half? The team which dominated the first ten minutes, or the one that all but disappeared for the middle 20? At first, it looked it would be the former as, from the kick-off, Wright and Max Jorgensen combined to break through and we ended up with a line-out right on their line. The Promised Land was right there, just waiting for a Wallaby forward to take up his rightful position – planting the ball down for defence on a patch of grass that grows green from the blood, sweat and tears of his 40 forebears.



Alas, that attack was snuffed out by a penalty and much of the rest went back to an aerial battle where we appeared to have a distinct lack of Spitfires, and Jerry was everywhere at once! Look, it was not simply that the All Blacks continued to put the ball up and then recover it, it was than when we put the ball up, we had no one of note rushing through to put a tenth of the pressure on them that had been put on us. The territory this delivered to the All Blacks was more than enough for them to plant their flag four more times behind our goal line in the next 35 minutes, taking the lead out to 43-14 as the match started to ebb. Leroy Carter of the All Blacks touches down for a try. Getty Images In that time, Wilson, Rob Valetini and Fraser McReight continued to impress, as did Jorgensen and Wright for at least knocking on the All Back door. But our side needed a whole lot more than mere impressions. It needed to defuse their bombs and blow up some our own, but could manage neither feat, until ... Until, wouldn’t you know it? With five minutes to go, at long bloody last, Suaalii did what we wanted him to do – what he should be asked to do every kick-off – run through, leap high and get us the bloody ball! The result? A Wallaby TRY!



Seriously. It was that simple an equation. When they won the aerial battles, they scored. When we did, we scored. We just won bugger-all of those aerial battles. Their final try, with seconds on the clock, to take it to 50-19 just upped the agony. All up, as disappointing as it was, at least it is bloody clear what training should consist of this week. Tell ’em, coach Les Kiss: Related Article Live

Bledisloe Cup Bledisloe heartache as All Blacks blow away Wallabies at Eden Park again “At least until Marky Mark gets here in a few weeks to take the marks, we need all of you, every day, all day, without fail, to practice the bloody high ball – otherwise we are wasting our time. And next week, the first bastard that calls out ‘YOURS!’ instead of ‘MINE!’ or makes no call at all, will be pulled from the field. We simply cannot compete without that.” And they really can’t. Most other parts of our game are seriously solid. That part is seriously shithouse. You heard me. And I know I shouldn’t say a bad word in a family newspaper. But kids, on this occasion, no other word will do.



Onwards to next week, at Homebush. Fix the high ball. Play ball! News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Bledisloe heartache as All Blacks blow away Wallabies at Eden Park again
World.content:
It’s the hope that kills you.

The long wait of Wallabies fans to see an Australian win over New Zealand at Eden Park will stretch into a 41st year after the All Blacks turned on another ruthless performance at their spiritual home to post a 50-19 victory.

Loading

The seven-tries-to-three victory ensured the All Blacks also retained the Bledisloe Cup for a 24th straight year, and gave Les Kiss his first defeat as Wallabies coach. On the flipside, it gave former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie his first taste from the elusive Bledisloe urn after several years of failure in gold.

The All Blacks have a habit of flossing their teeth with Australian optimism, and so it proved again in Auckland.

The Wallabies entered the match being talked up as a rising side with the potential to break some long-standing droughts at Eden Park, based on their last-start win over the Springboks and the Kiwis’ three-Test losing streak.

No Wallaby side has won at Eden Park since 1986, and no side has beaten the All Blacks there since 1994.

Those records rarely seemed threatened on a night that followed an all-too familiar script.

The Wallabies trailed by just 17-14 at the break, having stayed in touch with two tries despite being under siege for most the half.

Loading

Throughout the night, the Aussies were dominated in the aerial contests and using a passive defence, the Wallabies put the All Blacks under no linespeed pressure. The Kiwis waited patiently for their opportunity to strike and slice through a gap, or simply hold the ball for long enough to drive in a try.

In contrast, the verve shown by the Wallabies attack in the previous months was mostly missing, in an unusually listless and underwhelming performance.

Australia’s small window of staying in the game and potentially even winning came early in the second half, when they had several chances to score in the Kiwi quarter and take the lead.

But Irish referee Andrew Brace pinged the Wallabies for two 50-50 penalties, which piggybacked New Zealand into the Wallaby quarter. The Kiwis made no mistake with their territory and scored in the 49th minute and then again in the 54th minute. Now trailing by 16, the air went out of the Wallabies’ tyres.

Chasing the game to get back in the contest, the Wallabies then made errors in their own half and went on to concede another three tries in the last quarter. A late try to reserve hooker Josh Nasser was in the category of too little, too late.

To make matters worse on an already black night, star centre Len Ikitau came off the field with a concussion, which is likely to rule him out of the second Bledisloe Cup clash in Sydney next week.

Codie Taylor of the All Blacks celebrates scoring a try. Getty Images

The All Blacks led 17-14 after an opening half where the Wallabies started and finished the first well, but battled in the middle.

Australia dominated the early territory, and put pressure on the Kiwi line. Several attempted rolling mauls were repelled but slick work from the Wallabies’ backs saw the visitors open the scoring.

Under advantage, the Wallabies spun the ball left and a second-wave pass saw Ben Donaldson tap the ball onto the Max Jorgensen, who surged through a gap and passed to Tom Wright. The fullback had Suaalii on his outside but dummied and found a tiny gap, racing 20 metres to score.

The Kiwis responded quickly, however, when they finally got some possession and they were helped by the Wallabies’ passive defence and inability to win contestable kicks.

After one retake from Jordie Barrett, the Wallabies defence was caught sleepily retreating and disjointed, and Damian McKenzie sliced through. He found Peter Lakai in support for a 12th-minute try.

It was more of the same just three minutes later, when the Wallabies’ defensive line was again breached; this time through poor spacing. In their element against a retreating defence, the Kiwis kept punching and Tupou Vai’i ended up charging over in the 15th minute.

It was all a bit too easy, and things began to looking worrying for the Wallabies, who now also began turning the ball over when they got their hands on it.

The Kiwis began turned their favourite tap – the trusty pressure valve – and the Wallabies were lucky to not concede again when Will Jordan sliced through yet again in the 19th minute, but a long pass to support and a probable try went astray.

The Wallabies stayed in the fight but missed an easy penalty from in front in the 23rd minute. The All Blacks didn’t miss theirs though; they posted a 32nd minute kick to extend the lead to 10 points.

The visitors defended their line strongly in the last 10 minutes, and instead of conceding another try, which could have been a game-sealer already, the Wallabies shocked the crowd by scoring.

The All Blacks celebrate retaining the Bledisloe Cup. Getty Images

A penalty helped the Aussies into the All Black half, and again Donaldson got the ball out the back on attack. He slipped through the line and found skipper Harry Wilson in support. The skipper raced in under the sticks, bringing the deficit back to just three points at the break.

The Wallabies began the second half brightly, and counter-attacked down to the Kiwis line immediately. But they missed that chance, and missed another chance soon after, when a strong Rob Valetini run set up a chance for a lineout maul.

But referee Andrew Brace pinged the Wallabies for a pedantic obstruction penalty, and then pinged them again for holding on from a contestable kick. That gave the Kiwis entry to the Aussie quarter, and the Kiwis didn’t miss their chance.

Following a lineout maul – in which New Zealand went unpenalised by Brace for the same lifter obstruction – halfback Cam Roigard dived over from broken play.

By now, the Wallabies looked sapped and using a passive defensive line, were allowing the All Blacks to dictate terms at the contact zone. It seemed almost inevitable that the Kiwis would score again and they did in the 54th minute, when a long sequence of phases saw Codie Taylor break through and score.

The lead was now 16, with 20 minutes to go, and the night was as good as over for the Wallabies.

Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Jordan all rubbed more salt in the wounds with last-quarter tries.

World.title: Church victim accused of having ‘credibility of $3 note’ gets $2.2 million
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCatholic church Church victim accused of having ‘credibility of $3 note’ gets $2.2 million Cameron Houston October 10, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A survivor of shocking clerical abuse has been awarded more than $2.2 million by a Supreme Court jury, despite a series of contentious claims by the Marist Brothers’ legal team that he lied about his mental health and had the “credibility of a $3 note”. Greg Barclay was repeatedly accused of fabricating and exaggerating evidence during the civil trial, including a claim he faked details about two suicide attempts after he was sexually abused by brother John Anthony Skehan at the former St Colman’s College in Shepparton in 1970. Historical sexual abuse survivor Greg Barclay has been awarded more than $2.2 million. Justin McManus During a 12-day trial last month, barrister Jack Pappas, acting for the Trustees of the Marist Brothers, branded Barclay a “money-grubber” who was motivated by greed, while dismissing some of his testimony as “balderdash, piffle and rot”. “I suggest to you [there] was a performance by Mr Barclay on the morning of the second day of his evidence, unabashed display of faux emotion, gasping for air, huffing and puffing, struggling to get words out, the full enchilada,” Pappas told the jury.



“He pretended in front of you, and he pretended to doctors about the after effects and the continuing impact of the abuse upon him when he was 14 years old. He exaggerated symptoms and disabilities and consequences, all seeking sympathy and damages to which he is just not entitled.” Related Article Investigations Christian Brothers cry poor to abuse survivors after transferring elite schools for $1 However, a six-person jury emphatically rejected Pappas’ submission and awarded $2,248,974 to Barclay on October 1, while the Marist Brothers were also ordered to pay his legal costs. Barclay told this masthead he had been vindicated by the judgement, but was emotionally drained by the trial after more than three days giving evidence and facing cross-examination. “I knew they would come in hard, but it was just brutal. It was worse than I’d anticipated. To be accused of pretending to be a victim/survivor is just outrageous and that’s after the person who abused me was convicted in court,” Barclay told this masthead.



“There were so many comments that really struck me as disgusting. I was called a money-grabbing grub.” The court made no criticism of the conduct of the Marist Brother’s counsel in the judgement. Barclay, now 70, said there was a stark contrast between the public comments made by the Catholic order and its conduct in court. “This was consistent with how the Marist Brothers and the Catholic Church have behaved in the past. They publicly claim to support victims and apologise for the past, but when someone makes it to court they are accused of making it all up and [they say they] shouldn’t be believed,” he said. Barclay says he was disgusted by some of the claims by the Marist Brothers’ legal team in court. Justin McManus



However, the director of the Marist Brothers professional standards’ office, Domenic Pagano, defended the order’s legal response. He confirmed the Marist Brothers would appeal the recent judgement in favour of Barclay. “The Marist Brothers accepted that they were liable to pay Mr Barclay fair and reasonable compensation but believed, on a proper assessment of the evidence, that Mr Barclay was exaggerating aspects of his claim and that he had no claim for recovery of economic loss following an active and remunerative career as an educator and senior union official,” Pagano said. Related Article High Court of Australia Controversial High Court ruling could be used against sex abuse victims like Greg “The Marist Brothers’ counsel acted in court in a manner consistent with a robust challenge to a claim which the defendant believed to be deliberately overblown.” Pagano said the order had to be judicious in meeting the expanding legal demands of clerical abuse survivors and had an obligation as trustee of funds that also provide extensive education and care services.



In 2014, Skehan was convicted of indecently assaulting Barclay and handed a suspended eight-month prison sentence. He was previously convicted and placed on a suspended sentence in 2010 for the indecent assault of a young child in Broken Hill in the 1970s. In a press release after Skehan’s second conviction, the Marist Brothers said it was committed to “addressing the terrible effects of past abuse.” “We will continue to work with victims of abuse with care and compassion to help them achieve healing,” the statement read. In 2015, Barclay received an apology from then provincial leader Brother Peter Carroll. “I accept you were harmed through no fault of your own by the abusive actions of [Brother] John and that harm has extended into your adult life with adverse effects on your personal, work and social relationships,” Carroll said.



Barclay’s solicitor Laird Macdonald from Rightside Legal said the Marist Brothers deserved to pay a steep price for their treatment of his client during the trial. “The Marists told the jury to give him zero compensation for an impacted working life. To their credit, the jury saw through those ridiculous slurs and arguments,” Macdonald said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Calm before the storm: Why Nick Blakey’s path from Sydney to North remains uncertain
World.content:
Updated SportAFLTrading and drafting Calm before the storm: Why Nick Blakey’s path from Sydney to North remains uncertain Jon Pierik and Andrew Wu Updated October 10, 2026 — 6:57pm ,first published 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Nick Blakey’s path to North Melbourne remains uncertain as Sydney and the Kangaroos look to ramp up discussions over a blockbuster deal. Saturday was the calm before the storm, with neither club holding major discussions over Blakey’s future, according to two industry sources with knowledge of the matter. The Kangaroos’ pick No.6 in this year’s draft shapes as the key component of any trade to send Blakey to the club where his father John played 224 of his 359 games in the 1990s and early 2000s and won two premierships. Swans star Nick Blakey wants to continue his AFL career at North Melbourne. AFL Photos The pressure is on North Melbourne to secure a deal for Blakey, having made many unsuccessful bids to poach rival stars, including Richmond champion Dustin Martin, Collingwood star Jordan De Goey, GWS gun Josh Kelly, and Swans superstar Isaac Heeney.



Blakey has five years to run on his contract so they must find a package of picks to entice the Swans to release the All-Australian rebounding defender. Blakey wants to move to Arden Street but Essendon, Geelong and St Kilda have all expressed interest in him. Related Article Updated

Trading and drafting North board approved mammoth Blakey offer amid police investigation The Cats do not have the draft picks to entice the Swans, after parting ways with first-round picks for defender Jordan Ridley and ruckman Rowan Marshall, but the Saints have picks 10 and 16 this year, plus a future-first in 2028. The North Melbourne board, headed by president Sonja Hood, has signed off on a $12 million offer for Blakey, who was one of five players handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for his involvement in a night of wild partying at Melbourne’s Pullman East hotel in August.



A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. No charges have been laid, and all five Swans players who served season-ending suspensions denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. Elsewhere, Carlton and Collingwood are close to finalising a deal to turn young Blues ruckman Flynn Riley into a Magpie. The trade is likely to involve future picks. The Pies have a full suite of selections in 2027 and 2028 to work with to satisfy the Blues, who acquired Riley in this year’s mid-season draft. The Blues rated him highly enough to offer a two-year deal, but the Pies have offered more. Butters’ childhood dream comes true with Bulldogs move



Jon Pierik Boom recruit Zak Butters says the Western Bulldogs are on the cusp of “something special”, and revealed he turned to Marcus Bontempelli for advice throughout the year before making his decision to head to the Whitten Oval. Butters, 26, is officially a Bulldog on a record nine-year contract worth between $17 million and $17.5 million after the AFL on Friday approved a convoluted side deal involving five clubs and a series of first, second and later draft picks exchanged. The Butters contract is the biggest in AFL history in total, though he will earn less than the $2 million per season St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has made. Ready to start: Zak Butters is looking forward to getting to work with the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos



“It’s good to make the decision and be here, and, yeah, I feel like it was a long time getting to this point,” Butters said. Related Article Updated

Trading and drafting North board approved mammoth Blakey offer amid police investigation “And a few people told me along the journey that when you know, you know. And I felt like, yeah, once I knew, I just wanted to get it done, and get here and meet everyone and start my next journey.” Butters had already formed a friendship with Bontempelli, the Bulldogs’ skipper and legendary figure, which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the midfield gun that also involved Richmond and Geelong. “He’s obviously one that I am looking forward to playing with, and he’s been an inspiration of mine since I was a kid, and probably more so the more I got to know him, not just this year, but along the journey and playing against him,” Butters told the Bulldogs’ website.



“[I’m] trying to be the best, so you’re trying to learn off the best, and he’s he’s definitely one of them. So, over the last year as well, he’s just been a good sounding board and someone that you want to play footy with. Related Article AFL 2026 How Nick Blakey can get to the Roos and what it will cost them “I feel like, as much as I can add to the footy club, that I’ll learn a lot from him, and some other guys at the footy club as well. So, yeah, I’m really looking forward to learning and becoming better off guys like Marcus and Bevo [coach Luke Beveridge] as well.” Butters grew up following the Dogs, his family residing in Darley on the western metropolitan fringe. He played for the Western Jets before being taken by the Power with the 12th pick of the 2018 national draft. He said one of the highlights of his life had been attending the 2016 finals, when the Bulldogs unexpectedly stormed to their second club premiership.



“Yeah, I have loved the Bulldogs since I was a kid, had plenty of jumpers growing up, and loved a lot of different players. But, probably, 2016 is hard to top,” Butters said. “I remember catching the train in from Bacchus Marsh, and watching the finals, and was lucky enough to sneak a few tickets through friends and family. And yeah, I remember catching the train home after the ’16 granny [grand final], and, obviously, catching the train back through the west to get to Bacchus Marsh, it was pretty chaotic and loud. “It’s still one of my favourite days that I’ve had in footy. So it’d be cool to try and run that back.” Butters said he wants to be role model for youth in the western suburbs, reinforcing that they, too, can reach the heights of elite football.



He failed to play in a grand final in his eight years with the Power, and wants that to change at his new club. The Dogs’ 2026 campaign ended with an elimination final defeat to Adelaide. “It’s an exciting stage for the football club, and one that we can, hopefully, really challenge in,” Butters said. “And you want to bring members and all that along for the ride, and bring them in on the journey, and you want them to be there for the wins and the losses, and come along for the ride with us. And I feel like it could be something pretty special.” Get around our footy coverage
