World.title: Rookie claims Bathurst 1000 pole position in a Shootout shock
World.content:
SportMotorsportSupercars Rookie claims Bathurst 1000 pole position in a Shootout shock Frances Howe October 10, 2026 — 6:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Zach Bates will become the first rookie since 2001 to start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position after stunning Mount Panorama for the second day in a row to win the Top 10 Shootout qualifying competition. A day after clocking the fastest time around the circuit in this generation of supercars and earning provisional pole, 22-year-old Bates denied Brodie Kostecki the unprecedented feat of becoming the first driver to claim four successive pole positions in the Great Race. Zac Bates and co-driver Aaron Seton celebrate taking poll position. Getty Images The Top 10 Shootout pits the fastest 10 drivers from Friday’s qualifiers in a single solo lap around the Mount Panorama circuit. Their times set the first 10 positions on the grid for the main race on Sunday. On the verge of history, Kostecki led with just Bates left to drive on Saturday afternoon. Having started from pole in each of the last three years, Kostecki finished his lap 0.4942 seconds ahead of the next best driver. Only legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat have also claimed three successive poles, with neither able to claim a fourth.



With three drivers remaining, it looked like Kostecki was destined to become the first to achieve the feat. The third, Cooper Murray rounded the final turn, Murrays Corner, within a tenth of a second before ultimately crossing the finish line 0.2058 seconds slower than Kostecki. Then, Anton De Pasquale booted his Chevrolet Camaro around Mount Panorama only to finish 0.0384 seconds behind Kostecki’s time. Zach Bates in action. Getty Images Only Bates, who recorded the fastest qualifying time on Friday, was left. Bates gained on Kostecki at each split, crossing the line 0.2850 faster. The rookie was visibly emotional afterwards. After racing on Friday, Bates paid tribute to his mother and motorsport TV presenter Alison Drower, who died two weeks before his maiden Bathurst 1000 start last year as a wildcard entrant with veteran co-driver Craig Lowndes.



Speaking to reporters after the race, Bates was asked what his dad had to say to him in the pit.



“He didn’t say anything — he was crying,” Bates said. Loading Now in just his second start, he will start from pole – becoming just the third rookie, and the first since Marcos Ambrose in 2001, to do so. “It would’ve been cool, but I’d rather have my name engraved on the [Peter Brock] trophy,” Kostecki said of his failure to nab a fourth pole. Earlier, James Golding grazed the wall and finished with a time of 2:05:3028. It was better than the next attempt from former winner Matt Payne, who, despite being one of the best qualifiers in the Supercars Championship this year, finished the Shootout in 10th.



Full-season rookie Jayden Ojeda took the lead after three drivers, only to be knocked down a position when Jack Le Brocq finished ahead of him at the halfway mark, becoming the first driver of the day to record a sub 2:05 lap. A duck gatecrashed proceedings at one point during the afternoon’s practice session when it crossed the circuit with a number of ducklings in tow, forcing Mark Winterbottom to break. His Mustang was damaged when James Courtney then rear-ended him.

World.title: Michelle Payne was first to break racing’s glass ceiling. Rachel King is lining up to smash another
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Michelle Payne was first to break racing’s glass ceiling. Rachel King is lining up to smash another Danny Russell October 10, 2026 — 6:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Talented hoop Rachel King emerged on Saturday as a serious contender to win this year’s Cox Plate, a historic feat that would see the Sydney jockey smash one of racing’s unbroken glass ceilings. King could follow Michelle Payne and Jamie Melham into racing folklore if she becomes the first woman to salute in the country’s weight-for-age championship – to be staged at Flemington for the first time on Saturday week – after she became the first woman jockey to win the $3 million group 1 Caulfield Guineas. Rachel King celebrates winning the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven for trainer Bjorn Baker. Getty Images The 36-year-old King lobbed in Australia from the UK on a working holiday in 2014 and formed a formidable partnership with flamboyant Sydney-based New Zealand trainer Bjorn Baker. The pair were the toast of Melbourne racing fans on Saturday after combining to win the Guineas (1600 metres) on well-backed favourite Warwoven.



Related Article Victorian racing ‘We’re not a Big Build project’: Inside the $250 million Moonee Valley rebuild It was a win with the promise of more to come. Baker had long spruiked Warwoven’s credentials and the colt rocketed into third favouritism ($5) for the Cox Plate on the back of the Guineas victory. A win would see him become the first three-year-old galloper to capture the coveted $6 million event in 13 years. “I don’t think he has peaked. I think there’s still more there,” King said after her winning ride. “I’ve certainly never sat on a horse like this, and he’s pretty unbelievable.”



King has won 10 group 1s, but none of the sport’s majors. Payne became the first female jockey to win the Melbourne Cup in 2015, while Melham became the first woman to ride the winner of the Caulfield Cup on Half Yours last year, as well as the first female to take out the Cups double. Baker’s stable representative, Luke Hilton, praised King’s patient ride in the Guineas after she waited until the home turn before setting after second-favourite and another possible Cox Plate runner Blind Raise. Warwoven rockets into contention for the coming Cox Plate after winning the Caulfield Guineas. Getty Images “Over the past 24 hours she has copped a lot of instructions and running through the race play-by-play which she doesn’t appreciate because she is better off flying by the seat of her pants, but she did well, and it means a lot,” Hilton said “I see how hard she works and the ups and downs she goes through. It is an amazing game, and it can be very tough as well.”



Related Article Victorian racing ‘Jewish strength and solidarity’: The story behind Toorak runner’s changing colours Hinton labelled Warwoven an outstanding colt (by Sword Of State and out of Needle And Thread). “Bjorn has said for a long time that he could be one of those special horses that don’t come around too often. He’s proving him right so far,” he said. Further life was injected into this year’s Cox Plate when 70-1 outsider Land Legend caused one of the upsets of the spring by beating odds-on favourite Sheza Alibi by nose and putting away Birdman, a fancied runner with Carlton interests such as Chris Judd and Sam Docherty, in the $1 million group 1 Might And Power Stakes (2000m). No one expected the Ciaron Maher-trained Land Legend to win the race, a victory set up by a daring Ethan Brown front-running ride, least of all Sheza Alibi’s champion trainer Peter Moody. The seven-year-old gelding had not won a race in two years.



“As long as his ass points to the ground, he’d never beat her again,” Moody said of the upset, echoing the feelings of the race day crowd who let out an audible gasp when the fast-finishing Sheza Alibi failed by a matter of centimetres to run Land Legend down. “But he’s had his day in the sun, hasn’t he? So that’s life, and we’ll bounce back to fight another day.” Bouncing back might take more than Moody and co-trainer Katherine Coleman had originally planned, as they now turn their attention towards the $10 million Golden Eagle (1500m) at Randwick on October 31. “We followed Birdman, and unfortunately, he went terrible, and we were going to use him to drag us into the race, so it just didn’t pan out. So that’s life. We got beat on our merits,” Moody lamented. “We’ve got to sort of regroup and go back to Sydney in three weeks, and hopefully, we get the job done there.



“I am confident in her ability, but they ran a course record time. I would have liked a softer run today to go back to (1500m from 2000m) in three weeks, but we’ll let her guide the path and see how she does.” As for the reborn Land Legend, a French import formerly trained by Chris Waller to run in the big Cups, he had Maher tossing up between a run in this Saturday’s Caulfield Cup or the Cox Plate. “The Caulfield Cup can be a charge of the light-brigade to the first bend which wouldn’t really suit him,” Maher said. “So whether he runs in a Caulfield Cup and a Cox Plate, or whether he runs in the Cox Plate, it’s a good problem to have.” While King was the story of the day and injected extra spice into the Cox Plate narrative, the country’s best jockey, James McDonald, delivered the ride of the day at Caulfield by winning the $1 million group 1 Toorak Handicap (1600m) on the Waller-trained Lady Shenandoah, edging out Changing Colours by a nose.



“That was really one of the all-time greats, that ride,” Waller said of McDonald’s ability to barge between horses when he looked blocked for a run. “With 58-kilos for a mare, and awkward draw, there’s not an inch to spare, and he saved every inch he could. Kept the momentum. It was the difference between winning and not.”

World.title: History was there for the taking… until Wallabies bombed under a high-ball blitz
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion History was there for the taking… until Wallabies bombed under a high-ball blitz Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author October 10, 2026 — 7:37pm

October 10, 2026 — 7:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was going to be such a clever opener. “Let that be a lesson to world rugby,” I would exult, with echoes of Vitas Gerulaitis, “NO-ONE beats the Wallabies at the one ground 41 years in a row! 23 years and counting: The All Blacks retain the Bledisloe Cup. Getty Images Or maybe ... “Anyone can have a bad four decades, but that’s where the Wallabies really draw the line.”



It all turned, see, on the fact that our blokes had not won against the All Backs at Auckland’s Eden Park since 1986, and for the first part of this Bledisloe Cup Test match it really looked as if – hold my coat, Captain Cook – history was at hand. The Wallabies swept all before them. They carved them up in the backs, and stopped the hosts’ attack cold. They picked them off in the lineouts. The green and gold so dominated territory and possession that when our fullback Tom Wright sliced the defence wide open just seven minutes in to score, I was morally certain that for the next 40 years, I’d be able to boast: “I was there the night it all turned around, the beginning of the Green and Golden Age, after decades of All Blackness!” Tom Wright on his way to the tryline against the All Blacks. Getty Images But then those All Black boogers struck back, as they are ever wont to do, and one thing in particular did us real damage. The All Blacks kept putting up the high ball, and not only did none of the Wallabies appear to even call for it, many of them they didn’t even look particularly interested in claiming it.



It is a mystery to this despondent correspondent how a team so outstanding at so many other things continues to get this most basic of all required skills wrong. It is particularly confusing when Max Jorgensen and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii had been so great at it a fortnight ago against the Springboks. For the damage done by not swallowing whole the pills put up towards them was considerable, as the All Blacks quickly scored two converted tries and a penalty to lead 17-7. At least the fact our captain Harry Wilson restored a little order with a try just before halftime allowed us to hope, with the All Baddies only holding a 17-14 lead at the break. The Wallabies celebrate after Harry Wilson’s try before halftime. Getty Images Who would come out for the Wallabies in the second half? The team which dominated the first ten minutes, or the one that all but disappeared for the middle 20? At first, it looked it would be the former as, from the kick-off, Wright and Max Jorgensen combined to break through and we ended up with a line-out right on their line. The Promised Land was right there, just waiting for a Wallaby forward to take up his rightful position – planting the ball down for defence on a patch of grass that grows green from the blood, sweat and tears of his 40 forebears.



Alas, that attack was snuffed out by a penalty and much of the rest went back to an aerial battle where we appeared to have a distinct lack of Spitfires, and Jerry was everywhere at once! Look, it was not simply that the All Blacks continued to put the ball up and then recover it, it was than when we put the ball up, we had no one of note rushing through to put a tenth of the pressure on them that had been put on us. The territory this delivered to the All Blacks was more than enough for them to plant their flag four more times behind our goal line in the next 35 minutes, taking the lead out to 43-14 as the match started to ebb. Leroy Carter of the All Blacks touches down for a try. Getty Images In that time, Wilson, Rob Valetini and Fraser McReight continued to impress, as did Jorgensen and Wright for at least knocking on the All Back door. But our side needed a whole lot more than mere impressions. It needed to defuse their bombs and blow up some our own, but could manage neither feat, until ... Until, wouldn’t you know it? With five minutes to go, at long bloody last, Suaalii did what we wanted him to do – what he should be asked to do every kick-off – run through, leap high and get us the bloody ball! The result? A Wallaby TRY!



Seriously. It was that simple an equation. When they won the aerial battles, they scored. When we did, we scored. We just won bugger-all of those aerial battles. Their final try, with seconds on the clock, to take it to 50-19 just upped the agony. All up, as disappointing as it was, at least it is bloody clear what training should consist of this week. Tell ’em, coach Les Kiss: Related Article Live

Bledisloe Cup Bledisloe heartache as All Blacks blow away Wallabies at Eden Park again “At least until Marky Mark gets here in a few weeks to take the marks, we need all of you, every day, all day, without fail, to practice the bloody high ball – otherwise we are wasting our time. And next week, the first bastard that calls out ‘YOURS!’ instead of ‘MINE!’ or makes no call at all, will be pulled from the field. We simply cannot compete without that.” And they really can’t. Most other parts of our game are seriously solid. That part is seriously shithouse. You heard me. And I know I shouldn’t say a bad word in a family newspaper. But kids, on this occasion, no other word will do.



Onwards to next week, at Homebush. Fix the high ball. Play ball! News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Bledisloe heartache as All Blacks blow away Wallabies at Eden Park again
World.content:
It’s the hope that kills you.

The long wait of Wallabies fans to see an Australian win over New Zealand at Eden Park will stretch into a 41st year after the All Blacks turned on another ruthless performance at their spiritual home to post a 50-19 victory.

Loading

The seven-tries-to-three victory ensured the All Blacks also retained the Bledisloe Cup for a 24th straight year, and gave Les Kiss his first defeat as Wallabies coach. On the flipside, it gave former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie his first taste from the elusive Bledisloe urn after several years of failure in gold.

The All Blacks have a habit of flossing their teeth with Australian optimism, and so it proved again in Auckland.

The Wallabies entered the match being talked up as a rising side with the potential to break some long-standing droughts at Eden Park, based on their last-start win over the Springboks and the Kiwis’ three-Test losing streak.

No Wallaby side has won at Eden Park since 1986, and no side has beaten the All Blacks there since 1994.

Those records rarely seemed threatened on a night that followed an all-too familiar script.

The Wallabies trailed by just 17-14 at the break, having stayed in touch with two tries despite being under siege for most the half.

Loading

Throughout the night, the Aussies were dominated in the aerial contests and using a passive defence, the Wallabies put the All Blacks under no linespeed pressure. The Kiwis waited patiently for their opportunity to strike and slice through a gap, or simply hold the ball for long enough to drive in a try.

In contrast, the verve shown by the Wallabies attack in the previous months was mostly missing, in an unusually listless and underwhelming performance.

Australia’s small window of staying in the game and potentially even winning came early in the second half, when they had several chances to score in the Kiwi quarter and take the lead.

But Irish referee Andrew Brace pinged the Wallabies for two 50-50 penalties, which piggybacked New Zealand into the Wallaby quarter. The Kiwis made no mistake with their territory and scored in the 49th minute and then again in the 54th minute. Now trailing by 16, the air went out of the Wallabies’ tyres.

Chasing the game to get back in the contest, the Wallabies then made errors in their own half and went on to concede another three tries in the last quarter. A late try to reserve hooker Josh Nasser was in the category of too little, too late.

To make matters worse on an already black night, star centre Len Ikitau came off the field with a concussion, which is likely to rule him out of the second Bledisloe Cup clash in Sydney next week.

Codie Taylor of the All Blacks celebrates scoring a try. Getty Images

The All Blacks led 17-14 after an opening half where the Wallabies started and finished the first well, but battled in the middle.

Australia dominated the early territory, and put pressure on the Kiwi line. Several attempted rolling mauls were repelled but slick work from the Wallabies’ backs saw the visitors open the scoring.

Under advantage, the Wallabies spun the ball left and a second-wave pass saw Ben Donaldson tap the ball onto the Max Jorgensen, who surged through a gap and passed to Tom Wright. The fullback had Suaalii on his outside but dummied and found a tiny gap, racing 20 metres to score.

The Kiwis responded quickly, however, when they finally got some possession and they were helped by the Wallabies’ passive defence and inability to win contestable kicks.

After one retake from Jordie Barrett, the Wallabies defence was caught sleepily retreating and disjointed, and Damian McKenzie sliced through. He found Peter Lakai in support for a 12th-minute try.

It was more of the same just three minutes later, when the Wallabies’ defensive line was again breached; this time through poor spacing. In their element against a retreating defence, the Kiwis kept punching and Tupou Vai’i ended up charging over in the 15th minute.

It was all a bit too easy, and things began to looking worrying for the Wallabies, who now also began turning the ball over when they got their hands on it.

The Kiwis began turned their favourite tap – the trusty pressure valve – and the Wallabies were lucky to not concede again when Will Jordan sliced through yet again in the 19th minute, but a long pass to support and a probable try went astray.

The Wallabies stayed in the fight but missed an easy penalty from in front in the 23rd minute. The All Blacks didn’t miss theirs though; they posted a 32nd minute kick to extend the lead to 10 points.

The visitors defended their line strongly in the last 10 minutes, and instead of conceding another try, which could have been a game-sealer already, the Wallabies shocked the crowd by scoring.

The All Blacks celebrate retaining the Bledisloe Cup. Getty Images

A penalty helped the Aussies into the All Black half, and again Donaldson got the ball out the back on attack. He slipped through the line and found skipper Harry Wilson in support. The skipper raced in under the sticks, bringing the deficit back to just three points at the break.

The Wallabies began the second half brightly, and counter-attacked down to the Kiwis line immediately. But they missed that chance, and missed another chance soon after, when a strong Rob Valetini run set up a chance for a lineout maul.

But referee Andrew Brace pinged the Wallabies for a pedantic obstruction penalty, and then pinged them again for holding on from a contestable kick. That gave the Kiwis entry to the Aussie quarter, and the Kiwis didn’t miss their chance.

Following a lineout maul – in which New Zealand went unpenalised by Brace for the same lifter obstruction – halfback Cam Roigard dived over from broken play.

By now, the Wallabies looked sapped and using a passive defensive line, were allowing the All Blacks to dictate terms at the contact zone. It seemed almost inevitable that the Kiwis would score again and they did in the 54th minute, when a long sequence of phases saw Codie Taylor break through and score.

The lead was now 16, with 20 minutes to go, and the night was as good as over for the Wallabies.

Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Jordan all rubbed more salt in the wounds with last-quarter tries.

World.title: Church victim accused of having ‘credibility of $3 note’ gets $2.2 million
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCatholic church Church victim accused of having ‘credibility of $3 note’ gets $2.2 million Cameron Houston October 10, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A survivor of shocking clerical abuse has been awarded more than $2.2 million by a Supreme Court jury, despite a series of contentious claims by the Marist Brothers’ legal team that he lied about his mental health and had the “credibility of a $3 note”. Greg Barclay was repeatedly accused of fabricating and exaggerating evidence during the civil trial, including a claim he faked details about two suicide attempts after he was sexually abused by brother John Anthony Skehan at the former St Colman’s College in Shepparton in 1970. Historical sexual abuse survivor Greg Barclay has been awarded more than $2.2 million. Justin McManus During a 12-day trial last month, barrister Jack Pappas, acting for the Trustees of the Marist Brothers, branded Barclay a “money-grubber” who was motivated by greed, while dismissing some of his testimony as “balderdash, piffle and rot”. “I suggest to you [there] was a performance by Mr Barclay on the morning of the second day of his evidence, unabashed display of faux emotion, gasping for air, huffing and puffing, struggling to get words out, the full enchilada,” Pappas told the jury.



“He pretended in front of you, and he pretended to doctors about the after effects and the continuing impact of the abuse upon him when he was 14 years old. He exaggerated symptoms and disabilities and consequences, all seeking sympathy and damages to which he is just not entitled.” Related Article Investigations Christian Brothers cry poor to abuse survivors after transferring elite schools for $1 However, a six-person jury emphatically rejected Pappas’ submission and awarded $2,248,974 to Barclay on October 1, while the Marist Brothers were also ordered to pay his legal costs. Barclay told this masthead he had been vindicated by the judgement, but was emotionally drained by the trial after more than three days giving evidence and facing cross-examination. “I knew they would come in hard, but it was just brutal. It was worse than I’d anticipated. To be accused of pretending to be a victim/survivor is just outrageous and that’s after the person who abused me was convicted in court,” Barclay told this masthead.



“There were so many comments that really struck me as disgusting. I was called a money-grabbing grub.” The court made no criticism of the conduct of the Marist Brother’s counsel in the judgement. Barclay, now 70, said there was a stark contrast between the public comments made by the Catholic order and its conduct in court. “This was consistent with how the Marist Brothers and the Catholic Church have behaved in the past. They publicly claim to support victims and apologise for the past, but when someone makes it to court they are accused of making it all up and [they say they] shouldn’t be believed,” he said. Barclay says he was disgusted by some of the claims by the Marist Brothers’ legal team in court. Justin McManus



However, the director of the Marist Brothers professional standards’ office, Domenic Pagano, defended the order’s legal response. He confirmed the Marist Brothers would appeal the recent judgement in favour of Barclay. “The Marist Brothers accepted that they were liable to pay Mr Barclay fair and reasonable compensation but believed, on a proper assessment of the evidence, that Mr Barclay was exaggerating aspects of his claim and that he had no claim for recovery of economic loss following an active and remunerative career as an educator and senior union official,” Pagano said. Related Article High Court of Australia Controversial High Court ruling could be used against sex abuse victims like Greg “The Marist Brothers’ counsel acted in court in a manner consistent with a robust challenge to a claim which the defendant believed to be deliberately overblown.” Pagano said the order had to be judicious in meeting the expanding legal demands of clerical abuse survivors and had an obligation as trustee of funds that also provide extensive education and care services.



In 2014, Skehan was convicted of indecently assaulting Barclay and handed a suspended eight-month prison sentence. He was previously convicted and placed on a suspended sentence in 2010 for the indecent assault of a young child in Broken Hill in the 1970s. In a press release after Skehan’s second conviction, the Marist Brothers said it was committed to “addressing the terrible effects of past abuse.” “We will continue to work with victims of abuse with care and compassion to help them achieve healing,” the statement read. In 2015, Barclay received an apology from then provincial leader Brother Peter Carroll. “I accept you were harmed through no fault of your own by the abusive actions of [Brother] John and that harm has extended into your adult life with adverse effects on your personal, work and social relationships,” Carroll said.



Barclay’s solicitor Laird Macdonald from Rightside Legal said the Marist Brothers deserved to pay a steep price for their treatment of his client during the trial. “The Marists told the jury to give him zero compensation for an impacted working life. To their credit, the jury saw through those ridiculous slurs and arguments,” Macdonald said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Calm before the storm: Why Nick Blakey’s path from Sydney to North remains uncertain
World.content:
Updated SportAFLTrading and drafting Calm before the storm: Why Nick Blakey’s path from Sydney to North remains uncertain Jon Pierik and Andrew Wu Updated October 10, 2026 — 6:57pm ,first published 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Nick Blakey’s path to North Melbourne remains uncertain as Sydney and the Kangaroos look to ramp up discussions over a blockbuster deal. Saturday was the calm before the storm, with neither club holding major discussions over Blakey’s future, according to two industry sources with knowledge of the matter. The Kangaroos’ pick No.6 in this year’s draft shapes as the key component of any trade to send Blakey to the club where his father John played 224 of his 359 games in the 1990s and early 2000s and won two premierships. Swans star Nick Blakey wants to continue his AFL career at North Melbourne. AFL Photos The pressure is on North Melbourne to secure a deal for Blakey, having made many unsuccessful bids to poach rival stars, including Richmond champion Dustin Martin, Collingwood star Jordan De Goey, GWS gun Josh Kelly, and Swans superstar Isaac Heeney.



Blakey has five years to run on his contract so they must find a package of picks to entice the Swans to release the All-Australian rebounding defender. Blakey wants to move to Arden Street but Essendon, Geelong and St Kilda have all expressed interest in him. Related Article Updated

Trading and drafting North board approved mammoth Blakey offer amid police investigation The Cats do not have the draft picks to entice the Swans, after parting ways with first-round picks for defender Jordan Ridley and ruckman Rowan Marshall, but the Saints have picks 10 and 16 this year, plus a future-first in 2028. The North Melbourne board, headed by president Sonja Hood, has signed off on a $12 million offer for Blakey, who was one of five players handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for his involvement in a night of wild partying at Melbourne’s Pullman East hotel in August.



A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. No charges have been laid, and all five Swans players who served season-ending suspensions denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. Elsewhere, Carlton and Collingwood are close to finalising a deal to turn young Blues ruckman Flynn Riley into a Magpie. The trade is likely to involve future picks. The Pies have a full suite of selections in 2027 and 2028 to work with to satisfy the Blues, who acquired Riley in this year’s mid-season draft. The Blues rated him highly enough to offer a two-year deal, but the Pies have offered more. Butters’ childhood dream comes true with Bulldogs move



Jon Pierik Boom recruit Zak Butters says the Western Bulldogs are on the cusp of “something special”, and revealed he turned to Marcus Bontempelli for advice throughout the year before making his decision to head to the Whitten Oval. Butters, 26, is officially a Bulldog on a record nine-year contract worth between $17 million and $17.5 million after the AFL on Friday approved a convoluted side deal involving five clubs and a series of first, second and later draft picks exchanged. The Butters contract is the biggest in AFL history in total, though he will earn less than the $2 million per season St Kilda’s Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has made. Ready to start: Zak Butters is looking forward to getting to work with the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos



“It’s good to make the decision and be here, and, yeah, I feel like it was a long time getting to this point,” Butters said. Related Article Updated

Trading and drafting North board approved mammoth Blakey offer amid police investigation “And a few people told me along the journey that when you know, you know. And I felt like, yeah, once I knew, I just wanted to get it done, and get here and meet everyone and start my next journey.” Butters had already formed a friendship with Bontempelli, the Bulldogs’ skipper and legendary figure, which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the midfield gun that also involved Richmond and Geelong. “He’s obviously one that I am looking forward to playing with, and he’s been an inspiration of mine since I was a kid, and probably more so the more I got to know him, not just this year, but along the journey and playing against him,” Butters told the Bulldogs’ website.



“[I’m] trying to be the best, so you’re trying to learn off the best, and he’s he’s definitely one of them. So, over the last year as well, he’s just been a good sounding board and someone that you want to play footy with. Related Article AFL 2026 How Nick Blakey can get to the Roos and what it will cost them “I feel like, as much as I can add to the footy club, that I’ll learn a lot from him, and some other guys at the footy club as well. So, yeah, I’m really looking forward to learning and becoming better off guys like Marcus and Bevo [coach Luke Beveridge] as well.” Butters grew up following the Dogs, his family residing in Darley on the western metropolitan fringe. He played for the Western Jets before being taken by the Power with the 12th pick of the 2018 national draft. He said one of the highlights of his life had been attending the 2016 finals, when the Bulldogs unexpectedly stormed to their second club premiership.



“Yeah, I have loved the Bulldogs since I was a kid, had plenty of jumpers growing up, and loved a lot of different players. But, probably, 2016 is hard to top,” Butters said. “I remember catching the train in from Bacchus Marsh, and watching the finals, and was lucky enough to sneak a few tickets through friends and family. And yeah, I remember catching the train home after the ’16 granny [grand final], and, obviously, catching the train back through the west to get to Bacchus Marsh, it was pretty chaotic and loud. “It’s still one of my favourite days that I’ve had in footy. So it’d be cool to try and run that back.” Butters said he wants to be role model for youth in the western suburbs, reinforcing that they, too, can reach the heights of elite football.



He failed to play in a grand final in his eight years with the Power, and wants that to change at his new club. The Dogs’ 2026 campaign ended with an elimination final defeat to Adelaide. “It’s an exciting stage for the football club, and one that we can, hopefully, really challenge in,” Butters said. “And you want to bring members and all that along for the ride, and bring them in on the journey, and you want them to be there for the wins and the losses, and come along for the ride with us. And I feel like it could be something pretty special.” Get around our footy coverage

World.content:
If you’re not an Australian soccer sicko like me (and many others), you might be wondering why this game has been built up to be such a big deal.

We’ve got two pieces for you to read, explaining exactly why that’s the case. This isn’t just about the past meeting the present - it’s also about the future of the sport and the purpose of the A-League.

The day after South Melbourne clinched their spot in the final, a good three weeks ago, I wrote this story, which looks at how the Australia Cup (formerly FFA Cup) revived dormant conversations about promotion and relegation, a mooted national second division and the role of clubs outside of the top tier - and then why South vs Victory in particular is loaded with so much meaning.

And then yesterday (or in today’s papers), we’ve produced a closer look at South Melbourne’s recent transformation, and how realistic the prospects are of them getting an A-League licence, and when.

Enjoy.

World.title: Rookie claims Bathurst 1000 pole position in a Shootout shock
World.content:
SportMotorsportSupercars Rookie claims Bathurst 1000 pole position in a Shootout shock Frances Howe October 10, 2026 — 6:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Zach Bates will become the first rookie since 2001 to start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position after stunning Mount Panorama for the second day in a row to win the Top 10 Shootout qualifying competition. A day after clocking the fastest time around the circuit in this generation of supercars and earning provisional pole, 22-year-old Bates denied Brodie Kostecki the unprecedented feat of becoming the first driver to claim four successive pole positions in the Great Race. Zac Bates and co-driver Aaron Seton celebrate taking poll position. Getty Images The Top 10 Shootout pits the fastest 10 drivers from Friday’s qualifiers in a single solo lap around the Mount Panorama circuit. Their times set the first 10 positions on the grid for the main race on Sunday. On the verge of history, Kostecki led with just Bates left to drive on Saturday afternoon. Having started from pole in each of the last three years, Kostecki finished his lap 0.4942 seconds ahead of the next best driver. Only legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat have also claimed three successive poles, with neither able to claim a fourth.



With three drivers remaining, it looked like Kostecki was destined to become the first to achieve the feat. The third, Cooper Murray rounded the final turn, Murrays Corner, within a tenth of a second before ultimately crossing the finish line 0.2058 seconds slower than Kostecki. Then, Anton De Pasquale booted his Chevrolet Camaro around Mount Panorama only to finish 0.0384 seconds behind Kostecki’s time. Zach Bates in action. Getty Images Only Bates, who recorded the fastest qualifying time on Friday, was left. Bates gained on Kostecki at each split, crossing the line 0.2850 faster. The rookie was visibly emotional afterwards. After racing on Friday, Bates paid tribute to his mother and motorsport TV presenter Alison Drower, who died two weeks before his maiden Bathurst 1000 start last year as a wildcard entrant with veteran co-driver Craig Lowndes.



Speaking to reporters after the race, Bates was asked what his dad had to say to him in the pit.



“He didn’t say anything — he was crying,” Bates said. Loading Now in just his second start, he will start from pole – becoming just the third rookie, and the first since Marcos Ambrose in 2001, to do so. “It would’ve been cool, but I’d rather have my name engraved on the [Peter Brock] trophy,” Kostecki said of his failure to nab a fourth pole. Earlier, James Golding grazed the wall and finished with a time of 2:05:3028. It was better than the next attempt from former winner Matt Payne, who, despite being one of the best qualifiers in the Supercars Championship this year, finished the Shootout in 10th.



Full-season rookie Jayden Ojeda took the lead after three drivers, only to be knocked down a position when Jack Le Brocq finished ahead of him at the halfway mark, becoming the first driver of the day to record a sub 2:05 lap. A duck gatecrashed proceedings at one point during the afternoon’s practice session when it crossed the circuit with a number of ducklings in tow, forcing Mark Winterbottom to break. His Mustang was damaged when James Courtney then rear-ended him.

Talented hoop Rachel King emerged on Saturday as a serious contender to win this year’s Cox Plate, a historic feat that would see the Sydney jockey smash one of racing’s unbroken glass ceilings. King could follow Michelle Payne and Jamie Melham into racing folklore if she becomes the first woman to salute in the country’s weight-for-age championship – to be staged at Flemington for the first time on Saturday week – after she became the first woman jockey to win the $3 million group 1 Caulfield Guineas. Rachel King celebrates winning the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven for trainer Bjorn Baker. Getty Images The 36-year-old King lobbed in Australia from the UK on a working holiday in 2014 and formed a formidable partnership with flamboyant Sydney-based New Zealand trainer Bjorn Baker. The pair were the toast of Melbourne racing fans on Saturday after combining to win the Guineas (1600 metres) on well-backed favourite Warwoven.



Related Article Victorian racing ‘We’re not a Big Build project’: Inside the $250 million Moonee Valley rebuild It was a win with the promise of more to come. Baker had long spruiked Warwoven’s credentials and the colt rocketed into third favouritism ($5) for the Cox Plate on the back of the Guineas victory. A win would see him become the first three-year-old galloper to capture the coveted $6 million event in 13 years. “I don’t think he has peaked. I think there’s still more there,” King said after her winning ride. “I’ve certainly never sat on a horse like this, and he’s pretty unbelievable.”



King has won 10 group 1s, but none of the sport’s majors. Payne became the first female jockey to win the Melbourne Cup in 2015, while Melham became the first woman to ride the winner of the Caulfield Cup on Half Yours last year, as well as the first female to take out the Cups double. Baker’s stable representative, Luke Hilton, praised King’s patient ride in the Guineas after she waited until the home turn before setting after second-favourite and another possible Cox Plate runner Blind Raise. Warwoven rockets into contention for the coming Cox Plate after winning the Caulfield Guineas. Getty Images “Over the past 24 hours she has copped a lot of instructions and running through the race play-by-play which she doesn’t appreciate because she is better off flying by the seat of her pants, but she did well, and it means a lot,” Hilton said “I see how hard she works and the ups and downs she goes through. It is an amazing game, and it can be very tough as well.”



Related Article Victorian racing ‘Jewish strength and solidarity’: The story behind Toorak runner’s changing colours Hinton labelled Warwoven an outstanding colt (by Sword Of State and out of Needle And Thread). “Bjorn has said for a long time that he could be one of those special horses that don’t come around too often. He’s proving him right so far,” he said. Further life was injected into this year’s Cox Plate when 70-1 outsider Land Legend caused one of the upsets of the spring by beating odds-on favourite Sheza Alibi by nose and putting away Birdman, a fancied runner with Carlton interests such as Chris Judd and Sam Docherty, in the $1 million group 1 Might And Power Stakes (2000m). No one expected the Ciaron Maher-trained Land Legend to win the race, a victory set up by a daring Ethan Brown front-running ride, least of all Sheza Alibi’s champion trainer Peter Moody. The seven-year-old gelding had not won a race in two years.



“As long as his ass points to the ground, he’d never beat her again,” Moody said of the upset, echoing the feelings of the race day crowd who let out an audible gasp when the fast-finishing Sheza Alibi failed by a matter of centimetres to run Land Legend down. “But he’s had his day in the sun, hasn’t he? So that’s life, and we’ll bounce back to fight another day.” Bouncing back might take more than Moody and co-trainer Katherine Coleman had originally planned, as they now turn their attention towards the $10 million Golden Eagle (1500m) at Randwick on October 31. “We followed Birdman, and unfortunately, he went terrible, and we were going to use him to drag us into the race, so it just didn’t pan out. So that’s life. We got beat on our merits,” Moody lamented. “We’ve got to sort of regroup and go back to Sydney in three weeks, and hopefully, we get the job done there.



“I am confident in her ability, but they ran a course record time. I would have liked a softer run today to go back to (1500m from 2000m) in three weeks, but we’ll let her guide the path and see how she does.” As for the reborn Land Legend, a French import formerly trained by Chris Waller to run in the big Cups, he had Maher tossing up between a run in this Saturday’s Caulfield Cup or the Cox Plate. “The Caulfield Cup can be a charge of the light-brigade to the first bend which wouldn’t really suit him,” Maher said. “So whether he runs in a Caulfield Cup and a Cox Plate, or whether he runs in the Cox Plate, it’s a good problem to have.” While King was the story of the day and injected extra spice into the Cox Plate narrative, the country’s best jockey, James McDonald, delivered the ride of the day at Caulfield by winning the $1 million group 1 Toorak Handicap (1600m) on the Waller-trained Lady Shenandoah, edging out Changing Colours by a nose.



“That was really one of the all-time greats, that ride,” Waller said of McDonald’s ability to barge between horses when he looked blocked for a run. “With 58-kilos for a mare, and awkward draw, there’s not an inch to spare, and he saved every inch he could. Kept the momentum. It was the difference between winning and not.”

World.title: Opponents label National's fishing policy 'desperate' and a 'flip-flop'
World.content:
New Zealand First says National's fishing policy is desperate and unresearched, and would have huge impacts on employment and the costs of fish.

Meanwhile, environmental groups and parties to National's left say National cannot be trusted on the issue, given the party's track record this term.

After a spearfishing trip departing from Auckland's Takapuna Beach on Saturday, National leader Christopher Luxon announced the policy to ban ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf, establish a new Waiheke Island marine reserve, ban commercial sales of marlin, and review bottom trawling on sea mounts with a view to reducing use of the technique over time.

'Desperate and unresearched' - Peters

NZ First's Shane Jones has been championing the fishing industry this term of government, so the policy would appear to be a shot across his bow - and Luxon said he did not care what Jones might think of it.

NZ First leader Winston Peters, after what he said was a "wall to wall" public meeting in Invercargill, suggested the consequences had not been thought through.

"It's rather desperate and it's rather unresearched as to the consequences of what they propose to do, both with respect to the workers and the fishermen and fisherwomen, and everybody's involved in the market, but also the customers and the cost of fish going forward," Peters said.

"I don't understand why he's actually making that announcement because there's been a lot of work and a lot of research going into the total consequences of such decisions, and it's premature to arrive at that because the work in its totality hasn't been done."

However, he would not commit to opposing the policy in coalition negotiations.

"Look, we just heard about it today so we're not going to rush to judgement on it, but ... when you're forced to check out what you've just heard - to its authenticity and its veracity, and its utility and its workability - it's not going to survive that test.

"We'd be opposed to it but we need the time to work on that - but I was actually quite surprised that they would make such a premature announcement."

He said the policy went against what the government had been trying to do over the past term.

"We've tried to keep in mind two things: there are thousands of workers involved, and there are also hundreds of thousands of customers involved - and within a cost of living crisis like we have, those sorts of costs are significant."

'Really disappointing' - Forest and Bird

Forest and Bird spokesperson Bianca Ranson said Labour and the Greens had offered support to National on a ring-net ban for Hauraki, so there was "no need to compromise those high protection areas by allowing fishing in them".

She said the Waiheke Marine Reserve proposal had been "sitting on their desk" for nearly two years, and the decision could have been made already.

"It's great to see some energy around protection for the gulf, but it is very much a case of why did they not act on it this term?"

National seemed to be using the issue's popularity to score points, she said.

"It's very clear that bottom trawling on the Hauraki Gulf is an election issue, we've been campaigning hard on it. There's overwhelming social licence; people want to see action in the gulf ... what has been announced today could have been done this term. It feels quite unfair to hear they're announcing these things when they've literally had the power to be able to enact them."

National can't be trusted on oceans policy - Labour, Greens

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said National's time in government suggested it would do the opposite of what it campaigned on, and the party could not be trusted.

"When we announced protections around the Hauraki Gulf when we were in government, the National Party said that they didn't go far enough and they supported them, and then in government, undid much of the work that we were doing."

Hipkins said Labour was committed to banning bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf, but in terms of scaling up a ban in New Zealand's EEZ, there was more work to do.

"It can't be done immediately. There's a need for us still to fish. There's jobs associated with that. As new technology emerges, and we've invested as a country in quite a lot of research and development in this area, we need to do more of that so that we can work out how to do fishing more sustainably and with less environmental impact."

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick also said the policy showed National could not be trusted on oceans policy.

"When we were going through the amendment to the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act ... we ended up with a proposal for these high protection areas, and then at the 11th hour ministers of this government had a backroom meeting and decided to create carve-outs in those so-called high protection areas to allow ring-net commercial fishers to continue fishing.

"Now they're turning around, understanding how deeply unpopular this is and saying they're going to campaign on undoing it. You cannot trust the National Party when it comes to conservation."

Opportunity Party welcomes shift

The Opportunity Party also noted much of the policy could have been progressed in the last three years, but welcomed the new approach.

Oceans and fisheries spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said National did not need to rely on New Zealand First in the first place to get the legislation that created the high protection areas - including the exemptions - over the line.

"Parties on the other side of the House would have supported it. There was absolutely no need to exempt commercial fishing from those two areas in the first place. So I think it's pretty interesting to see that National's now campaigning on reversing a decision it didn't actually have to make in the last term."

One of Opportunity's five bottom lines is an immediate end to bottom trawling in inshore areas such as the Hauraki Gulf, followed by a complete phase-out.

Leader Qiulae Wong said National had "clearly been led astray by some of their coalition partners" this term and wanted to see the party go further.

World.title: Youth homelessness a 'growing reality' as Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day
World.content:
Youth homelessness is "getting younger", with support workers warning more rangatahi are going without basic necessities and safe places to stay.

Rangatahi, youth advocates and housing providers gathered in West Auckland on Saturday to mark World Homeless Day, calling for better support for young people experiencing homelessness.

The event was organised by Manaaki Rangatahi, a kaupapa Māori-led collective working to address youth housing insecurity and homelessness in Aotearoa.

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa, from Mā Te Huruhuru Charitable Trust, works with the organisation's Manukura outreach team, connecting with taitamariki experiencing homelessness across Tāmaki Makaurau.

He said the situation was changing, with younger children increasingly needing support. The night before the event, his team had connected with a 12-year-old who had been homeless for more than nine months.

"I've not seen homelessness like this before. It's a different homelessness now. It's getting younger.

"The need is more, and there's not a hell of a lot of support out there for them."

He said many young people lacked access to basic necessities, while the proportion of rangatahi Māori and Pacific young people experiencing homelessness was particularly concerning.

"I would say 90 percent are of Māori whakapapa or are from Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa," he said.

"It hurts. It shouldn't be a reality for us as people of the land, as tangata whenua. We shouldn't be experiencing this.

"It is really hard to swallow sometimes to see our own people out there."

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa says homeless youth are getting younger and needing more support. RNZ / Coco Lance

Mā Te Huruhuru's Manukura outreach vehicle, or 'waka', allows kaimahi to go directly to young people rather than requiring them to find their way to a service.

The team provides food, hygiene products, phone-charging equipment and a safe space for rangatahi to sit down and talk.

Raising awareness was an important first step towards finding lasting solutions, Panapa said.

"We need to normalise the conversation and have more kōrero, and work collectively to come up with sustainable solutions for our taitamariki and our whānau who are currently homeless."

As Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day, Panapa wants New Zealanders to understand that homelessness and youth homeless is "a reality".

"Homelessness is not our future. It should not be our future, for our taitamariki, for our mokopuna and for our whānau."

Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal, 18, says finding support helped her work towards a safer future for herself and her baby Kaos. RNZ / Coco Lance

'Change can happen'

18-year-old Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal knows what it is like to experience homelessness and the importance of having somewhere safe to turn.

Morgan-Neal said she experienced "deep addiction" and an abusive relationship before seeking support from Grace Foundation, a charitable trust providing accommodation and rehabilitation services.

She said she had been sober for five months and was working towards a better future for herself and her baby.

Before seeking help, she had spent time sleeping in stolen cars and abandoned houses when she was only 12 years old up until she was 16.

"I felt neglected and broken. I didn't grow up with my parents."

A key kaupapa of this year's World Homeless Day was 'What does Home mean or look like to you?' RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Morgan-Neal said losing touch with her Māori culture while growing up had also affected her, but reconnecting through pōwhiri, wānanga and kapa haka at Grace Foundation had been an important part of her journey.

She said the support helped her rebuild trust and focus on herself and her child.

"I didn't want to give my baby the life that I had. I wanted to give him better."

For her, a safe home had "healthy connections, love, caring ... and respecting and loving one another".

"Connecting with one another. That's what I think home is."

Her message to others experiencing similar challenges and addiction was to reach out for support.

"Change can happen. Change is worth it. Reach out for help. Speaking up is not wrong."

Manaaki Rangatahi chief executive Bianca Johanson is calling for more youth housing and a national strategy to address youth homelessness. RNZ / Coco Lance

Home is more than a roof

Community Housing Aotearoa's most recent report on severe housing deprivation found Māori made up 28.8 percent of people

experiencing homelessness, despite accounting for 17.1 percent of the population.

Pacific people accounted for 22.6 percent of those experiencing homelessness, despite making up about 8 percent of the population.

The report also highlighted the scale of youth homelessness, with more than half of people experiencing homelessness under the age of 24.

It warned youth homelessness could become a pathway into adult homelessness without early, age-appropriate support and changes to barriers that prevent young people accessing housing.

The World Homeless Day art exhibition by Kākano Youth Arts Collective reflects the lived experiences of rangatahi, capturing journeys from a “trap house to a home”. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

21-year-old Georgia, a member of Kākano Youth Arts Collective, said youth homelessness could be difficult to recognise because many young people were not sleeping on the street.

She had supported someone close to her who moved between homes, including a period when they slept together on a mattress in a garage.

"Just because you don't see youth on the street begging for change or sleeping in a blanket on the street doesn't mean it doesn't exist," she said.

"Youth homelessness is quite often jumping from couch to couch, staying at friends' houses, sleeping on horrible mattresses in people's garages."

Georgia said young people could end up staying in unsafe environments because they had nowhere else to go.

"It's quite a dangerous situation to be in, but you're so desperate to be somewhere that's not your own home because you don't want to be in your own home."

She said the lack of visibility meant youth homelessness could be pushed aside, even when young people were experiencing significant housing insecurity.

"Just because they're in a house doesn't mean they're actually safe, and that still classes as homeless because if you're couch surfing, it's not stable."

20-year-old youth advocate Platinum says homelessness goes beyond sleeping rough, with many rangatahi couch surfing or living in unsafe homes. RNZ / Coco Lance

Platinum, a 20-year-old rangatahi MC at the event, reiterated that homelessness was much broader than sleeping rough, with many young people moving between houses or living in unsafe environments.

"Homelessness is just an umbrella word for so many things. Homelessness is when you live in a house that has way too many people. Homelessness is when you are couch surfing, going from home to home," she said.

"People aren't choosing to be homeless."

Platinum said a home should be a safe place where people felt protected, heard and seen.

"Home isn't just a place, it's a life."

Manaaki Rangatahi is calling for greater investment in youth housing and a coordinated national response to homelessness.

World.title: Otago dominate Hawke's Bay on home turf, earning spot in NPC semifinals
World.content:
Otago got their revenge over Hawke's Bay and continued to defend their home ground fortress with a 50-14 win in their NPC quarter-final in Dunedin.

Earlier this season, Hawke's Bay pulled off a come from behind victory over the southerners but could not do the same on Saturday with a place in the semifinals on the line.

Otago made their intentions clear early with no.8 Christian Lio-Willie powering over from the back of a scrum to open the scoring in the seventh minute.

The home side had doubled their lead when halfback Kieran McClea marked his return to the starting lineup with a try in the 16th minute.

Hawke's Bay replied through their halfback Folau Fakatava, when he finished off a break from winger Nic Benn, but Otago restored their lead through tighthead prop Saula Ma'u who crashed over after some strong work from his forwards and took a 24-7 lead into halftime.

After the break Henry Bell extended the lead when he also scored off the back of a maul.

The visitors were awarded a penalty try and Joseva Tamani was sent to the sinbin for playing the ball on the ground and preventing Fakatava scoring his second in the 50th minute.

However, the home side could not be slowed down as Sam Nemec-Vial sprinted in to score, even though his team were still down to 14 men.

Replacement back Joel Lam scored his first try of the season as Otago kept piling on the points.

Hawke's Bay made mass changes on the hour mark but could not turn around their fortunes.

Otago's final try came after a couple of players came close but it was Harry Irving who got the ball down over the line.

The win also reinforced Otago's strength on their home ground, with a record of one loss in their last 12 games at Forsyth Barr Stadium.

World.title: Ruthless Taranaki clinch NPC semifinal spot after Bradley Slater hat-trick against North Harbour
World.content:
Taranaki have continued their high-scoring late season form and secured a place in the NPC semifinals with a 50-31 win over North Harbour on the North Shore.

In the first meeting between these teams this season, Taranaki hooker Bradley Slater was once again the star with a hat-trick of tries in his side's eight-try rout.

Slater had also scored three tries against Harbour last season.

In a tit for tat first half, Harbour winger Rory Taylor scored in the second minute of the match when he was on the end of a move that began at a lineout, went through several sets of hands, and was sealed with him crossing the try line in the corner to give the home side a dream start.

However, 10 minutes later Taranaki struck back on the counter when pacy winger Kini Naholo outran the defenders to score in the left corner. The try was not converted and Harbour held on to the lead.

Just after the half-hour mark, Taranaki were temporarily reduced to 14 men when centre Meihana Grindlay got a yellow card for no clear release at the breakdown.

While Harbour had the numerical advantage, Taylor ran in his second try, but again Taranaki hit back minutes later through Slater, who scored off the back of a maul.

Taranaki then took the lead for the first time in the match while still a man down - flanker Michael Loft went over in the corner after the hooter in the first half to go into the sheds ahead 17-14.

After a back and forth first half, Taranaki unleashed in the second.

Naholo scored his second try four minutes after halftime, off some solid work by the forwards.

Slater then scored twice in six minutes after getting driven over the line both times before getting subbed at the 60-minute mark.

Jacob Ratumaitavuki-Kneepkens got in on the try scoring action, as did Vereniki Tikoisolomone.

Back Sam Wye came off the bench and scored for the home side in the 65th minute.

There was a delay in play when Harbour's Zinzan Hansen was stretchered off with a leg injury after playing just over 15 minutes.

Fullback Hunter Rice scored two late tries but it would be too little too late.

In further late drama, Taranaki also played out the final minutes of the game with 14 men as Kaylum Boshier was sinbinned.
